Comment by Associate Examiner Fan, Instructor: In discussing the distinction made in recording the meeting and the absence of laudatory wording, he expounds the meaning of the commentary in detail…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
明春秋文字正當如此
考試官教諭林　批〔分義嚴明人臣觀之自消希望之心〕
考試官學正毛　批〔詞條義盡宰孔范鞅等有知亦〕
自無辭
冢宰會霸春秋待之以常列卿勤王春秋待之
以正夫莫嚴於君臣之分莫重於君臣之義也
春秋於宰孔於列卿之會肯少假溢於其間哉
諸侯曷會乎葵丘也齊桓脩尋盟之好宰孔將
賜胙之命也是役也孔以冢宰上兼三公方之
===
大禹上兼師保周公下行端揆若不異矣曷春
秋不殊會之耶蓋先王制禮正分别嫌正以謹
嚴等殺也孔也論道啓沃統正百官責任固曰
重矣規以大義夫非盡人之臣歟是故以終始
則有進退之節以出入則有均勞之義位非世
及貴非常尊烏可與王世子等論哉春秋秩分
庸禮故不以殊會書之者以此若後世以位加
王世子之上者非春秋待宰孔之義矣諸侯大
夫曷會乎黃父也范獻子警早圖之策趙簡子
punctuated:
明，春秋文字正當如此。
考試官教諭林批〔分義嚴明，人臣觀之，自消希望之心。〕
考試官學正毛批〔詞條義盡，宰孔、范鞅等有知，亦〕自無辭。
冢宰會霸，《春秋》待之以常；列卿勤王，《春秋》待之以正。夫莫嚴於君臣之分，莫重於君臣之義也。《春秋》於宰孔、於列卿之會，肯少假溢於其間哉？
諸侯曷會乎葵丘也？齊桓脩尋盟之好，宰孔將賜胙之命也。是役也，孔以冢宰上兼三公，方之大禹上兼師保、周公下行端揆，若不異矣。曷《春秋》不殊會之耶？蓋先王制禮，正分别嫌，正以謹嚴等殺也。孔也論道啓沃，統正百官，責任固曰重矣。規以大義，夫非盡人之臣歟？是故以終始則有進退之節，以出入則有均勞之義。位非世及，貴非常尊，烏可與王世子等論哉？《春秋》秩分庸禮，故不以殊會書之者以此。若後世以位加王世子之上者，非《春秋》待宰孔之義矣。
諸侯大夫曷會乎黃父也？范獻子警早圖之策，趙簡子
translation_en:
…clear. Writing on the Spring and Autumn Annals should indeed be like this.
Examiner Lin, an Instructor, comments: 〔The distinctions of status and the obligations they entail are rigorously clarified. Ministers who read this will naturally relinquish thoughts of aspiring beyond their station.〕
Examiner Mao, a School Director, comments: 〔The language is orderly and the meaning fully developed. If Zai Kong, Fan Yang, and the others were aware of it, they too〕 would naturally have nothing to say in objection.
When the Grand Steward meets with the hegemon, the Spring and Autumn Annals treats him according to the ordinary rules; when the ranked ministers exert themselves in the king’s service, the Annals treats them according to what is proper. Nothing is more inviolable than the distinction between ruler and minister, and nothing weightier than the obligations between them. In recording the meetings attended by Zai Kong and by the ranked ministers, would the Annals allow them even the slightest unwarranted elevation?
Why did the feudal lords meet at Kuiqiu? Duke Huan of Qi was renewing the friendship of their covenant, and Zai Kong was conveying the command to bestow sacrificial meat. On this occasion, Kong, as Grand Steward, concurrently held the higher standing of one of the Three Dukes. Compared with the Great Yu concurrently assuming the higher roles of Grand Preceptor and Grand Guardian, or the Duke of Zhou undertaking the lower duties of chief minister, this would seem no different. Why, then, does the Annals not distinguish his participation in the meeting by recording it separately? The former kings established ritual to rectify distinctions of status and distinguish potentially confusing cases, precisely so as to maintain strict gradations of rank. Kong discussed the Way and enlightened the ruler, overseeing and rectifying the conduct of all officials: his responsibilities were certainly weighty. Yet, measured against the greater obligations, was he not wholly another man’s minister? Thus, regarding the beginning and end of service, there were prescribed rules for entering office and retiring; regarding service at court or away from it, there was the obligation to share the toil equally. His position was not hereditary, nor was his exalted standing permanently assured. How could he be discussed on equal terms with the king’s heir apparent? The Annals orders distinctions of status and applies ritual: this is why it does not record his participation as a separate meeting. Those in later ages who placed such an official above the king’s heir apparent did not follow the principle by which the Annals treated Zai Kong.
Why did the feudal lords’ grand masters meet at Huangfu? Fan Xianzi urged a strategy of planning early, and Zhao Jianzi…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
布勤王之令也是役也謀輸王粟且具戍人擬
之齊桓翼戴世子晉文尊奬王室若同功矣曷
春秋無美詞耶蓋先王公天下建侯封國因以
藩屛王室也令也宗周弗靖小國之懼大國之
憂伯國謀之夫豈異人之任歟是故輸之粟則
壤之賦也具之戍力役之征也分所當爲義所
當盡豈能逃於天地間哉春秋正誼明道故無
美詞者以此後世臣子受當爲之賞而不辭者
非春秋待黃父之旨矣是則待以常禮則人臣
===
知分之當守責以常分則人臣知分之當爲春
秋教後世之爲人臣者如此也抑春秋之待五
霸爲世道計也權也桓非受命之伯又不朝周
重臣賜胙止於登拜已耳晉爲盟主宗周有隕
不能奔問官守舉義昭職徐徐數年淺言圖會
律以先王之法齊晉將能免乎春秋尚美葵丘
之盟不貶黃父之會聖人豈得已哉
公會晉師于瓦〔定公八年〕
張雲路
punctuated:
布勤王之令也。是役也，謀輸王粟，且具戍人，擬之齊桓翼戴世子、晉文尊奬王室，若同功矣。曷春秋無美詞耶？蓋先王公天下，建侯封國，因以藩屛王室也。令也，宗周弗靖，小國之懼，大國之憂，伯國謀之，夫豈異人之任歟？是故輸之粟，則壤之賦也；具之戍，力役之征也。分所當爲，義所當盡，豈能逃於天地間哉？春秋正誼明道，故無美詞者以此。後世臣子受當爲之賞而不辭者，非春秋待黃父之旨矣。是則待以常禮，則人臣知分之當守；責以常分，則人臣知分之當爲。春秋教後世之爲人臣者如此也。抑春秋之待五霸，爲世道計也，權也。桓非受命之伯，又不朝周，重臣賜胙，止於登拜已耳。晉爲盟主，宗周有隕，不能奔問，官守舉義昭職，徐徐數年，淺言圖會。律以先王之法，齊晉將能免乎？春秋尚美葵丘之盟，不貶黃父之會，聖人豈得已哉？
公會晉師于瓦〔定公八年〕
張雲路
translation_en:
…issued the command to serve the king. In this undertaking, they planned to send grain to the king and also to supply men for garrison duty. Compared with Duke Huan of Qi’s support for the heir apparent and Duke Wen of Jin’s honoring and assisting the royal house, their achievement would seem equivalent. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals offer no words of praise? The former kings treated All-under-Heaven as a public trust, establishing lords and enfeoffing states to serve as protective barriers for the royal house. Now [?], when the Zhou royal realm was unsettled, this was a source of fear for small states and concern for great ones, and the hegemonic state was to devise a response. Could this responsibility belong to anyone else? Thus, the grain they sent was the levy upon their lands, and the garrison troops they supplied were their obligation of labor service. These were acts required by their station and duties demanded by righteousness. How could they evade them anywhere between Heaven and Earth? The Spring and Autumn Annals rectifies righteousness and illuminates the Way: this is why it offers no words of praise. Subjects in later ages who accept rewards for doing what they ought to do, without declining them, depart from the purport of its treatment of Huangfu. Thus, when subjects are treated according to the ordinary rites, they know the bounds of their station that they must observe; when held accountable for their ordinary obligations, they know the duties of their station that they must perform. Such is the instruction that the Spring and Autumn Annals gives to subjects of later ages.
Yet its treatment of the Five Hegemons takes account of the condition of the age: it is an expedient judgment. Duke Huan was not a hegemon appointed by royal command, nor did he attend court at Zhou. When a high minister bestowed sacrificial meat upon him, he merely ascended the steps and bowed. Jin was the leader of the covenant, yet when calamity befell the Zhou royal realm, it could not hasten there to inquire after it. Its officials upheld righteousness and made manifest their duties [?], yet several years passed in leisurely fashion, with only slight talk of planning a meeting [?]. Judged by the laws of the former kings, could Qi and Jin escape blame? That the Spring and Autumn Annals nevertheless praises the covenant at Kuiqiu and does not disparage the meeting at Huangfu—could the Sage have had any other choice?
The duke met the army of Jin at Wa. 〔Eighth year of Duke Ding〕
Zhang Yunlu.

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭范　批〔詳玩傳文前曰其書公會晉師後曰言晉師而不書士鞅作者類多今拗此作提點明白文亦足以發之有見有見〕
考試官教諭林　批〔義意謹嚴正是明經待用之學〕
考試官學正毛　批〔重衆謹權令人悚息〕
春秋於霸臣之將兵示重衆之義寓專兵之戒
甚矣民不可易權不可忽也春秋致謹於瓦之
會焉意其遠哉昔者晉以衛叛盟之隙以䁹齊
人士鞅間西鄙之兵以救魯患我定往逆瓦亭
===
有會茲行也寔以鞅也春秋書會晉師不書士
鞅何耶蓋觀容民畜衆之訓則知軍旅之事君
與大夫皆以師為重也宜矣鞅也入聞晉政出
馭三軍其視師徒藐乎微矣殊不知民惟邦本
勢切安危之機佳兵不祥事關悔吝之戒大夫
敢以貴重少之乎今也輕舉大衆妄與遠役督
丘民以犯兇器驅無罪以赴險危借曾仇齊動
搖邦本殆見旗旄所指利害伏焉其機其戒不
亦為可懼乎又觀履霜堅冰之戒則知世祿之
punctuated:
同考試官教諭范　批〔詳玩傳文，前曰其書公會晉師，後曰言晉師而不書士鞅，作者類多。今拗此作，提點明白，文亦足以發之。有見！有見！〕
考試官教諭林　批〔義意謹嚴，正是明經待用之學。〕
考試官學正毛　批〔重衆謹權，令人悚息。〕
春秋於霸臣之將兵，示重衆之義，寓專兵之戒。甚矣，民不可易，權不可忽也！春秋致謹於瓦之會焉，意其遠哉！昔者晉以衛叛盟之隙，以䁹齊人。士鞅間西鄙之兵，以救魯患，我定往逆，瓦亭有會。茲行也，寔以鞅也。春秋書會晉師，不書士鞅，何耶？蓋觀容民畜衆之訓，則知軍旅之事，君與大夫皆以師為重也宜矣。鞅也入聞晉政，出馭三軍，其視師徒，藐乎微矣。殊不知民惟邦本，勢切安危之機；佳兵不祥，事關悔吝之戒。大夫敢以貴重少之乎？今也輕舉大衆，妄與遠役，督丘民以犯兇器，驅無罪以赴險危，借曾仇齊，動搖邦本。殆見旗旄所指，利害伏焉。其機其戒，不亦為可懼乎？又觀履霜堅冰之戒，則知世祿之
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Fan, Instructor, comments: 〔Read the commentary closely: first it says that the text records “the duke met the army of Jin”; later it speaks of “the army of Jin” without recording Shi Yang. Many writers have treated this similarly. This composition now takes a different approach [?], pointing out the issue clearly, and its prose adequately develops it. Insightful! Insightful!〕
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: 〔The interpretation and argument are scrupulous and rigorous. This is precisely the learning of one who understands the Classics and awaits employment.〕
Examiner Mao, Director of Studies, comments: 〔Respect for the multitude and caution concerning power: this makes one shudder and sigh.〕
When a minister of a hegemonic state commands troops, the Spring and Autumn Annals demonstrates the duty to value the multitude and conveys a warning against monopolizing military command. How grave a matter it is: the people must not be treated lightly, and power must not be disregarded! The Spring and Autumn Annals treats the meeting at Wa with particular care. How far-reaching its purpose!
Formerly, Jin took advantage of Wei’s breach of the covenant to watch for an opening against Qi. Shi Yang, amid the fighting on the western frontier [?], came to relieve Lu’s troubles. Our Duke Ding went to meet him, and a meeting took place at Wating. This journey was indeed on account of Yang. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals record a meeting with the army of Jin without recording Shi Yang?
Consider the instruction to “shelter the people and nurture the multitude”: one then knows that, in military affairs, ruler and grand officers alike should give weight to the army. Yang participated in Jin’s government at court [?] and commanded its three armies in the field; he regarded the troops as insignificant. He utterly failed to understand that the people are the foundation of the state, their condition intimately bound up with the turning point between security and peril; fine weapons are inauspicious, and their use calls for heed to the warning against remorse and humiliation. Dare a grand officer, relying on his own exalted standing, slight them?
Now he lightly mobilizes the masses and recklessly commits them to distant service, pressing the common people forward against deadly weapons and driving the innocent into danger. Even supposing that he thereby opposed Qi [?], he shook the foundations of the state. Wherever his banners pointed, benefit and harm lay concealed. Were not that turning point and that warning truly to be feared? Consider also the warning, “Treading on frost, hard ice is coming”: one then knows that those who receive hereditary stipends …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
臣植根膠固其辨之於早也宜矣鞅也席有卿
位間晉中微其將兵出會來也久矣殊不知天
下大事積於至微夫人常情忽於未兆國家可
以尋常忽之乎今也授之節鉞專制車徒兵權
在手威福隨之細民習於耳目而不察大幾失
於勢重而難反殆見童牛不梏扞格及矣其積
其兆不亦爲可憂乎春秋至是義繫於師矣所
以書會晉師而不書士鞅也有是哉此義行則
人君慎於用衆而忽兵貪兵牛羊其民者可免
===
矣慎於馭臣而公車公徒散復於丘甸者可復
矣此春秋垂鑑之意也大抵三綱軍政之大智
者察之仁者行之魯昭久寄於晉境魯定受制
於世臣晉也既不能急於方伯之義又且沮於
貪利之臣今齊之病魯未甚魯之報齊尚力顧
因背盟之故假救魯之聲其止也以利其行也
以私其機也以臣其君莫之察也軍政之本何
在哉宜其失諸侯不能主盟也歟
禮記
punctuated:
臣植根膠固，其辨之於早也宜矣。鞅也席有卿位，間晉中微，其將兵出會來也久矣。殊不知天下大事積於至微，夫人常情忽於未兆，國家可以尋常忽之乎？今也授之節鉞，專制車徒，兵權在手，威福隨之。細民習於耳目而不察，大幾失於勢重而難反，殆見童牛不梏，扞格及矣。其積其兆，不亦爲可憂乎？春秋至是，義繫於師矣，所以書會晉師而不書士鞅也。有是哉！此義行，則人君慎於用衆，而忽兵貪兵、牛羊其民者可免矣；慎於馭臣，而公車公徒散復於丘甸者可復矣。此春秋垂鑑之意也。大抵三綱，軍政之大，智者察之，仁者行之。魯昭久寄於晉境，魯定受制於世臣。晉也既不能急於方伯之義，又且沮於貪利之臣。今齊之病魯未甚，魯之報齊尚力，顧因背盟之故，假救魯之聲。其止也以利，其行也以私，其機也以臣，其君莫之察也。軍政之本何在哉？宜其失諸侯，不能主盟也歟！

禮記
translation_en:
…ministers put down roots and become firmly entrenched; it is therefore fitting to discern the danger early. Yang occupies a ministerial position and takes advantage of Jin’s decline; he has long commanded troops on expeditions to join allied forces. Yet he fails to understand that great affairs under Heaven grow from the smallest beginnings. Ordinary people habitually overlook things before any sign appears, but can a state dismiss them with such commonplace indifference? Now he is granted the command tally and battle-axe, with sole authority over chariots and infantry. Military power rests in his hands, and the power to punish and reward follows it. The common people grow accustomed to what they see and hear and fail to discern the danger. The decisive moment is missed, and his power becomes too great to reverse. We may well see that, when the young bull is left unrestrained, the time soon comes when it resists all restraint. Are not this accumulation of power and these emerging signs cause for anxiety? At this point, the moral significance of the Spring and Autumn Annals rests upon the army. That is why it records a meeting with “the army of Jin” rather than with Shi Yang. Such indeed is its meaning! If this principle is observed, rulers will exercise care in mobilizing their people, and may avoid treating warfare lightly, coveting warfare, and treating their people like cattle and sheep. They will exercise care in controlling their ministers, and the ducal chariots and infantry dispersed among the territorial levies [?] may be recovered. This is the intention of the Spring and Autumn Annals in leaving a warning for posterity.

In general, the Three Bonds are fundamental to military administration: the wise discern them, and the humane put them into practice. Duke Zhao of Lu long sojourned within Jin’s borders, while Duke Ding of Lu was subject to hereditary ministers. Jin not only failed to attend urgently to its duties as leader of the regional lords, but was also obstructed by ministers greedy for profit. At this time, Qi had not yet gravely afflicted Lu, and Lu still had strength to retaliate against Qi. Yet Jin used the breach of the covenant as a pretext and claimed to be rescuing Lu. Its halts were dictated by profit, its advances by private interests, and its decisions by ministers; its ruler discerned none of this. Where were the foundations of military administration? Was it not fitting that Jin should lose the allegiance of the regional lords and prove unable to preside over their covenants?

Book of Rites

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
君子耆老不徒行庶人耆老不徒食
陽紹先
同考試官教授徐　批
〔就題遣語而化民成俗之意躍如盖讀禮而得其肯綮者〕
考試官教諭林　批
〔不窘不泛亙有發明〕
考試官學正毛　批
〔雅健〕
觀王政之優老而貴賤各得其所焉夫老者安
之聖人之政也貴賤各得其所而王道成矣記
王制者意謂先王之制養老爲先然其德教之
===
行蓋有化民成俗者焉彼六十曰耆七十曰老
者老以君子稱言有爵也服命既列於縉紳名
位不同於鄉族有常尊焉是故命駕於朝所以
貴德也而行無徒步之勞懸車於館所以賜謝
也而出無無輿之歎體貌尊於齊民冠蓋崇於
道路非侈也蓋其分之所當有而義之所當安
矣徒行者何有乎耆老以庶人稱言在下也負
戴既非其所勤指使惟隨其所願有常養焉是
故道其妻子可使貳膳也而晨昏遂甘旨之懽
punctuated:
君子耆老不徒行，庶人耆老不徒食。

陽紹先

同考試官教授徐　批〔就題遣語，而化民成俗之意躍如，盖讀禮而得其肯綮者。〕

考試官教諭林　批〔不窘不泛，亙有發明。〕

考試官學正毛　批〔雅健。〕

觀王政之優老，而貴賤各得其所焉。夫老者安之，聖人之政也。貴賤各得其所，而王道成矣。記王制者，意謂先王之制，養老爲先。然其德教之行，蓋有化民成俗者焉。彼六十曰耆、七十曰老者，老以君子稱，言有爵也。服命既列於縉紳，名位不同於鄉族，有常尊焉。是故命駕於朝，所以貴德也，而行無徒步之勞；懸車於館，所以賜謝也，而出無無輿之歎。體貌尊於齊民，冠蓋崇於道路，非侈也。蓋其分之所當有，而義之所當安矣。徒行者何有乎？耆老以庶人稱，言在下也。負戴既非其所勤，指使惟隨其所願，有常養焉。是故道其妻子，可使貳膳也，而晨昏遂甘旨之懽。
translation_en:
“Elderly gentlemen do not travel on foot; elderly commoners do not eat meals without meat.”

Yang Shaoxian

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Professor: 〔The wording addresses the topic directly, vividly conveying the intention to transform the people and establish good customs. Here is someone who has read the rites and grasped their essential points.〕

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: 〔Neither constrained nor diffuse; it offers illuminating insights throughout [?].〕

Comment by Examiner Mao, School Director: 〔Elegant and vigorous.〕

Observe how royal government treats the elderly generously, so that noble and humble alike receive their proper due. Giving the aged peace and comfort is the government of the sage. When noble and humble alike receive their proper due, the Kingly Way is realized. The author of “Royal Regulations” meant that, in the institutions of the former kings, caring for the elderly came first. Yet the implementation of their moral instruction also served to transform the people and establish good customs. Those aged sixty are called qi, and those aged seventy lao. When the elderly are termed “gentlemen,” this means that they possess rank. Through their robes and appointments they have entered the ranks of officials; their standing differs from that of their fellow villagers and clansmen, and they receive enduring honor. Thus, ordering carriages for them at court honors their virtue, and they travel without the toil of walking. When they hang up their carriages at their residences in retirement, provision is made for their withdrawal [?], and when they go out they have no cause to lament the lack of a conveyance. The ceremonial respect accorded them sets them above ordinary people; their caps and carriage canopies command honor along the roads. This is no extravagance. It is what their station properly entitles them to possess and what righteousness permits them to enjoy with an easy mind. How could there be any question of their traveling on foot?

When the elderly are termed “commoners,” this means that they occupy a lowly station. Carrying loads on their backs or heads is no longer their work; they need only give directions according to their wishes, and they receive regular support. Thus, by guiding their wives and children, one can ensure that they have additional dishes, so that morning and evening they enjoy the pleasure of savory food…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
敎之樹畜可使食肉也而口體備珍羞之奉頤
養適於引年飲食豐於庋閣非僭也蓋其身之
所當得而民之所當爲矣徒食者何有乎是則
不徒行老老之化行於貴不徒食老老之化行
於賤王道之成可想見矣傳曰上老老而民興
孝明王以孝治天下而民興焉虞之燕夏之饗
殷之食周人兼而脩之皆是也此其治隆俗美
而四代之盛所以不可及歟噫不法王道而能
言治者否也孟軻氏所以拳拳於齊梁也
===
然後聖人作爲父子君臣以爲紀綱紀綱
既正天下大定天下大定然後正六律
和五聲弦歌詩頌此之謂德音德音之
謂樂
司杷
同考試官敎授徐 批〔有聖人而後可以制禮禮制而後樂作 此篇體認親切足以發明子夏論樂之意〕
考試官敎諭林 批〔明暢無長語〕
考試官學正毛 批〔有斷制〕
punctuated:
敎之樹畜，可使食肉也，而口體備珍羞之奉。頤養適於引年，飲食豐於庋閣，非僭也，蓋其身之所當得，而民之所當爲矣。徒食者何有乎？是則不徒行，老老之化行於貴；不徒食，老老之化行於賤。王道之成，可想見矣。傳曰：「上老老而民興孝。」明王以孝治天下，而民興焉。虞之燕，夏之饗，殷之食，周人兼而脩之，皆是也。此其治隆俗美，而四代之盛所以不可及歟！噫！不法王道而能言治者，否也。孟軻氏所以拳拳於齊梁也。

然後聖人作爲父子君臣，以爲紀綱。紀綱既正，天下大定；天下大定，然後正六律，和五聲，弦歌詩頌。此之謂德音，德音之謂樂。

司杷

同考試官敎授徐，批〔有聖人而後可以制禮，禮制而後樂作。此篇體認親切，足以發明子夏論樂之意。〕

考試官敎諭林，批〔明暢，無長語。〕

考試官學正毛，批〔有斷制。〕
translation_en:
…Teach them to cultivate plants and raise livestock, and the elderly can be provided with meat, with delicacies to nourish their bodies and please their palates. Their care is suited to their advancing years, and their stores are plentiful with food and drink. This is no overstepping of their station: it is what they themselves ought to receive and what the people ought to provide. How could any be left eating only plain fare? Thus, when the elderly need not travel on foot, the transforming influence of honoring the aged extends to the noble; when they need not eat only plain fare, it extends to the lowly. One can envision the fulfillment of the Kingly Way. The commentary says: “When those above honor the aged, the people are stirred to filial devotion.” Enlightened kings govern all under Heaven through filial devotion, and the people are moved by it. The convivial feasts of Yu, the ceremonial banquets of Xia, the meals of Yin, and the Zhou people's combined observance of all these practices exemplify this. Is this not why their government flourished and their customs were fine, and why the splendor of those four dynasties cannot be matched? Alas! Those who fail to model themselves on the Kingly Way cannot speak competently of governing. This is why Meng Ke urged it so earnestly upon Qi and Liang.

“Then the sages established the relationships between father and son and between ruler and minister as the guiding principles of order. Once these principles were properly established, all under Heaven became fully settled. Only then did they set the six pitch standards correctly, harmonize the five notes, and sing the poems and hymns to stringed accompaniment. This is called the sound of virtue; the sound of virtue is called music.”

Si Pa 司杷 [?].

Associate Examiner Xu, Professor, comments: “Only after sages appear can ritual be instituted; only after ritual is instituted does music arise. This essay grasps the matter closely and aptly, and fully elucidates the meaning of Zixia's discussion of music.”

Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: “Clear and fluent, without superfluous words.”

Examiner Mao, School Instructor, comments: “It shows decisive judgment.”

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
記者卽聖樂之所由作著古樂之所由名夫萬
物得其理而後和樂之所由作也古樂之名其
以是夫子夏荅魏文侯問樂至此若謂音與樂
異而衆庶昧焉若古之聖人也豈茍焉哉乗夫
大當之時作爲斯民之極內則父子外則君臣
三綱六紀秩然而有條紀綱旣正則百姓以親
五品以遜天下四方翕然而順治天下旣定則
禮備而樂可興焉由是酌元聲以正律參伍乎
相生損益之宜比六律以和聲曲盡乎清濁高
===
下之變協之弦歌至德於是乎流通被之詩頌
太和以之而宣布所謂德音者非歟是故優柔
平中德之盛也極情文之備所以移風易俗者
是矣天下化中治之至也兼功德之隆所以平
心宣化者是矣不謂之樂而何是則序之以禮
和之以樂聖人作樂之始終而古樂見矣彼徒
音非樂君何聽焉雖然音樂非二也樂不離乎
音而音所以宣樂惟夫音易好樂難知不知則
厭而溺音代變正樂日荒此子夏所以有爲而
punctuated: 記者卽聖樂之所由作，著古樂之所由名。夫萬物得其理而後和，樂之所由作也。古樂之名，其以是夫！子夏荅魏文侯問樂，至此若謂：音與樂異，而衆庶昧焉。若古之聖人也，豈茍焉哉？乗夫大當之時，作爲斯民之極，內則父子，外則君臣，三綱六紀，秩然而有條。紀綱旣正，則百姓以親，五品以遜，天下四方，翕然而順治。天下旣定，則禮備而樂可興焉。由是酌元聲以正律，參伍乎相生損益之宜；比六律以和聲，曲盡乎清濁高下之變。協之弦歌，至德於是乎流通；被之詩頌，太和以之而宣布。所謂德音者非歟？是故優柔平中，德之盛也；極情文之備，所以移風易俗者是矣。天下化中，治之至也；兼功德之隆，所以平心宣化者是矣。不謂之樂而何？是則序之以禮，和之以樂，聖人作樂之始終，而古樂見矣。彼徒音非樂，君何聽焉？雖然，音樂非二也。樂不離乎音，而音所以宣樂。惟夫音易好，樂難知，不知則厭，而溺音代變，正樂日荒。此子夏所以有爲而
translation_en:
The recorder explains why ancient music bears its name by considering how the sages’ music came to be created. Only when the myriad things attain their proper principles do they become harmonious: this is the basis on which music is created. Surely ancient music owes its name to this! At this point in Zixia’s reply to Marquis Wen of Wei’s question about music, he seems to say: tones and music differ, yet ordinary people fail to understand this. Could the ancient sages have acted carelessly? Taking advantage of a time of great fitness [?], they established the ultimate standard for the people: within the family, the relationship of father and son; outside it, that of ruler and minister. The Three Bonds and Six Relationships were ordered and clearly articulated. Once these guiding relationships were set right, the people lived in affection, and the five human relationships were conducted with deference. All under Heaven, in every quarter, united in obedience and good order. Once the realm was settled, ritual was complete and music could arise.

Accordingly, they considered the fundamental tone to set the pitch standards correctly, comparing and verifying the appropriate ways of generating pitches from one another by diminution and augmentation. They aligned the six pitch standards to harmonize the sounds, fully encompassing the variations of clarity and depth, height and lowness. They coordinated these with strings and singing, through which consummate virtue flowed freely; they embodied them in poems and hymns, through which supreme harmony was diffused. Is this not what is called the sound of virtue? Thus, gentleness and ease, balance and centeredness, constitute the fullness of virtue. Bringing feeling and its patterned expression to their fullest realization is how music transforms prevailing practices and changes customs. When all under Heaven is transformed toward centeredness, government reaches its highest achievement. Combining the abundance of accomplishment and virtue is how music brings peace to people’s hearts and spreads moral transformation. What could this be called if not music?

Thus, ordering people through ritual and harmonizing them through music comprise the whole process by which the sages created music; therein ancient music becomes apparent. Those other sounds are merely tones, not music: why should you, my lord, listen to them? Nevertheless, tones and music are not two separate things. Music cannot exist apart from tones, and tones are the means by which music is expressed. It is simply that tones are easy to enjoy, while music is difficult to understand. Without understanding it, people grow weary of it; seductive tones change from age to age, while proper music falls daily into neglect. This is why Zixia, with a particular purpose in mind, …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
二之也苟知樂如知音則聞韶者忘味觀舞者
擬德而古樂復矣故曰今之樂猶古之樂
第貳場
論
聖人愼重之意
劉廷臣
同考試官教諭李　批〔圓融活潑警言策自見眞一倡三歎〕
〔而有遺音者矣健羨健羨〕
同考試官教諭毛　批〔淵然之光蒼然之色奪于珠璧當〕
===
〔爲子敛衽〕
考試官教諭林　批〔得言本旨〕
考試官學正毛　批〔朗誦動色輕忽自失〕
論曰明王欲有以動天下莫難乎其始也始之
弗難而終無以應是以聖人憂焉夫以天下之
大而欲以一人之身握其樞要運其機栝以奔
走天下而使之帖然竦服則非令無以動之也
何也勢之散者未可以易合事之異者未可以
易同人之睽者未可以易孚聖人者洞察其幾
punctuated:
二之也。苟知樂如知音，則聞韶者忘味，觀舞者擬德，而古樂復矣。故曰：「今之樂，猶古之樂。」

第貳場
論
聖人愼重之意
劉廷臣

同考試官教諭李批〔圓融活潑，警言策自見眞，一倡三歎〕〔而有遺音者矣。健羨，健羨！〕
同考試官教諭毛批〔淵然之光，蒼然之色，奪于珠璧，當〕〔爲子敛衽。〕
考試官教諭林批〔得言本旨。〕
考試官學正毛批〔朗誦動色，輕忽自失。〕

論曰：明王欲有以動天下，莫難乎其始也。始之弗難，而終無以應，是以聖人憂焉。夫以天下之大，而欲以一人之身握其樞要，運其機栝，以奔走天下，而使之帖然竦服，則非令無以動之也。何也？勢之散者，未可以易合；事之異者，未可以易同；人之睽者，未可以易孚。聖人者，洞察其幾
translation_en:
…thus distinguishing the two. If one understood music as one understands sounds, then those who heard the Shao music would forget the taste of food, and those who watched its dances would emulate its virtue; ancient music would thereby be restored. Thus it is said: “The music of today is like the music of antiquity.”

Second Session
Discourse
The Sage’s Intention in Exercising Caution
Liu Tingchen

Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “Well rounded and lively; its striking words and admonitions reveal the truth of themselves [?]. One voice leads and three respond, leaving lingering echoes. How admirable, how admirable!”

Associate Examiner Mao, Instructor, comments: “Its profound radiance and venerable hue outshine pearls and jade discs. I ought to gather my robes in reverence before you.”

Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: “It captures the original purport of the saying.”

Examiner Mao, School Instructor, comments: “Reading it aloud, my expression changes; my own carelessness leaves me discomfited.”

The discourse reads: When an enlightened king wishes to move all under Heaven to action, nothing is more difficult than the beginning. If he treats the beginning as easy but in the end has no means of responding, this is what causes the sage concern. Given the vastness of all under Heaven, if a single person wishes to grasp its essential pivots and operate its mechanisms, setting all under Heaven in motion and bringing it to tranquil and reverent submission, he has no means of moving it except through commands. Why is this? Dispersed forces cannot readily be brought together; divergent affairs cannot readily be made uniform; estranged people cannot readily be brought to trust. The sage perceives their incipient workings with penetrating insight…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
而深曉其故于是乎有命令之說焉葢王者命
令則若進天下之人而與之對談于當宁之上
而吾之精神藴奥亦若有以親授於四海之遠
九圍之內者在上無隱情而在下無伏機故王
言布而萬國傾心絲綸敷而神道默運其散者
異者睽者固已連絡而統屬之矣又何俟乎躬
役萬機之勞哉是令者人君所以動天下之微
權也然令出之非難而謹始之惟難而聖人者
則又欲其慎之而不敢忽重之而不敢輕此其
===
故何哉誠以始發之也乃所以率天下之人以
就吾法而俾之我從以歸于極使其擬議未足
以合道而弛張未足以中情則人心必不樂于
我而事勢或有乖其常起而强爲之將有以鼓
天下大難之端而莫吾應矣不得已而亟爲之
易則又恐不足以取信于衆而紛更之譏卒不
免于天下之口此聖人所以拳拳于其始而明
王亦自知所警惕矣元城劉氏之論書曰慎乃
出令令出惟行弗惟反易曰渙汗其大號傳曰
punctuated: 而深曉其故，于是乎有命令之說焉。葢王者命令，則若進天下之人而與之對談于當宁之上，而吾之精神藴奥，亦若有以親授於四海之遠、九圍之內者。在上無隱情，而在下無伏機，故王言布而萬國傾心，絲綸敷而神道默運，其散者、異者、睽者，固已連絡而統屬之矣，又何俟乎躬役萬機之勞哉？是令者，人君所以動天下之微權也。然令出之非難，而謹始之惟難。而聖人者，則又欲其慎之而不敢忽，重之而不敢輕，此其故何哉？誠以始發之也，乃所以率天下之人以就吾法，而俾之我從，以歸于極。使其擬議未足以合道，而弛張未足以中情，則人心必不樂于我，而事勢或有乖其常。起而强爲之，將有以鼓天下大難之端，而莫吾應矣。不得已而亟爲之易，則又恐不足以取信于衆，而紛更之譏，卒不免于天下之口。此聖人所以拳拳于其始，而明王亦自知所警惕矣。元城劉氏之論：「《書》曰：『慎乃出令，令出惟行，弗惟反。』《易》曰：『渙汗其大號。』《傳》曰：
translation_en:
…and thoroughly understands their causes; hence the teaching concerning commands and ordinances. When a king issues commands, it is as though he summoned the people of the realm and conversed with them face to face at his place before the palace hall. The deepest workings of his spirit likewise seem to be personally imparted to all within the nine regions, even to the farthest reaches of the Four Seas. Those above conceal no intentions, and those below harbor no hidden designs. Thus, when the king’s words are promulgated, the myriad states turn their hearts toward him; when his silken pronouncements are disseminated, his spiritual influence operates silently. Those who were scattered, different, or estranged have already been joined together and brought under unified authority. What need is there, then, for him personally to undertake the toil of the myriad affairs of government? Commands are thus the subtle means by which a ruler moves the realm.

Yet issuing commands is not difficult; taking care at the outset is what is difficult. The sage therefore wishes the ruler to approach them cautiously, never negligently, and to treat them gravely, never lightly. Why is this? It is because their initial promulgation serves to lead the people of the realm to conform to his laws, to follow him, and to return to the supreme standard. If his deliberations do not adequately accord with the Way, and his measures of relaxation and restriction do not properly fit the circumstances, the people’s hearts will surely be displeased with him, and affairs may depart from their normal course. Should he then proceed to impose his will by force, he will set in motion the beginnings of great calamity throughout the realm, with no one responding to him. If, having no alternative, he hastily changes his commands, he must again fear that he will fail to secure the people’s trust, and in the end he will not escape their criticism for incessant alteration. This is why the sage is so deeply concerned about the outset, and why the enlightened king himself knows where he must exercise vigilance.

In the discussion by Master Liu of Yuancheng: “The Book of Documents says, ‘Be cautious in issuing your commands. Once issued, commands are to be carried out, not reversed.’ The Book of Changes says, ‘He disperses his great proclamations as sweat is dispersed.’ The Commentary says: …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
令重則君尊又曰國之安危在出令凡此皆聖
人愼重之意也嗚呼其知命令之道乎夫人君
者深居九重之中而欲化行萬里之外禮以正
分樂以導和刑以懲姦政以廣惠固必愼號令
以昭畫一重政令以垂法守新天下之耳目而
使之不能鼓天下之心志而使之不敢懈而
天下之人亦自知所持循以蹈吾法而不亂然
後可以厚望於天下之治是以古之善觀人國
者不視其勢之盛衰而先察其令之弛張未論
===
其政之醇疵而先審其令之繁簡柰何後之言
治者功利之念與而圖治之過銳務勝之心熾
而好名之日急故當其事幾之初動也慮之未
暇熟而處之未暇安則皇皇然以速令于天下
曰如此而爲禮如此而爲樂如此而爲刑與政
冀驅天下一日以入于太平之域及其令甫達
而變易頻數遠者一二歲近者期月之間甚者
朝行而夕改吏莫知所守民莫知所從是盖人
情有所未盡事理有所未通或牽于好惡之私
punctuated:
「令重則君尊。」又曰：「國之安危在出令。」凡此皆聖人愼重之意也。嗚呼，其知命令之道乎！夫人君者，深居九重之中，而欲化行萬里之外，禮以正分，樂以導和，刑以懲姦，政以廣惠，固必愼號令以昭畫一，重政令以垂法守，新天下之耳目而使之不能，鼓天下之心志而使之不敢懈，而天下之人亦自知所持循，以蹈吾法而不亂，然後可以厚望於天下之治。是以古之善觀人國者，不視其勢之盛衰，而先察其令之弛張；未論其政之醇疵，而先審其令之繁簡。
柰何後之言治者，功利之念與而圖治之過銳，務勝之心熾而好名之日急。故當其事幾之初動也，慮之未暇熟，而處之未暇安，則皇皇然以速令于天下，曰：「如此而爲禮，如此而爲樂，如此而爲刑與政。」冀驅天下一日以入于太平之域。及其令甫達，而變易頻數，遠者一二歲，近者期月之間，甚者朝行而夕改。吏莫知所守，民莫知所從。是盖人情有所未盡，事理有所未通，或牽于好惡之私，
translation_en:
…“When commands carry weight, the ruler is honored.” It also says: “The security or peril of the state depends on the issuing of commands.” All these statements express the sages’ concern for caution and gravity. Ah, how well they understood the proper way of issuing commands! A ruler dwells deep within the palace’s ninefold enclosure, yet wishes his transforming influence to reach ten thousand li away. Ritual rectifies distinctions, music fosters harmony, punishments restrain wrongdoing, and government extends benefits. He must therefore exercise caution in issuing commands to make uniform standards clear, and attach weight to administrative orders to establish rules that can be upheld. He must renew what all under Heaven see and hear, making them unable to … [?], and stir their hearts and purposes so that they dare not slacken. The people throughout the realm will then themselves know what to uphold and follow, observing our laws without disorder. Only then can one entertain high hopes for good order throughout the realm. Thus, those in antiquity skilled at judging another’s state did not look first at whether its power was flourishing or declining, but first examined whether its commands were lax or strict. Before discussing the merits and defects of its administration, they first considered whether its commands were numerous or few.
Why, then, did later advocates of good government become excessively eager in pursuing it as thoughts of achievement and profit arose [?], while their burning desire to surpass others made them ever more impatient for renown? When the first signs of an affair appeared, before they had time to consider it thoroughly or settle on an appropriate response, they hurried anxiously to issue commands throughout the realm, saying: “Ritual is to be conducted thus; music is to be performed thus; punishments and government are to be administered thus.” They hoped to drive the whole realm into a condition of great peace in a single day. Yet scarcely had their commands arrived before they were repeatedly changed: after one or two years at the longest, within a month at the shortest, and in extreme cases implemented in the morning and altered that evening. Officials did not know what to uphold, and the people did not know what to follow. This was presumably because human feelings had not been fully considered and the principles governing affairs had not been fully understood, or because they were swayed by their private likes and dislikes …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
惑溺于迎合之說故一人言之而遽爲之紛更
也是果可以語治平乎哉或者曰法度之廢置
吾不必其已見之爲是政事之因革吾不必其
已成之難更惟求其義理之所在而徐爲之圖
果可易歟則更其所可更而不嫌于違俗果可
守歟則守其所可守而無憚于襲故此亦無不
可者而又何以紛更爲議耶吁非後之更者之
過也始之不愼者爲之非後之易者之非也始
之不重者爲之蓋令而至於更易以求治則亦
===
不得已之計耳而可乎哉君人者苟能澄神于
未事之先而周諮于圖事之始慮之既臧謀之
既定發之不妄而持以必行則天下之人聞吾
之令如聞雷霆之聲傾耳聳聽而不敢有侮易
之心信吾之令如信神明之鑒悉心厭服而不
敢有違戾之志禮之令于天下也因情以定制
順則以立軌而民莫不整然以守曰此明王之
所以達吾分也固不必戶揭以禮而父子君臣
之秩其常上下內外之理其敘僭踰消焉綱維
punctuated:
惑溺于迎合之說，故一人言之而遽爲之紛更也。是果可以語治平乎哉？或者曰：「法度之廢置，吾不必其已見之爲是；政事之因革，吾不必其已成之難更。惟求其義理之所在，而徐爲之圖。果可易歟，則更其所可更，而不嫌于違俗；果可守歟，則守其所可守，而無憚于襲故。此亦無不可者，而又何以紛更爲議耶？」吁！非後之更者之過也，始之不愼者爲之；非後之易者之非也，始之不重者爲之。蓋令而至於更易以求治，則亦不得已之計耳，而可乎哉？
君人者苟能澄神于未事之先，而周諮于圖事之始，慮之既臧，謀之既定，發之不妄，而持以必行，則天下之人聞吾之令，如聞雷霆之聲，傾耳聳聽，而不敢有侮易之心；信吾之令，如信神明之鑒，悉心厭服，而不敢有違戾之志。禮之令于天下也，因情以定制，順則以立軌，而民莫不整然以守，曰：「此明王之所以達吾分也。」固不必戶揭以禮，而父子君臣之秩其常，上下內外之理其敘，僭踰消焉，綱維
translation_en:
…beguiled and ensnared by words calculated to please, so that at a single person’s suggestion he hastily makes a welter of changes. Can this really be called bringing about good government and peace? Someone might say: “In abolishing or establishing institutions, I need not insist that what has already appeared is right; in retaining or reforming governmental practices, I need not insist that what is already established is difficult to change. I seek only where moral principle lies and deliberate upon it at leisure. If something truly can be changed, I change what can be changed, without misgivings about departing from customary practice. If something truly can be maintained, I maintain what can be maintained, without shrinking from following precedent. There is nothing impermissible in any of this. Why, then, criticize frequent changes?” Ah! The fault lies not with those who make changes afterward: it is caused by those who were incautious at the outset. The error lies not with those who alter things afterward: it is caused by those who failed to give them due weight at the outset. Once commands must be changed in the pursuit of good government, this is merely a measure adopted because no alternative remains. How can it be acceptable?
If the ruler of men can clear his mind before undertaking affairs and consult widely when first planning them, then, once his deliberations are sound and his plans settled, he will issue no commands rashly and will hold firmly to their execution. The people throughout the realm will hear my commands as they hear the sound of thunder, straining their ears in rapt attention and daring harbor no thought of contempt or disregard. They will trust my commands as they trust the scrutiny of the spirits, submitting wholeheartedly and daring harbor no intention of defiance. When commands concerning ritual are issued throughout the realm, institutions are determined in accordance with human feelings and standards established in conformity with proper norms. The people all observe them in orderly fashion, saying: “This is how the enlightened king makes our respective duties clear.” There is certainly no need to post ritual instructions at every household: the ranks of father and son, ruler and minister attain their constancy, and the proper relationships of superior and inferior, inner and outer attain their order. Usurpation and overstepping disappear, and the bonds of order…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
張焉樂之令于天下也本和以正律協律以諧
聲而民莫不欣然以承曰此明王之所以穆吾
風也固不必家喻以樂而弦歌詩頌之得其章
政俗風化之萃其美躁心釋焉慾心平焉刑政
之令于天下也欽恤而不濫漸被而不狹而民
莫不歡乎以順從曰此明王之所以弼吾違而
惠吾疇也固不待網織之法煩細之條而閭閻
小民已洽好生之德海隅蒼生各遂咸若之願
㷀宄屛焉大化行焉此豈有他哉令審於始事
===
而機達於莫遏故其鼓舞之餘將有不怒而威
不動而變而轉移變化之妙莫知其所以然者
天下之人亦將惟吾之禮樂是圉焉耳刑政是
服焉耳而亦不能以自已是王者一令之頒有
以關天下之安危一命之布有以係生民之休
戚而可不思所以愼重之乎此自古帝王之所
以兢兢業業而不敢以忽於其令審之而不輕
發守之而不輕變以示不惑於觀聽而求成于
治功也雖然爲天下主者天也繼天者君也君
punctuated:
張焉。樂之令于天下也，本和以正律，協律以諧聲，而民莫不欣然以承，曰：「此明王之所以穆吾風也。」固不必家喻以樂，而弦歌詩頌之得其章，政俗風化之萃其美，躁心釋焉，慾心平焉。刑政之令于天下也，欽恤而不濫，漸被而不狹，而民莫不歡乎以順從，曰：「此明王之所以弼吾違而惠吾疇也。」固不待網織之法、煩細之條，而閭閻小民已洽好生之德，海隅蒼生各遂咸若之願，㷀宄屛焉，大化行焉。此豈有他哉？令審於始事，而機達於莫遏，故其鼓舞之餘，將有不怒而威、不動而變，而轉移變化之妙，莫知其所以然者。天下之人亦將惟吾之禮樂是圉焉耳，刑政是服焉耳，而亦不能以自已。是王者一令之頒，有以關天下之安危；一命之布，有以係生民之休戚，而可不思所以愼重之乎？此自古帝王之所以兢兢業業，而不敢以忽於其令，審之而不輕發，守之而不輕變，以示不惑於觀聽，而求成于治功也。
雖然，爲天下主者，天也；繼天者，君也。君
translation_en:
…are set firmly in place. When commands concerning music are issued throughout the realm, harmony is taken as the basis for rectifying the pitch standards, and the pitch standards are coordinated to harmonize the sounds. The people all receive them gladly, saying: “This is how the enlightened king brings harmony to our customs.” There is certainly no need to explain music to every household: songs accompanied by strings, poems, and hymns attain their proper form; government, customs, and moral instruction display their collective beauty. Restless hearts are calmed, and desires are stilled. When commands concerning punishments and government are issued throughout the realm, they show reverent care and compassion without excess, and their influence spreads without narrow restriction. The people all gladly obey, saying: “This is how the enlightened king corrects our transgressions and bestows kindness on our kind.” There is certainly no need to wait for laws woven into a net or burdensomely detailed regulations: the common people in the lanes and villages are already steeped in the virtue that cherishes life, and the people even in the remotest coastal regions each fulfill their wish that all should fare well. Wrongdoers [?] are banished, and the great transforming influence takes effect. Could there be any other reason for this? Commands are carefully considered at the outset of an undertaking, and their motive force operates without obstruction. Thus, as their inspiring influence continues, there will be authority without anger and transformation without movement; no one will know how such wondrous changes and transformations come about. The people throughout the realm, too, will find themselves bounded solely by our rites and music [?], and submit solely to our punishments and government, unable to do otherwise. Thus, the promulgation of a single command by a king bears upon the security or peril of the realm, and the issuance of a single order bears upon the well-being or suffering of the people. Can one fail to consider how to exercise caution in this? This is why, since antiquity, emperors and kings have been vigilant and conscientious, never daring to treat their commands lightly. They scrutinize them and do not issue them rashly; they uphold them and do not change them lightly. In this way they give clear guidance to all who see and hear, and seek success in the work of government.
Nevertheless, the master of all under Heaven is Heaven itself; the one who succeeds Heaven is the ruler. The ruler …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
代天出命者也臣代君行命者也君出命固不
可違天之道臣行命亦不可侵君之事人君繼
天以出治苟非純心以建極燭理以制欲則出
命之際是非或可以下或可以投
其隙威命不免於下移而政權將流於多門矣
不亦可懼哉故曰大哉王言一哉王心令也者
其天下之機乎心也者其人君之本乎先儒謂
人君之心惟在所養可爲有國者鑒矣
同前
===
萬化
同考試官教諭杜　批〔詞暢而豊意妥而盡他日從容論議十　廟堂之上舍子其誰〕
考試官教諭林　批〔明白正大得立言意〕
考試官學正毛　批〔有源委有發揮有斷制用並錄出〕
聖人一天下之令而神天下之化者要於其心
焉得之心也者令之所從出也聖人不能與天
下相忘於無言而其所恃以爲鼓舞之術者本
諸其心而布之於天下君臣上下相與由之而
punctuated:
代天出命者也，臣代君行命者也。君出命，固不可違天之道；臣行命，亦不可侵君之事。人君繼天以出治，苟非純心以建極，燭理以制欲，則出命之際，是非或可以下，或可以投其隙，威命不免於下移，而政權將流於多門矣。不亦可懼哉？故曰：「大哉王言，一哉王心！」令也者，其天下之機乎！心也者，其人君之本乎！先儒謂人君之心惟在所養，可爲有國者鑒矣。

同前。
萬化
同考試官教諭杜　批〔詞暢而豊，意妥而盡。他日從容論議十　廟堂之上，舍子其誰？〕
考試官教諭林　批〔明白正大，得立言意。〕
考試官學正毛　批〔有源委，有發揮，有斷制，用並錄出。〕

聖人一天下之令而神天下之化者，要於其心焉得之。心也者，令之所從出也。聖人不能與天下相忘於無言，而其所恃以爲鼓舞之術者，本諸其心而布之於天下，君臣上下相與由之而
translation_en:
…issues commands on Heaven’s behalf; the minister carries out commands on the ruler’s behalf. In issuing commands, the ruler must certainly not violate Heaven’s Way; in carrying them out, the minister likewise must not encroach upon the ruler’s responsibilities. The ruler succeeds Heaven in bringing forth good government. Unless he purifies his heart to establish the supreme standard and illuminates principle to restrain desire, then, when commands are issued, judgments of right and wrong may come from below [?], and some may exploit the opening. Authority over commands will inevitably shift downward, and governmental power will pass into many hands. Is this not frightening? Thus it is said: “How great are the king’s words! How undivided is the king’s heart!” Commands—are they not the pivot of all under Heaven? The heart—is it not the foundation of the ruler? Earlier Confucian scholars said that everything depends upon how the ruler’s heart is nurtured. This may serve as a mirror for those who possess a state.

Same topic as the preceding answer.
Wan Hua 萬化
Associate Examiner Du 杜, Instructor, comments: “The language is fluent and abundant; the ideas are well judged and fully expressed. In days to come, who but you will deliberate with composure at the imperial court [?]?”
Examiner Lin 林, Instructor, comments: “Clear, upright, and correct; it grasps the purpose of setting forth an argument.”
Examiner Mao 毛, School Director, comments: “It traces origins and ramifications, develops its ideas, and offers decisive judgments. Accordingly, it is included here along with the others.”

That the sage unifies the commands of all under Heaven and works a wondrous transformation throughout the realm depends essentially on what he achieves within his heart. The heart is the source from which commands issue. The sage cannot remain with all under Heaven in mutual unawareness, without words. Rather, the means upon which he relies to inspire and stir the people are rooted in his heart and promulgated throughout the realm. Ruler and ministers, those above and those below, follow them together and…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
不變焉是故天下之化可成而聖人之心始慰
否則徒爲文具而無眞誠專慤之意貫徹於其
間上無道揆下無法守而其爲令也不足以動
天下而適所以病天下將有不勝其弊者矣故
曰聖人愼重之意元城劉氏誠有見於時之好
繁其令而欲其求端於心也且上古結繩而治
無所謂命令者聖人無庸心也綱維世道樹風
聲而陳藝極凡以爲天下生民慮者二三聖人
豈無所用其心哉天下相忘於道化之中而不
===
知其誰之所使雖謂之忘言可也自是而誓誥
諄諄惟恐人之不吾聽且信者於是乎始有疑
而叛者矣是非民之疑且叛也淳龎之俗降而
道德之意微聖人於此始有不容已於言者矣
聖人不容於言而其所以令之而使行風之而
使動蓋有不可以苟焉者是故不求之於下而
求之於上不求之於言而求之於心故其所爲
說者曰君子以申命行事言乎其善入也曰令
出惟行弗惟反言乎其必行也曰王言如綸其
punctuated: 不變焉。是故天下之化可成，而聖人之心始慰。否則徒爲文具，而無眞誠專慤之意貫徹於其間，上無道揆，下無法守，而其爲令也不足以動天下，而適所以病天下，將有不勝其弊者矣。故曰：「聖人愼重之意。」元城劉氏誠有見於時之好繁其令，而欲其求端於心也。且上古結繩而治，無所謂命令者，聖人無庸心也？綱維世道，樹風聲而陳藝極，凡以爲天下生民慮者，二三聖人豈無所用其心哉？天下相忘於道化之中，而不知其誰之所使，雖謂之忘言可也。自是而誓誥諄諄，惟恐人之不吾聽且信者，於是乎始有疑而叛者矣。是非民之疑且叛也，淳龎之俗降而道德之意微，聖人於此始有不容已於言者矣。聖人不容於言，而其所以令之而使行、風之而使動，蓋有不可以苟焉者。是故不求之於下，而求之於上；不求之於言，而求之於心。故其所爲說者曰：「君子以申命行事。」言乎其善入也。曰：「令出惟行，弗惟反。」言乎其必行也。曰：「王言如綸，其
translation_en: …without changing. Thus the transformation of all under Heaven can be accomplished, and only then is the sage’s heart satisfied. Otherwise, commands become mere paperwork, with no truly sincere and single-minded earnestness running through them. Those above lack the Way as their measure; those below lack laws to uphold. Their commands cannot move all under Heaven but serve instead to afflict them, producing abuses too great to bear. Hence the phrase, “the sage’s intention to proceed with care.” Master Liu of Yuancheng truly perceived his age’s fondness for multiplying commands and wished people to seek their source in the heart. Moreover, in highest antiquity, government was conducted by knotted cords, and there were no so-called commands. Did this mean that the sages had no need to apply their minds? In maintaining order in the world, establishing an exemplary influence, and setting forth standards, those few sages devoted their care to the living people of all under Heaven. How could they have had no occasion to apply their minds? All under Heaven lived unselfconsciously amid the transforming influence of the Way, unaware of who had brought this about. One might indeed call this forgetting words. Thereafter, oaths and proclamations became earnest and insistent, as rulers feared only that people would neither heed nor trust them; it was then that doubt and rebellion first arose. This was not simply a matter of the people being distrustful and rebellious: customs of generous simplicity had declined, and the spirit of the Way and virtue had grown faint. Only then did the sages find themselves unable to refrain from speaking. When the sages could not refrain from words [?], the means by which they commanded people and secured action, influenced them and moved them, were certainly matters in which they could not proceed carelessly. Therefore they sought the source above rather than below, in the heart rather than in words. Thus the explanations say: “The noble man reiterates commands and carries out affairs.” This speaks of their capacity to penetrate effectively. They say: “Once a command is issued, it must be carried out, not reversed.” This speaks of its necessarily being put into effect. They say: “The king’s words are like a silken cord; their …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
出如綍言乎其末流之甚也此慎重之意也至
於所謂訏謨定命遠猷辰告者尤可以見聖人
之心焉何也謨之訏也則不便於其身而有天
下國家之慮矣命之定也則不疑於其心而有
僉謀從衆之長矣猷之遠也則不爲目前而有
百千萬年之計矣告之辰也則不爲急遽而無
慢令致期之賊矣夫是四者令之所以爲善內
而庭除之近外而蠻方之遠細而寢興洒掃之
常大而車馬戎兵之變慮無不周備無不飭夫
===
焉有僨事者乎傳曰令重則君尊又曰國之安
危在出令嗚呼其亦可懼也哉是故不敢以忽
心乘之懼其慮之弗熟也不敢以私心參之懼
其謀之弗臧也不敢以欺心二之懼其發之或
妄也不敢以怠心留之懼其行之弗篤也夫心
弗怠而能勇於義矣弗欺而能信於民矣弗私
而能公於人矣弗忽而能謹於度矣審令之道
何以加此故曰君子出其言善則千里之外應
之況其邇者乎由是禮樂明備而天地官刑政
punctuated: 出如綍，言乎其末流之甚也。此慎重之意也。至於所謂「訏謨定命，遠猷辰告」者，尤可以見聖人之心焉。何也？謨之訏也，則不便於其身，而有天下國家之慮矣；命之定也，則不疑於其心，而有僉謀從衆之長矣；猷之遠也，則不爲目前，而有百千萬年之計矣；告之辰也，則不爲急遽，而無慢令致期之賊矣。夫是四者，令之所以爲善。內而庭除之近，外而蠻方之遠，細而寢興洒掃之常，大而車馬戎兵之變，慮無不周，備無不飭，夫焉有僨事者乎？傳曰：「令重則君尊。」又曰：「國之安危在出令。」嗚呼，其亦可懼也哉！是故不敢以忽心乘之，懼其慮之弗熟也；不敢以私心參之，懼其謀之弗臧也；不敢以欺心二之，懼其發之或妄也；不敢以怠心留之，懼其行之弗篤也。夫心弗怠，而能勇於義矣；弗欺，而能信於民矣；弗私，而能公於人矣；弗忽，而能謹於度矣。審令之道，何以加此？故曰：「君子出其言善，則千里之外應之，況其邇者乎？」由是禮樂明備而天地官，刑政
translation_en:
…when issued, become like a thick rope.” This speaks of how greatly their effects grow as they spread. Such is the intent of exercising caution and care. As for the saying, “Make broad plans and settle commands; devise far-reaching policies and announce them at the proper time,” here especially we can discern the sages’ intentions. Why is this? When plans are broad, one considers the realm and the state rather than one’s own convenience. When commands are settled, one has no doubts in one’s heart and gains the benefit of consulting all and following the collective judgment. When policies reach far, one plans for hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of years rather than merely for the present moment. When announcements are timely, one avoids haste and the cruelty of being slow to issue orders yet demanding compliance by a fixed deadline. These four things are what make commands good. Whether concerning matters within, as near as the courtyard steps, or beyond, as distant as the lands of the non-Chinese peoples; whether small, like the daily routines of sleeping, rising, sprinkling water, and sweeping, or great, like the extraordinary affairs of chariots, horses, and warfare: nothing is omitted from consideration, and no preparation is left unregulated. How, then, could affairs come to ruin?

A transmitted text says, “When commands carry weight, the ruler is honored.” It also says, “The security or peril of a state depends on the issuing of commands.” Alas, is this not cause for fear! Thus one dares not let carelessness take hold, fearing that deliberation may be insufficiently mature; one dares not let selfishness intrude, fearing that plans may be unsound; one dares not introduce duplicity through deceit, fearing that what one issues may be false; and one dares not allow indolence to cause delay, fearing that implementation may lack earnestness. When the heart is free from indolence, one can act courageously for righteousness; free from deceit, one can gain the people’s trust; free from selfishness, one can treat others impartially; free from carelessness, one can scrupulously observe proper standards. How could the way of carefully considering commands surpass this? Thus it is said, “When the gentleman issues good words, people respond from a thousand li away; how much more those nearby!” Through this, rites and music are made manifest and complete, Heaven and Earth assume their proper functions, and punishments and government…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
脩齊而人心服道德合一而風俗同唐虞純懿
之美三代有道之長皆是物也而豈他有一說
以爲粉飾籠絡之具哉後世之爲令者吾惑焉
本於中者無真誠專慤之心而發於外者多二
三苟且之說令則益繁而化則益窒紛更之患
起數易之弊生遠不過一二歲近或期月甚者
朝行而夕改亦有前詔未頒後令錮除者吏斯
眩而民斯疑焉蓋由其不知所慎重之道是非
取舍無所折衷君臣上下相與優游而卒無補
===
於理譬之泛江河亡維楫而一任其風波之所
之其能免於覆溺之患者能幾何哉雖然忘言
之化不可見矣唐虞三代不可及矣知聖人慎
重之意而致之天下焉亦可以爲令矣宋之中
葉仁宗之休養不足以供神宗之作用哲宗嗣
位之初正涵養休息之時也其善者不可變其
不善者亦當以漸而復事體安妥人心帖服而
不覺其爲變更斯善之善者斯固元城劉氏之
意也非固膠於一定而不知通也要於其當而
punctuated:
脩齊而人心服，道德合一而風俗同。唐虞純懿之美，三代有道之長，皆是物也，而豈他有一說以爲粉飾籠絡之具哉？後世之爲令者，吾惑焉。本於中者無真誠專慤之心，而發於外者多二三苟且之說。令則益繁，而化則益窒；紛更之患起，數易之弊生。遠不過一二歲，近或期月，甚者朝行而夕改，亦有前詔未頒、後令錮除者。吏斯眩而民斯疑焉。蓋由其不知所慎重之道，是非取舍無所折衷，君臣上下相與優游，而卒無補於理。譬之泛江河，亡維楫，而一任其風波之所之，其能免於覆溺之患者能幾何哉？
雖然，忘言之化不可見矣，唐虞三代不可及矣。知聖人慎重之意而致之天下焉，亦可以爲令矣。宋之中葉，仁宗之休養不足以供神宗之作用。哲宗嗣位之初，正涵養休息之時也。其善者不可變，其不善者亦當以漸而復。事體安妥，人心帖服，而不覺其爲變更，斯善之善者。斯固元城劉氏之意也，非固膠於一定而不知通也，要於其當而
translation_en:
…are cultivated and brought into order, and the people's hearts submit; the Way and virtue are united, and customs become uniform. The pure and excellent beauty of the ages of Tang and Yu, and the enduring rule of the Three Dynasties when they possessed the Way, all consist in this. Could there be some other doctrine serving merely as an instrument of embellishment and manipulation? I am perplexed by those who issued commands in later ages. Inwardly, they lacked a heart of genuine sincerity and single-minded honesty; outwardly, what they proclaimed was often inconsistent and expedient. Commands grew ever more numerous, while moral transformation became ever more obstructed. The troubles of incessant alteration arose, and the evils of repeated revision developed. At most, commands lasted only a year or two; sometimes merely a month. In extreme cases, they were implemented in the morning and changed by evening; there were even cases in which an earlier edict had not yet been promulgated before a later command suppressed and annulled it [?]. Officials were bewildered, and the people became distrustful. This was because those responsible did not understand the way of caution and deliberation, and had no standard for judging right and wrong or deciding what to adopt and reject. Ruler and ministers, superiors and inferiors, drifted along together and ultimately contributed nothing to good government. It was like floating on a river without ropes or oars, surrendering entirely to wherever the wind and waves might carry one. How many could escape capsizing and drowning?
Nevertheless, transformation that dispenses with words is no longer to be seen, and the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties can no longer be attained. Yet if one understands the sage's intention in exercising caution and deliberation and puts it into practice throughout the realm, one can still issue commands properly. In the middle period of the Song, the recuperation fostered under Renzong was insufficient to sustain Shenzong's undertakings. When Zhezong first succeeded to the throne, it was precisely a time for nurturing strength and allowing repose. What was good should not have been changed; what was not good should have been restored gradually. To leave affairs settled and secure and people's hearts contentedly submissive, without their even perceiving that a change was taking place—this was the best of good courses. This was indeed the intention of Master Liu of Yuancheng. He was not stubbornly attached to a fixed arrangement and ignorant of how to adapt. What mattered was its appropriateness…

Thus it is said: “The sage endures in his Way, and the world is transformed and brought to completion.” It is also said: “Should there be successors to the Zhou, even a hundred generations hence they can be known.” These words express the sage’s caution; this is the concern of seasoned men deliberating on affairs of state. Memorial
A Memorial in the Person of Zhang Sixun of the Song, Presenting a New Armillary Sphere 〔Fourth year of Taiping Xingguo [979]〕
By Zhang Yaobi.
Associate Examiner Du, Instructor, comments: 〔It traces the beginnings and comprehends the outcome, lucid and fluent, elegant and beautiful. Reading it, one sees the armillary sphere before one’s eyes. Who could accomplish this without understanding both the Way and its concrete instruments? Admirable! Admirable!〕
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: 〔Well-paired parallel prose.〕
Examiner Mao, Education Director, comments: 〔Classical and exemplary.〕

On this day of this month in the fourth year of Taiping Xingguo, your servant Zhang Sixun, a student of the Directorate of Astronomy, having completed a new armillary sphere, respectfully presents it to the throne. Your servant Sixun, in utmost fear and trembling, bows his head to the ground and repeatedly kowtows, submitting these words:

I humbly consider that Heaven and Earth disclose their mysteries, and the sage king esteems their images to make the seasons clear; the pearl-like and jade-disc-like luminaries suspend their patterns above, and this illustrious dynasty examines Heaven to establish the calendar. Calculations take their origin from the seven luminaries; the instrument sets right the positions of the three celestial lights—the sun, moon, and stars. In calculating their motions, I have exhausted what my narrow observation can reveal; with writing brush and tablet, I have merely recorded measurements made with the gnomon. Following inherited precedents, I restore antiquity; by devising an instrument, I bring renewal. For ever since Pao Xi took Heaven as his model and observed the changes of the sun, moon, and stars…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
而軒轅推筴順陰陽天地之占重黎世掌
璣衡羲和始終曆象降觀于後寖失其初
宣夜之制莫傳周髀爲術靡驗張衡靈憲
妄擬蓋天一行銅游浪傳圭土地難尺度
空聞五行之三十三家天不可階徒似陰
陽之二十一術是以渾儀之制久爲棄璧
之文野獻爲勤杞憂未釋玆蓋伏遇
○○○○
聖神撫運
===
聰明憲天奎聚河清識
太平之有象
龍行虎步觀
帝德之罔愆治先敬天以勤民道欲
登三而邁五稽古定制不廢保章之官觀象
玩占尚錄司天之後顧臣箕裘末業術數
世流嘗因星曆之過差欲究古今之同異
仰觀俯察有覺雖丸計往推來因窺磨蟻
木游取則于令瓚銅儀效法乎淳風天體
punctuated: 而軒轅推筴，順陰陽天地之占；重黎世掌璣衡，羲和始終曆象。降觀于後，寖失其初。宣夜之制莫傳，周髀爲術靡驗。張衡靈憲，妄擬蓋天；一行銅游，浪傳圭土。地難尺度，空聞五行之三十三家；天不可階，徒似陰陽之二十一術。是以渾儀之制，久爲棄璧之文。野獻爲勤，杞憂未釋。玆蓋伏遇○○○○聖神撫運，聰明憲天。奎聚河清，識太平之有象；龍行虎步，觀帝德之罔愆。治先敬天以勤民，道欲登三而邁五。稽古定制，不廢保章之官；觀象玩占，尚錄司天之後。顧臣箕裘末業，術數世流。嘗因星曆之過差，欲究古今之同異。仰觀俯察，有覺雖丸；計往推來，因窺磨蟻。木游取則于令瓚，銅儀效法乎淳風。天體
translation_en:
…and Xuanyuan calculated with counting rods, following the prognostications of yin and yang, Heaven and Earth. Zhong and Li held hereditary charge of the astronomical instruments; Xi and He maintained calendrical reckoning and celestial observations from beginning to end. Looking down through later ages, we find that the original methods were gradually lost. The system of the Vast Night theory was no longer transmitted, and the methods of the Zhou Gnomon proved ineffective. Zhang Heng’s Spiritual Constitution presumptuously modeled a canopy heaven; Yixing’s bronze revolving instrument vainly transmitted methods involving the gnomon and the earth [?]. The earth is difficult to measure: we hear only of the thirty-three schools of the Five Phases. Heaven cannot be reached by steps: there remain merely the twenty-one techniques of yin and yang [?]. Thus the design of the armillary sphere has long remained in writings discarded like a precious jade. Diligently offering this humble contribution, I have yet to dispel my anxiety, like that of the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall.
This is because I have reverently encountered ○○○○ Your Majesty, sagely and divine, presiding over the fortunes of the age, discerning and enlightened, taking Heaven as your model. The gathering of stars in Kui and the clearing of the Yellow River reveal auspicious signs of Great Peace; your dragonlike bearing and tigerlike stride manifest imperial virtue without fault. In government, you put reverence for Heaven first, thereby diligently caring for the people; your Way seeks to equal the Three Sovereigns and surpass the Five Emperors. Examining antiquity to establish institutions, you have retained the office of the Keeper of Celestial Phenomena; observing celestial configurations and pondering their prognostications, you still employ the descendants of those who administered astronomy.
As for your servant, I carry on the modest occupation inherited from my forebears, belonging to a lineage versed in mathematical and divinatory arts. Having repeatedly encountered discrepancies in astronomical and calendrical calculations, I wished to investigate the similarities and differences between ancient and present methods. Looking upward and examining below, I gained some understanding, though only of a sphere [?]; reckoning the past and extrapolating the future, I gained insight through the analogy of an ant on a millstone. For the wooden revolving instrument I took Lingzan as my model; for the bronze instrument I followed Chunfeng. The celestial body…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄

至圓周三百六十五度四分度之一渾儀
