五德之運因儀察變定洪範之稽疑觀象授
時示豳風之播穀陰陽定而寒暑時九疇
punctuated: 至圓，周三百六十五度四分度之一。渾儀左運，盡一丈九寸五分寸之三。設架閣於崇臺，運圓機於密室。二儀異道，七政同觀。地隱天中，盡地足、地輪、地軸；奩浮水上，周中關、小關、定關。植水銀於三樞，轉木人于七直。循環不息，自爲鐘鼓之聲；隱見可觀，擬作樓臺之狀。氣朔具瞻於咫尺，乾坤不出于戶庭。運機物範兩儀，范睟昔嘗稱其妙；窮天地侔造化，崔玉無所容其談。是蓋聖世運會之所成，豈謂微臣心思之能到？閉門數歲，僅見一斑；抱瑟三投，自慚千慮。昔晉臣不棄記里之鼓，周家獨藏指南之車。而況棄龜可以占年，飛灰亦能候氣。輒忘狂瞽，自獻芻蕘，仰垂乙夜之觀，用觀五德之運。因儀察變，定《洪範》之稽疑；觀象授時，示《豳風》之播穀。陰陽定而寒暑時，九疇
translation_en:
…is perfectly round, with a circumference of three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees. The armillary instrument turns to the left, spanning one zhang, nine cun, and three-fifths of a cun. A supporting frame is set upon a lofty terrace, and the revolving mechanism operates within an enclosed chamber. Heaven and earth follow different courses, while the seven celestial luminaries can be observed together. The earth is concealed within the heavens, with its supporting feet, wheel, and axle all included [?]; a case floats upon water, encompassing the central joint, small joint, and fixed joint [?]. Mercury is placed at the three pivots, and wooden figures revolve at the seven stations [?]. Cycling without cease, it sounds bells and drums of itself; its appearances and disappearances can be watched, arranged in the likeness of towers and terraces. The solar terms and new moons are all visible within the space of a few inches; heaven and earth do not extend beyond the household courtyard. Its moving mechanism models the things of heaven and earth [?], and Fan Sui once praised its ingenuity; it exhausts the workings of heaven and earth and rivals creation itself, leaving Cui Yu no room for further discourse.

Surely this achievement comes from the auspicious convergence of circumstances in Your Majesty’s sagely age: how could your humble servant’s own thought have attained it? Secluding myself for several years, I have gained only a partial glimpse; presenting myself with my zither three times, I feel ashamed of my thousand deliberations [?]. In former times, a minister of Jin did not discard the distance-recording drum, and the house of Zhou alone preserved the south-pointing carriage. Moreover, even a discarded tortoise can foretell the year’s harvest [?], and flying ashes can indicate the seasonal qi. Presuming to forget my rashness and blindness, I offer this woodcutter’s counsel, humbly hoping that you will deign to inspect it during the second watch of the night, and thereby observe the revolutions of the Five Powers. By examining changes through the instrument, you may settle doubts as prescribed in the “Great Plan”; by observing celestial phenomena and promulgating the seasons, you may indicate when to sow grain, as in the “Airs of Bin.” When yin and yang are settled, cold and heat arrive in their proper seasons; the Nine Categories…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
敘而三綱正伏覩
天地定位
聖人成能水火金木惟脩歲月日時無易
昭六文于
帝極有穆泰階
升萬國于大猷同歸黃道臣無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屏營之至謹以所製新渾儀隨
表上
進以
聞
===
第叁場
策
第一問
同考試官教諭李　批
劉廷臣
聖學之要在正本審幾子能歷敘湯武建中建極與
祖宗丕顯丕承之盛終篇復以洪範五事爲
punctuated:
敘而三綱正。伏覩天地定位，聖人成能，水火金木惟脩，歲月日時無易。昭六文于帝極，有穆泰階；升萬國于大猷，同歸黃道。臣無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹以所製新渾儀隨表上進以聞。

第叁場
策
第一問
同考試官教諭李　批
劉廷臣
聖學之要，在正本審幾。子能歷敘湯武建中建極，與祖宗丕顯丕承之盛，終篇復以洪範五事爲
translation_en:
…are put in order, and the Three Bonds are rectified. I humbly behold Heaven and Earth taking their appointed places, and the sage bringing their capacities to fulfillment. Water, fire, metal, and wood are duly regulated; years, months, days, and hours suffer no displacement. The six celestial patterns [?] shine about the imperial pole, and the Three Steps constellation is harmonious and serene. The myriad states are raised to the Great Way, all converging upon the Yellow Path. Your servant, gazing up at Heaven and reverently looking toward Your Majesty, cannot contain his fervent emotion and profound trepidation. I respectfully submit the newly constructed armillary sphere together with this memorial for Your Majesty’s consideration.

Third Session
Policy Essays
First Question
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor
Liu Tingchen

The essentials of sagely learning lie in rectifying the foundation and discerning the first stirrings of things. You have successively recounted how Tang and Wu established the Mean and the Supreme Standard, together with the flourishing achievements of the imperial ancestors in gloriously manifesting and continuing their legacy. At the end of the essay, you further take the Five Activities of the “Great Plan” as …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
欽蓋涵泳有素而不負所學者
同考試官教諭毛　批〔組織事實而規頌之意藹然非特華於文也敬服敬服〕
考試官教諭林　批〔援古證今條答無遺〕
考試官學正毛　批〔攷據詳實敷對洋洋三晉之俊非子而誰〕
聖王之學在正其本而已聖學之要在審
其幾而已夫人君一心天下萬化之本也
本不正則無以建天下之極而作則以昭
遠端緒微茫天下萬事之幾也幾不審則
===
無以制天下之動而謹微以成務故帝王
之學不在於章句之末而以正本爲先能
養其心則端本澄源之道得矣聖學之要
不待於事爲之著而以審幾爲先能愼其
獨則防微杜漸之功密矣是知審天下之
幾者能正天下之本者也正天下之本者
能致天下之化者也知乎此則自古帝王
精一之傳與我
聖祖
punctuated:
欽。蓋涵泳有素，而不負所學者。

同考試官教諭毛批〔組織事實，而規頌之意藹然，非特華於文也。敬服！敬服！〕
考試官教諭林批〔援古證今，條答無遺。〕
考試官學正毛批〔攷據詳實，敷對洋洋，三晉之俊，非子而誰？〕

聖王之學，在正其本而已；聖學之要，在審其幾而已。夫人君一心，天下萬化之本也。本不正，則無以建天下之極，而作則以昭遠。端緒微茫，天下萬事之幾也。幾不審，則無以制天下之動，而謹微以成務。故帝王之學，不在於章句之末，而以正本爲先。能養其心，則端本澄源之道得矣。聖學之要，不待於事爲之著，而以審幾爲先。能愼其獨，則防微杜漸之功密矣。是知審天下之幾者，能正天下之本者也；正天下之本者，能致天下之化者也。知乎此，則自古帝王精一之傳，與我聖祖
translation_en:
…reverence [?]. Clearly, he has long steeped himself in these teachings and has lived up to what he has learned.

Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, Instructor: 〔He marshals historical facts, and an evident spirit of admonition and praise pervades his writing. This is more than literary elegance. Admirable! Admirable!〕
Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: 〔He invokes antiquity to substantiate the present and answers each point without omission.〕
Comment by Examiner Mao, Instructor: 〔His investigation of the sources is detailed and sound, and his response is expansive. Who but you could be the outstanding talent of the Three Jin regions?〕

The learning of sage kings consists simply in rectifying its foundation; the essential point of sagely learning consists simply in discerning the first stirrings of things. The ruler’s single mind is the foundation of all transformations under Heaven. If that foundation is not rectified, there is no means to establish the supreme standard for the world or to provide an example whose illumination reaches afar. Beginnings, faint and indistinct, are the first stirrings of all affairs under Heaven. If these stirrings are not discerned, there is no means to govern the world’s movements or to attend carefully to minute signs so as to accomplish affairs. Thus, the learning of emperors and kings does not lie in the peripheral details of textual divisions and phrases, but gives priority to rectifying the foundation. If one can nurture one’s mind, one has attained the way of setting the root upright and making the source clear. The essential point of sagely learning does not wait until affairs and actions become manifest, but gives priority to discerning their first stirrings. If one can be watchful over oneself when alone, one’s efforts to guard against minute beginnings and forestall their gradual development will be thorough. Hence we know that those who discern the first stirrings of affairs under Heaven can rectify the foundation of all under Heaven; those who rectify that foundation can bring about the transformation of all under Heaven. Once this is understood, the teaching of refinement and single-mindedness transmitted by emperors and kings since antiquity, together with our sagely ancestor…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
神禄心學源流之妙淵衷敬畏之誠豈不同條
而共貫哉敢敬陳之以復明問之萬一嘗
謂人主之心天下所視以爲治忽萬幾所
視以爲理亂一念之不謹或貽四海之憂
一時之未愼或致無窮之患其關係豈小
哉書曰人心惟危道心惟微惟精惟一允
執厥中是非正心之謂歟然微妙之體易
昏而難見衆欲之攻易引而難遏隄防一
弛則潰裂四至而莫爲之所此其幾又不
===
謂之至要至要者乎易曰知幾其神乎知
微知彰知柔知剛萬夫之望是非審幾之
謂歟是以古之聖帝明王莫不祈天永命
而問學緝熙廓其大公之量而不牿于形
器之小使心之湛然澄一而常爲一身之
主本然之體與天地同大者無一理之不
明瑩然明淨而超然物欲之表本然之用
與天地流通者無一息之不生而又且凝
神定慮反巳靜觀淵衷抑畏不遑縱逸察
punctuated: 神禄心學源流之妙，淵衷敬畏之誠，豈不同條而共貫哉？敢敬陳之，以復明問之萬一。嘗謂人主之心，天下所視以爲治忽，萬幾所視以爲理亂。一念之不謹，或貽四海之憂；一時之未愼，或致無窮之患。其關係豈小哉？《書》曰：「人心惟危，道心惟微，惟精惟一，允執厥中。」是非正心之謂歟？然微妙之體，易昏而難見；衆欲之攻，易引而難遏。隄防一弛，則潰裂四至，而莫爲之所。此其幾，又不謂之至要至要者乎？《易》曰：「知幾其神乎！知微知彰，知柔知剛，萬夫之望。」是非審幾之謂歟？是以古之聖帝明王，莫不祈天永命，而問學緝熙，廓其大公之量，而不牿于形器之小，使心之湛然澄一，而常爲一身之主。本然之體，與天地同大者，無一理之不明；瑩然明淨，而超然物欲之表。本然之用，與天地流通者，無一息之不生。而又且凝神定慮，反巳靜觀，淵衷抑畏，不遑縱逸，察
translation_en:
…the divine blessings [?], the wondrous origins and transmission of the learning of the mind, and the sincerity of reverence and awe deep within the heart—do these not belong to the same lineage and share a common thread? I venture respectfully to set this forth, answering even a ten-thousandth part of your discerning question. I have long held that the ruler’s mind determines whether all under Heaven enjoys good government or suffers neglect, and whether the myriad incipient affairs lead to order or disorder. A single unguarded thought may bequeath sorrow to all within the Four Seas; a moment’s lack of caution may bring endless calamity. Can its consequences be slight? The Book of Documents says: “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle. Be discerning, be single-minded, and hold faithfully to the mean.” Is this not what is meant by rectifying the mind? Yet its subtle essence is easily obscured and difficult to perceive; the assaults of multitudinous desires readily draw one in and are difficult to restrain. Once the embankments are relaxed, breaches occur on every side, leaving no means of coping. Must not these incipient stirrings be called supremely, supremely important? The Book of Changes says: “To know the incipient—is this not divine? Knowing the subtle and the manifest, knowing the yielding and the firm: such a person is looked up to by the multitude.” Is this not what is meant by scrutinizing incipient stirrings?

Thus the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity all prayed to Heaven for an enduring mandate and, through inquiry and learning, continually increased their illumination. They enlarged their capacity for complete impartiality, without being confined by the narrowness of tangible forms, making the mind profoundly clear, pure, and undivided, so that it constantly governed the whole person. In its original essence, as vast as Heaven and Earth, there was no principle it failed to illuminate; radiant and clear, it rose above material desires. In its original functioning, circulating freely with Heaven and Earth, there was not a single moment in which it ceased to generate life. Moreover, they concentrated their spirit and settled their thoughts, turned inward to contemplate themselves quietly, and maintained humble awe in the depths of their hearts, allowing themselves no leisure for indulgence or ease, discerning…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
天理人欲之分致擴充遏絶之力敬畏于
是乎崇逸欲于是乎戒是故以湯武之聖
而承萬世心學之傳懋昭大德不邇聲色
道已至矣而憂勤之念未已不泄不邇克
慎明德德已至矣而惕勵之意尚存訂几
杖以示義而敬怠義欲之訓翼然于觸目
之餘也銘盤盂以昭警而日新又新之諭
竦然于沐浴之際也蓋其動察於理欲之
間而辯不可以不早分析於天人之限而
===
幾不可以不防顧諟之誠殆爲緝熙光明
之助而嚴師之主籍爲祈天永命之休乃
聖人不自滿假無敢暇豫之心也而豈但
動則左史書之言則右史書之瞽箴于幾
聲矇誦于臨事而已哉嗣是而後心學失
傳歷漢而唐而宋英君誼辟各以所見爲
學養心慎獨之功寂然無聞忠諫之屛帝
範之篇規誨若切也而徇名責實之道或
踈丹扆有箴敬天有圖取法若善也而靜
punctuated:
天理人欲之分，致擴充遏絶之力，敬畏于是乎崇，逸欲于是乎戒。是故以湯武之聖，而承萬世心學之傳，懋昭大德，不邇聲色，道已至矣，而憂勤之念未已；不泄不邇，克慎明德，德已至矣，而惕勵之意尚存。訂几杖以示義，而敬怠義欲之訓，翼然于觸目之餘也；銘盤盂以昭警，而日新又新之諭，竦然于沐浴之際也。蓋其動察於理欲之間，而辯不可以不早；分析於天人之限，而幾不可以不防。顧諟之誠，殆爲緝熙光明之助，而嚴師之主，籍爲祈天永命之休，乃聖人不自滿假、無敢暇豫之心也。而豈但動則左史書之，言則右史書之，瞽箴于幾聲，矇誦于臨事而已哉？

嗣是而後，心學失傳，歷漢而唐而宋，英君誼辟各以所見爲學，養心慎獨之功寂然無聞。忠諫之屛、帝範之篇，規誨若切也，而徇名責實之道或踈；丹扆有箴，敬天有圖，取法若善也，而靜
translation_en:
…the distinction between Heaven’s principle and human desires, exerting themselves to expand the former and cut off the latter. Reverence and awe were thereby heightened, and indulgence and desire guarded against. Thus Tang and Wu, with their sagely wisdom, inherited the learning of the mind transmitted through myriad generations. They assiduously manifested their great virtue and kept away from sensual music and beauty: their Way had reached perfection, yet their concern and diligence never ceased. Neither lax nor drawn to sensual pleasures, they carefully tended their luminous virtue: their virtue had reached perfection, yet their vigilance and resolve remained. They set admonitions upon their armrests and staffs to display what was right [?], so that teachings concerning reverence and negligence, righteousness and desire stood vividly before their eyes. They inscribed their basins and bowls to make warnings plain, so that the injunction to renew themselves daily, and yet again each day, stirred them to vigilance as they bathed. In their activity they scrutinized the distinction between principle and desire, which had to be discerned early; they analyzed the boundary between Heaven and the human, whose incipient stirrings had to be guarded against. Their sincerity in constantly attending to this luminous virtue surely helped them continually to brighten its radiance; their commitment to honoring teachers furnished the means of seeking Heaven’s enduring mandate [?]. Such was the mind of the sages, never complacent or self-satisfied, never daring to indulge in leisure and ease. How could it have consisted merely in having the Recorder of the Left record their actions and the Recorder of the Right record their words, or in having blind musicians offer admonitions at the first stirrings of sound [?] and blind reciters chant counsel when affairs arose?

Thereafter, the transmission of the learning of the mind was lost. Through the Han, Tang, and Song, gifted rulers and righteous sovereigns each pursued learning according to their own understanding, but nothing was heard of their efforts to nurture the mind and remain vigilant when alone. Screens bearing loyal remonstrances and the chapters of the Model for Emperors seemed earnest in their admonitions, yet the practice of following names and demanding corresponding realities was sometimes neglected. There were Admonitions for the Vermilion Screen and a Diagram of Reverence for Heaven: the models they adopted seemed good, yet in their quiet…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
言庸違之失不免是不過粉飭於太平而
無以恢弘乎治理此治功之就所以止於
雜夷雜伯而不能以復隆古之盛也仰惟
皇天篤生
聖祖膺明命于淮甸奮起之餘正綱常于腥穢
蕩除之後
獨稟全智
功高千古
盛德大業不可殫述
===
睿資遠邁百王
精義尚友先聖
兢業恒存而不恥然于幽獨得肆之地
嚴畏中切而不怡然于宮闈燕閑之時
知人心出入之幾固無其時也則建
觀心亭於隙地所以存天理而遏人欲正心
之功何極
知誠意正心之道固不可間也
書衍義篇于兩廡所以崇敬畏而戒逸欲愼
punctuated:
言庸違之失不免，是不過粉飭於太平，而無以恢弘乎治理。此治功之就所以止於雜夷雜伯，而不能以復隆古之盛也。
仰惟皇天篤生聖祖，膺明命于淮甸奮起之餘，正綱常于腥穢蕩除之後，獨稟全智，功高千古，盛德大業不可殫述。睿資遠邁百王，精義尚友先聖。兢業恒存，而不恥然于幽獨得肆之地；嚴畏中切，而不怡然于宮闈燕閑之時。知人心出入之幾固無其時也，則建觀心亭於隙地，所以存天理而遏人欲，正心之功何極！知誠意正心之道固不可間也，書衍義篇于兩廡，所以崇敬畏而戒逸欲，愼
translation_en:
…they could not escape the fault of acting contrary to their words. This amounted merely to embellishing an appearance of peace, without any means of enlarging the achievement of good government. Thus their accomplishments in government remained mixed with barbarian ways and hegemonic practices, unable to restore the flourishing order of high antiquity.
We reverently reflect that August Heaven generously brought forth the Sage Founder. He received Heaven’s luminous mandate after rising in the Huai region, and rectified the cardinal bonds and constant norms after sweeping away foul corruption. Uniquely endowed with consummate wisdom, his achievements surpassed those of a thousand ages; his abundant virtue and great undertakings cannot be fully recounted. His sagely endowments far exceeded those of the hundred kings; by penetrating moral principles, he took the sages of old as his companions. He remained constantly vigilant and diligent, and did not become heedless [?] in secluded places where he might indulge himself. Solemn awe pressed urgently within him, and he did not grow complacent during leisure within the palace. Knowing that the subtle movements by which the human heart goes out or returns have no fixed time, he built the Pavilion for Observing the Heart on an unoccupied plot, thereby preserving heavenly principle and restraining human desires. How boundless was his effort to rectify the heart! Knowing that the way of making intentions sincere and rectifying the heart must never be interrupted, he inscribed passages from the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning on the two side galleries, thereby honoring reverence and awe and guarding against indolence and desire. His vigilance…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
獨之功何容其
精一執中之傳正心慎獨之學誠足以上匹
帝王之美而非漢唐宋諸君之所彷彿矣
列聖相承守而弗失
懋契心學先後一致肆我
皇上以天縱之資纘溥將之緒益隆
聖祖之心學遠接帝王之道統註范氏之箴卽
惟危惟微之旨須敬一之訓卽精一執中
之傳
===
天章宸翰曠百世而同符
宏詞奥義越萬年而僅見其他凡所更創則
必
定議新名大揭昭示恭舉其所聞之大者言
之如成于
文華殿者
齋則以九五名矣
室則以恭默名矣九五乾象也辭曰飛龍在
天利見大人〔是蓋〕〔秉剛〕健不息之强其純
punctuated:
獨之功何容其？精一執中之傳，正心慎獨之學，誠足以上匹帝王之美，而非漢唐宋諸君之所彷彿矣。列聖相承，守而弗失，懋契心學，先後一致。肆我皇上以天縱之資，纘溥將之緒，益隆聖祖之心學，遠接帝王之道統。註范氏之箴，卽惟危惟微之旨；須敬一之訓，卽精一執中之傳。天章宸翰，曠百世而同符；宏詞奥義，越萬年而僅見。

其他凡所更創，則必定議新名，大揭昭示。恭舉其所聞之大者言之，如成于文華殿者，齋則以九五名矣，室則以恭默名矣。九五，乾象也。辭曰：「飛龍在天，利見大人。」〔是蓋〕〔秉剛〕健不息之强，其純
translation_en:
…the work of vigilance in solitude—how could it admit of such [?]? The transmitted teaching of refinement, singleness, and holding fast to the Mean, and the learning of rectifying the mind and being vigilant in solitude, are indeed sufficient to match the excellence of the ancient emperors and kings. The rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song could not approach this. Successive sage sovereigns preserved it without loss, diligently accorded with the learning of the mind, and remained consistent from one reign to the next. Thus our Emperor, endowed by Heaven, has continued the grand inherited enterprise, further exalted the Sagely Progenitor’s learning of the mind, and reached back to carry on the orthodox transmission of the Way from the ancient emperors and kings. His annotations to Master Fan’s Admonition embody the purport of “the human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle.” His instruction on reverent singleness [?] embodies the transmitted teaching of refinement, singleness, and holding fast to the Mean. His imperial compositions and writings accord with those of antiquity across a hundred generations; such magnificent language and profound meaning are scarcely seen even in ten thousand years.

Moreover, whenever he renovates or establishes anything, he invariably settles upon a new name and prominently displays it for all to see. Let us respectfully mention the most significant examples of which we have heard. Among those completed in the Hall of Literary Brilliance, the study was named “Nine in the Fifth Place,” and the chamber “Reverent Silence.” “Nine in the Fifth Place” is an image from the hexagram Qian. Its statement reads: “A flying dragon in the heavens. It is beneficial to see the great man.” 〔This presumably means〕 〔possessing firmness〕 and the strength of unceasing vigor, and the purity of …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
粹中正之德而後可以與此誠於此而留
神焉則所以奮終日之乾效夕惕之厲以
統天凝命者無不至矣至於恭默思道非
商高宗之所以中興者乎溫溫恭人維德
之基惟玄惟默守道之極又皆君人者之
所當澄神靜慮以培其存養之功者也至
構于西苑者
亭則以豳風名矣
殿則以無逸名矣豳風周詩也傳曰事上愛
===
下養老慈幼是蓋有勤儉仁厚之風先王
遺澤之遠而後可以語此誠於是而省覽
焉則所以知小人之依崇力穡之効以開
國重民者無不至矣至於所其無逸非周
公所以告成王者乎所其無逸乃有逸民
惟邦本本固邦寧又皆君人者之所當存
神加志以厚其涵濡之體者也是知
聖學淵源而存養省察之精無異於几杖之戒
神功溥博而體驗擴充之大不殊於盤盂之銘
punctuated:
粹中正之德，而後可以與此。誠於此而留神焉，則所以奮終日之乾、效夕惕之厲，以統天凝命者，無不至矣。至於恭默思道，非商高宗之所以中興者乎？「溫溫恭人，維德之基」，「惟玄惟默，守道之極」，又皆君人者之所當澄神靜慮，以培其存養之功者也。
至構于西苑者，亭則以豳風名矣，殿則以無逸名矣。豳風，周詩也。傳曰：「事上愛下，養老慈幼。」是蓋有勤儉仁厚之風、先王遺澤之遠，而後可以語此。誠於是而省覽焉，則所以知小人之依、崇力穡之効，以開國重民者，無不至矣。至於所其無逸，非周公所以告成王者乎？「所其無逸，乃有逸」，「民惟邦本，本固邦寧」，又皆君人者之所當存神加志，以厚其涵濡之體者也。
是知聖學淵源，而存養省察之精，無異於几杖之戒；神功溥博，而體驗擴充之大，不殊於盤盂之銘。
translation_en:
…pure, balanced, and correct virtue: only then can one participate in this. If Your Majesty truly attends to this, then nothing will be lacking in the means of exerting oneself diligently throughout the day and emulating the vigilance of remaining watchful at night, thereby presiding over all under Heaven and securing the Mandate. As for being reverent and silent while contemplating the Way, was this not how Gaozong of Shang brought about a restoration? “Gentle and reverent is the man: this is the foundation of virtue”; “In profundity and silence lies the utmost attainment of preserving the Way.” These, too, are matters in which a ruler should clear his mind and quiet his thoughts, cultivating the work of preserving and nourishing his moral nature.
As for the buildings erected in the Western Park (Xiyuan), the pavilion is named Winds of Bin (Binfeng), and the hall Against Idleness (Wuyi). The Winds of Bin are poems of the Zhou. The commentary says: “Serve those above and cherish those below; support the aged and care tenderly for the young.” Only where there is a spirit of diligence, frugality, benevolence, and generosity, and the far-reaching legacy of the former kings’ beneficence, can one speak of this. If Your Majesty truly reflects upon and examines these matters, then nothing will be lacking in the means of understanding what the common people depend upon and honoring the achievements of diligent farming, thereby establishing the state and giving due weight to the people. As for making freedom from idleness one’s abiding principle, was this not how the Duke of Zhou admonished King Cheng? “Make freedom from idleness your abiding principle, and then there will be ease”; “The people are the foundation of the state; when the foundation is firm, the state is at peace.” These, too, are matters to which a ruler should devote his mind and direct his purpose, deepening the substance of his cultivation through sustained moral nurture.
From this we know that Your Majesty’s sagely learning has deep sources: its refinement in preserving and nourishing the moral nature and in reflective self-examination is no different from the admonitions inscribed on armrests and staffs. Your Majesty’s divine accomplishments are vast and comprehensive: their greatness in putting learning into practice and extending it fully is no different from the inscriptions on basins and bowls.

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
聖祖
神孫心傳之盛豈不有以上追乎隆古天下臣
工欽仰之誠豈不有以舞蹈于風動耶然
人心易放而難存幾微難燭而易昧伏願
讀書以窮理爲先養心以愼獨爲要
益嚴祗畏更切氷兢
講明義理之歸閑塞私邪之路
奉若天道中心無爲務使
貌之恭足以作肅言之從足以作乂視之明
足以作哲聽之聰足以作謀思之睿足以
作聖然後以八柄馭羣臣以八統馭萬民
而遠無不至邇無不服矣四方於穆之休
萬世太平之治又豈不復見於
今日哉謹對
第二問
===
同考試官學正孫　批　〔水旱堯湯不免貴有以弭之耳此〕
張淑勵
〔篇敘述詳悉行入漢唐二臣論義殊得章法末引經訓歸之力行一〕
punctuated:
聖祖神孫心傳之盛，豈不有以上追乎隆古？天下臣工欽仰之誠，豈不有以舞蹈于風動耶？然人心易放而難存，幾微難燭而易昧。伏願讀書以窮理爲先，養心以愼獨爲要，益嚴祗畏，更切氷兢，講明義理之歸，閑塞私邪之路，奉若天道，中心無爲。務使貌之恭足以作肅，言之從足以作乂，視之明足以作哲，聽之聰足以作謀，思之睿足以作聖。然後以八柄馭羣臣，以八統馭萬民，而遠無不至，邇無不服矣。四方於穆之休，萬世太平之治，又豈不復見於今日哉？謹對。

第二問

同考試官學正孫，批：〔水旱堯湯不免，貴有以弭之耳。此〕
張淑勵
〔篇敘述詳悉，行入漢唐二臣論義，殊得章法。末引經訓，歸之力行，一〕
translation_en:
Could not the glorious transmission of the mind’s teaching from the sagely ancestor to his divine descendant rival that of high antiquity? Could not the sincere reverence and admiration of officials throughout the realm move them to dance for joy under its transforming influence? Yet the human mind is easily let loose and difficult to preserve; subtle incipient movements are difficult to illuminate and easily obscured. I humbly wish that Your Majesty would make fathoming principle the priority in reading and vigilance in solitude the essential point in nurturing the mind; deepen reverence and awe, and exercise still greater caution, as though treading on ice. Clarify the import of moral principles, block the paths of selfishness and perversity, follow the Way of Heaven reverently, and remain free of contrived action within your heart. Strive to ensure that reverence in demeanor produces gravity, accordance in speech produces order, clarity of vision produces discernment, acuity of hearing produces sound deliberation, and penetration of thought produces sageliness. Then employ the eight instruments of authority to govern the assembled officials and the eight bonds of unity to govern the myriad people: none afar will remain beyond your reach, and none nearby will fail to submit. Would not the sublime blessings enjoyed throughout the four quarters, and a reign of great peace lasting ten thousand generations, then appear again today? Respectfully submitted in reply.

Second Question

Associate Examiner Sun, Instructor, comments: 〔Even Yao and Tang could not escape floods and droughts; what matters is having the means to mitigate them. This〕
Zhang Shuli
〔essay gives a detailed and comprehensive account. It proceeds into the arguments of two ministers of the Han and Tang dynasties [?], displaying an excellent command of composition. At the end it cites the teachings of the Classics and brings the matter back to vigorous practice; a single …〕

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
大延之上者
言尤爲簡盡蓋熟於策學而可以對揚于
考試官教諭林　批〔抑揚取舍卓有定見〕
考試官學正毛　批〔董子觀春秋有見於天人相與之可畏此荅良得其意〕
對以人驗天善言天者也以人應天善事
天者也天人之分雖殊感應之機則一不
知人之未始不爲天天之未始不爲人不
足以言天不知和氣之足以致祥乖氣之
===
足以致異不足以事天是故人感而天應
理之常也災變之未生脩德以格之而已
矣人定而勝天數之極也災變之旣生脩
政以禳之而已矣舍其當爲之事而委
於或然之數而曰天也非人也數也非政
也是豈人君之所以事天而天之所以
愛之意亦虚矣執事以天變策士而有及
乎邇者雷火之警蓋欲講求所以弭變之
術而上下同致其憂勤也敢不敬應夫天
punctuated:
大延之上者，言尤爲簡盡，蓋熟於策學而可以對揚于。
考試官教諭林，批〔抑揚取舍，卓有定見。〕
考試官學正毛，批〔董子觀春秋，有見於天人相與之可畏，此荅良得其意。〕
對：以人驗天，善言天者也；以人應天，善事天者也。天人之分雖殊，感應之機則一。不知人之未始不爲天、天之未始不爲人，不足以言天；不知和氣之足以致祥、乖氣之足以致異，不足以事天。是故，人感而天應，理之常也；災變之未生，脩德以格之而已矣。人定而勝天，數之極也；災變之旣生，脩政以禳之而已矣。舍其當爲之事，而委於或然之數，而曰：「天也，非人也；數也，非政也。」是豈人君之所以事天？而天之所以愛之意亦虚矣。執事以天變策士，而有及乎邇者雷火之警，蓋欲講求所以弭變之術，而上下同致其憂勤也。敢不敬應？夫天
translation_en:
…those at the great court [?]. The wording is especially concise and comprehensive; evidently he is well versed in policy essays and capable of responding to and proclaiming imperial commands at… [?]
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: 〔In his praise and criticism, acceptance and rejection, he displays remarkably firm judgment.〕
Examiner Mao, Instructor, comments: 〔Master Dong, in studying the Spring and Autumn Annals, perceived how fearsome the interaction between Heaven and humanity could be. This answer truly captures his meaning.〕
In reply: To examine Heaven through human affairs is to speak well of Heaven; to respond to Heaven through human conduct is to serve Heaven well. Although Heaven and humanity occupy distinct spheres, the mechanism of stimulus and response is one. Unless one understands that humanity has never been separate from Heaven, and Heaven has never been separate from humanity, one cannot adequately speak of Heaven. Unless one understands that harmonious qi can bring auspicious signs, and discordant qi can bring anomalies, one cannot adequately serve Heaven. Thus, that human actions move Heaven and Heaven responds is the constant principle. Before calamities and anomalies arise, one need only cultivate virtue to forestall them. That humanity, through settled resolve, can prevail over Heaven marks the ultimate limit of destiny. Once calamities and anomalies have arisen, one need only reform government to avert them. If one abandons the tasks one ought to undertake, leaves matters to uncertain fate, and says, “This is Heaven, not humanity; this is destiny, not government,” can this be how a ruler serves Heaven? Heaven’s intention of showing him care would thereby also be frustrated.
You, honored examiners, have tested candidates with a policy question on celestial anomalies, touching upon the recent warning of thunder and fire. Your intention, surely, is to investigate the means of averting such anomalies, so that those above and below may alike exert themselves in anxious diligence. How could I dare fail to respond respectfully? Now, Heaven…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
人相與之際甚可畏也書曰惟吉凶不僭
在人惟天降災祥在德又曰天視自我民
視天聽自我民聽夫天之災祥民之視聽
邈乎其不相及也而響應若此則人君居
萬民之上而所以因政以得民因民以得
天者其可以易而爲之耶董仲舒之告武
帝曰天出災變見天心之仁愛人君而欲
止其亂也雨暘之災山川之變不見於有
道之國而且以爲仁愛蓋變不虛生所以
示戒也人君克謹天戒則天意回天意回
===
則治道興而人君致治之德益成然則非
天成之耶是之謂仁愛是故九年之水堯
非不仁也然而懷襄之勢使禹治之八年
于外而九州攸同四隩旣宅九山刋旅九
澤旣陂則所以遺堯之憂而成平成之治
者未必非天成之也如此而謂之天之仁
愛於堯可也三年之旱湯非不德也然而
桑林之禱六事自責曰政不節歟民失職
punctuated: 人相與之際，甚可畏也。《書》曰：「惟吉凶不僭，在人；惟天降災祥，在德。」又曰：「天視自我民視，天聽自我民聽。」夫天之災祥，民之視聽，邈乎其不相及也，而響應若此，則人君居萬民之上，而所以因政以得民、因民以得天者，其可以易而爲之耶？董仲舒之告武帝曰：「天出災變，見天心之仁愛人君，而欲止其亂也。」雨暘之災，山川之變，不見於有道之國，而且以爲仁愛，蓋變不虛生，所以示戒也。人君克謹天戒，則天意回；天意回，則治道興，而人君致治之德益成。然則非天成之耶？是之謂仁愛。是故九年之水，堯非不仁也。然而懷襄之勢，使禹治之，八年于外，而九州攸同，四隩旣宅，九山刋旅，九澤旣陂，則所以遺堯之憂而成平成之治者，未必非天成之也。如此而謂之天之仁愛於堯，可也。三年之旱，湯非不德也。然而桑林之禱，六事自責，曰：「政不節歟？民失職
translation_en:
…the interaction between Heaven and humanity is greatly to be feared. The Book of Documents says: “Good and ill fortune never err: they depend on people. Heaven’s sending down calamities or blessings depends on virtue.” It also says: “Heaven sees through what our people see; Heaven hears through what our people hear.” Heaven’s calamities and blessings and the people’s seeing and hearing seem so remote as to have no connection. Yet they respond to one another like an echo. Thus, when the ruler stands above the myriad people, can he take lightly the means by which he wins the people through government and wins Heaven through the people?

Dong Zhongshu told Emperor Wu: “Heaven sends forth calamities and anomalies to reveal its benevolent love for the ruler and its desire to put a stop to his disorder.” Disasters of excessive rain or prolonged sunshine, and disturbances in mountains and rivers, do not appear in a state that possesses the Way. Yet these too are regarded as benevolent love, for anomalies do not arise without cause: they serve to convey warnings. If the ruler can heed Heaven’s warnings with due care, Heaven’s intentions will turn. When Heaven’s intentions turn, good government flourishes, and the ruler’s virtue in bringing about good government becomes still more complete. Is this not, then, Heaven bringing it to completion? This is what is meant by benevolent love.

Thus, the nine years of flooding did not mean that Yao lacked benevolence. Nevertheless, faced with the overwhelming floodwaters, he ordered Yu to bring them under control. Yu spent eight years away from home; the Nine Provinces were brought into accord, the lands in all four quarters became habitable, the nine mountains had their trees cleared and sacrifices offered upon them, and the nine marshes were embanked. The means by which Yao’s anxiety was relieved [?] and peaceful, orderly government achieved may indeed have been Heaven’s work. Understood in this way, it is fitting to call this Heaven’s benevolent love for Yao.

The three years of drought did not mean that Tang lacked virtue. Nevertheless, in his prayer at the Mulberry Grove, he reproached himself on six counts, saying: “Has my government lacked restraint? Have the people lost their livelihoods …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
歟宮室崇歟女謁盛歟苞苴行歟讒夫昌
歟則所以勤湯之省而致永懷之化者未
必非天致之也如此而謂天之仁愛於湯
可也仲舒之言蓋取諸此乃若唐康澄之
論事於明宗則以三辰失行天象變見小
人訛言山崩川竭水旱蟲蝗五者爲不足
畏夫五者之爲災莫大焉而以爲不足畏
豈非啓人君戲豫之心而漫視於天人之
際哉然澄之言亦自有見蓋人之所能者
===
人也其所不能者天也聖如堯湯而不能
使天下之無水旱而水旱亦不能免於堯
湯之世則其所可畏者在天而不在我而
我方且恐然以求之於茫渺冥昧之中而
不求其實於天下國家之事則亦何益之
有是何也畏其所難畏而忘其機之在我
耳故曰天作孽猶可違者此也蘇軾所謂
星墜木鳴川竭谷湮彼之咎者此也其視
王安石所謂天變不足畏人言不足恤祖
punctuated: 歟？宮室崇歟？女謁盛歟？苞苴行歟？讒夫昌歟？則所以勤湯之省而致永懷之化者，未必非天致之也。如此而謂天之仁愛於湯，可也。仲舒之言，蓋取諸此。乃若唐康澄之論事於明宗，則以三辰失行、天象變見、小人訛言、山崩川竭、水旱蟲蝗五者爲不足畏。夫五者之爲災，莫大焉，而以爲不足畏，豈非啓人君戲豫之心，而漫視於天人之際哉？然澄之言亦自有見。蓋人之所能者，人也；其所不能者，天也。聖如堯湯，而不能使天下之無水旱，而水旱亦不能免於堯湯之世，則其所可畏者在天而不在我。而我方且恐然，以求之於茫渺冥昧之中，而不求其實於天下國家之事，則亦何益之有？是何也？畏其所難畏，而忘其機之在我耳。故曰：「天作孽，猶可違」者，此也。蘇軾所謂「星墜木鳴，川竭谷湮，彼之咎」者，此也。其視王安石所謂「天變不足畏，人言不足恤，祖
translation_en:
…? Are the palaces too grand? Is influence exerted through women too prevalent? Are bribes circulating? Are slanderers flourishing?」 Thus, what prompted Tang to examine himself diligently and brought about a transforming influence of enduring solicitude may indeed have been brought about by Heaven. Understood in this way, it is permissible to speak of Heaven’s benevolent love for Tang. Zhongshu’s words presumably drew upon this.

As for Kang Cheng of the Tang, when discussing affairs with Emperor Mingzong, he held that five things were insufficient cause for fear: the sun, moon, and stars departing from their courses; anomalies appearing in celestial phenomena; rumors spread by petty people; mountains collapsing and rivers drying up; and floods, droughts, insect pests, and locusts. No calamities are greater than these five; yet he considered them insufficient cause for fear. Does this not encourage a ruler’s inclination toward idle amusement and cause him to treat the relationship between Heaven and humanity carelessly? Yet Cheng’s words also contain an insight. What lies within human capacity belongs to the human sphere; what lies beyond it belongs to Heaven. Even sages such as Yao and Tang could not keep the world free of floods and droughts, nor could their ages escape such disasters. Thus, the cause for fear lies with Heaven, rather than with oneself. But if, in alarm, one seeks it amid the obscure and unfathomable, without seeking its practical substance in the affairs of the realm and the state, what benefit can there be? Why is this? It is simply that one fears what is difficult to guard against and forgets that the means of responding lie within oneself. This is the meaning of the saying, “Calamities wrought by Heaven may still be avoided.” This is also what Su Shi meant by “Stars fall and trees cry out; rivers dry up and valleys are engulfed: the fault lies with Heaven.” Compare this with Wang Anshi’s saying, “Heavenly anomalies are insufficient cause for fear; people’s words are insufficient cause for concern; ancestral …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
宗法不足守則其虛名實行堅志强辯以
釀成新法之禍古人所謂一言而喪邦者
也豈君子至當之論哉澄之言又以賢士
藏匿四民遷業上下相徇廉恥道消毀譽
亂眞直言不聞六者爲深可懼夫六者之
爲害若隱焉而以爲深可懼豈非以其有
可懼之實無可懼之形哉然澄之言誠爲
知本蓋人君當制治於未亂也保邦於未
危也治如堯湯猶且兢業以行道檢身如
===
不及而當時四凶之未去慚德之未釋則
其所可懼者在我而不在天而我方且肆
然以自足於豐亨豫大之世而忘其憂勤
惕厲之心則亦何足爲恃是何也懼其所
當懼而盡其道之在我耳故曰自作孽不
可逭者此也蘇軾所謂德薄道虧政荒民
散我之咎者此也其與湯之六事自責以
義制事以禮制心而成有商格天之治者
異詞同符又豈得以澄之言而盡廢之哉
punctuated: 宗法不足守」，則其虛名實行、堅志强辯，以釀成新法之禍，古人所謂「一言而喪邦」者也，豈君子至當之論哉？澄之言，又以賢士藏匿、四民遷業、上下相徇、廉恥道消、毀譽亂眞、直言不聞六者爲深可懼。夫六者之爲害若隱焉，而以爲深可懼，豈非以其有可懼之實、無可懼之形哉？然澄之言誠爲知本，蓋人君當制治於未亂也，保邦於未危也。治如堯湯，猶且兢業以行道，檢身如不及，而當時四凶之未去、慚德之未釋，則其所可懼者在我而不在天。而我方且肆然以自足於豐亨豫大之世，而忘其憂勤惕厲之心，則亦何足爲恃？是何也？懼其所當懼，而盡其道之在我耳。故曰「自作孽，不可逭」者，此也。蘇軾所謂「德薄道虧，政荒民散，我之咎」者，此也。其與湯之六事自責、以義制事、以禮制心，而成有商格天之治者，異詞同符，又豈得以澄之言而盡廢之哉？
translation_en:
…“ancestral institutions need not be preserved”: his empty claims and practical measures, his obstinate resolve and forceful arguments [?], thus brewed the calamity of the New Policies. This was what the ancients called “a single utterance that ruins a state.” How could it be the supremely fitting judgment of a gentleman?

Cheng (Kang Cheng), moreover, identified six things as deeply to be feared: worthy scholars remaining in hiding; the four classes of the people abandoning their occupations; superiors and subordinates accommodating one another improperly; integrity and shame falling away; praise and blame obscuring the truth; and forthright words going unheard. The harm caused by these six things seems hidden, yet he considered them deeply frightening. Was this not because they possess the substance of something to be feared without its visible form? Cheng’s words indeed show an understanding of the root. A ruler should establish order before disorder arises and preserve his state before it is endangered.

Even with government like that of Yao and Tang, they still acted with vigilance and diligence in carrying out the Way, examining themselves as though they fell short. While the Four Evildoers had yet to be removed and grounds for shame over one’s virtue had yet to be dispelled, what was to be feared lay in oneself, not in Heaven. Yet if I complacently content myself with an age of abundance, prosperity, ease, and grandeur, forgetting the disposition of anxious diligence and vigilant self-discipline, what would there be to rely upon? Why is this? One must fear what ought to be feared and fully carry out the Way insofar as it lies within oneself. This is the meaning of the saying, “Calamities you bring upon yourself cannot be escaped.” It is also what Su Shi meant by “Virtue is scant, the Way is impaired, government is neglected, and the people scatter: these are our own faults.”

Compared with Tang’s reproaching himself on six counts, regulating affairs through righteousness and regulating his mind through ritual propriety, thereby achieving the Shang dynasty’s government that moved Heaven, these statements differ in wording but accord in meaning. How, then, could Cheng’s words justify rejecting them all?

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
是則仲舒之言推天以示人康澄之論以
人而事天而介甫之辯則棄天褻天之甚
者也方今
聖明在上禮備樂和其視堯湯之世後先一揆
然近日雷火之災隨發隨滅而
益加抑畏引咎責躬
明詔下頒期以實應是其上天之所以仁愛於
皇上者即堯湯之水旱也而其所以
事天之孝即堯湯洚水之儆六事之責也然愚
===
又何贅焉夫爲政不在多言顧力行何如
耳書曰勑天之命惟時惟幾又曰先王克
謹天戒易曰君子以恐懼脩省詩曰天命
降監不敢怠豫又曰小心翼翼以事上帝
此先王愼重天戒有如此者洪惟我
太祖高皇帝立國之初憂思深遠每遇水旱則
謂省臣曰豈刑罰失中武事未息宜輔朕
脩省以消變異又遇星變謂羣臣曰四方
災異或匿不以聞或舉不以實今宜以實
punctuated:
是則仲舒之言，推天以示人；康澄之論，以人而事天；而介甫之辯，則棄天褻天之甚者也。方今聖明在上，禮備樂和，其視堯湯之世，後先一揆。然近日雷火之災，隨發隨滅，而益加抑畏，引咎責躬，明詔下頒，期以實應。是其上天之所以仁愛於皇上者，即堯湯之水旱也；而其所以事天之孝，即堯湯洚水之儆、六事之責也。然愚又何贅焉？夫爲政不在多言，顧力行何如耳。《書》曰：「勑天之命，惟時惟幾。」又曰：「先王克謹天戒。」《易》曰：「君子以恐懼脩省。」《詩》曰：「天命降監，不敢怠豫。」又曰：「小心翼翼，以事上帝。」此先王愼重天戒有如此者。

洪惟我太祖高皇帝立國之初，憂思深遠，每遇水旱，則謂省臣曰：「豈刑罰失中，武事未息？宜輔朕脩省，以消變異。」又遇星變，謂羣臣曰：「四方災異，或匿不以聞，或舉不以實，今宜以實
translation_en:
Thus Zhongshu’s words invoke Heaven to instruct men; Kang Cheng’s argument concerns serving Heaven through human conduct; but Jiefu’s contention represents the utmost abandonment and profanation of Heaven. Today our sage and enlightened sovereign reigns above; ritual is complete and music harmonious. Compared with the ages of Yao and Tang, earlier and later ages follow a single standard. Yet the recent calamities of thunder and fire, though extinguished as soon as they arose, have prompted His Majesty to exercise still greater humility and reverence, take blame upon himself, and reproach his own conduct. An enlightened edict has been issued, calling for a response in actual deeds. The loving concern that Heaven thus shows toward His Majesty is the same as that manifested in the floods and droughts of Yao and Tang; and the filial devotion with which he serves Heaven is the same as Yao’s vigilance in the face of the great flood and Tang’s self-reproach concerning six matters. What further words need an ignorant man like me add? Governing does not depend on much talk, but only on how earnestly one acts. The Book of Documents says: “Attend reverently to Heaven’s mandate, watching the times and the first signs of change.” It also says: “The former kings were able to heed Heaven’s warnings.” The Book of Changes says: “The gentleman, in fear and apprehension, cultivates himself and examines his conduct.” The Book of Odes says: “Heaven’s mandate descends to oversee us; we dare not be idle or seek ease.” It also says: “With care and reverence, he served the Lord on High.” Such was the seriousness with which the former kings regarded Heaven’s warnings.

We reverently reflect that, at the founding of the state, our Emperor Taizu Gao pondered deeply and looked far ahead. Whenever floods or droughts occurred, he would say to the officials of the Secretariat: “Could it be that punishments have failed to strike the proper balance, or that military operations have not ceased? You should assist me in self-cultivation and self-examination, so as to dispel these anomalies.” Again, when a celestial anomaly occurred, he told his assembled officials: “Calamities and anomalies throughout the realm are sometimes concealed and not reported, or reported without truthfulness. Henceforth, you should truthfully…”

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
上聞此
祖宗愼重天戒有如此此者若今日之事能以堯
湯之心爲心六經之訓爲訓
祖宗之法爲法
躬行於上而責成於下應之以實而不應之
以文舉其所當因而釐其所當革如此則
可以事天可以弭變董子之所謂正朝廷
以正百官正百官以正萬民萬民正遠近
莫不一於正而諸福之物可致之祥皆畢
===
至矣公孫弘所謂心和則氣和氣和則形
和形和則聲和聲和而天地之和應矣否
則可懼者舍之而不懼而不可畏者日見
其可畏矣其如弭變何哉漆室之憂野芹
之獻執事或不以爲迂而汜焉庶幾土壤
細流之足錄云謹對
第三問
孟顏
同考試官教諭杜　批〔易畫經世同者亦異〕〔異者本同辨〕
punctuated:
上聞。此祖宗愼重天戒有如此此者。若今日之事，能以堯湯之心爲心，六經之訓爲訓，祖宗之法爲法，躬行於上而責成於下，應之以實而不應之以文，舉其所當因而釐其所當革，如此則可以事天，可以弭變。董子之所謂「正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民，萬民正，遠近莫不一於正，而諸福之物、可致之祥皆畢至矣」。公孫弘所謂「心和則氣和，氣和則形和，形和則聲和，聲和而天地之和應矣」。否則，可懼者舍之而不懼，而不可畏者日見其可畏矣，其如弭變何哉？漆室之憂，野芹之獻，執事或不以爲迂而汜焉，庶幾土壤細流之足錄云。謹對。

第三問
孟顏
同考試官教諭杜批〔易畫、經世，同者亦異〕〔異者本同，辨〕
translation_en:
…report truthfully to the throne. Such was the ancestral emperors’ care in heeding Heaven’s warnings [the transcription repeats 此]. In dealing with affairs today, if one could take the minds of Yao and Tang as one’s own mind, the teachings of the Six Classics as one’s teachings, and the ancestral emperors’ methods as one’s methods; personally put these into practice above and hold those below responsible for accomplishing them; respond with substance rather than mere formalities; and uphold what ought to be retained while rectifying what ought to be reformed—then one could serve Heaven and avert ominous anomalies. This is what Master Dong meant when he said: “Rectify the court in order to rectify the officials; rectify the officials in order to rectify the people. Once the people are upright, those far and near will all be united in uprightness, and all blessed things and auspicious signs that can be brought about will arrive.” It is also what Gongsun Hong meant when he said: “When the heart is harmonious, the vital force is harmonious; when the vital force is harmonious, the bodily form is harmonious; when the bodily form is harmonious, the voice is harmonious; and when the voice is harmonious, the harmony of Heaven and Earth responds.” Otherwise, if what should be feared is disregarded without fear, even what need not be feared will daily appear fearsome. How could this avert ominous anomalies?

Mine is the anxiety of the woman of Qishi, and this offering is but wild celery—a humble gift offered in sincerity. If you, sir, do not dismiss it as impractical and will take note of it [?], I hope that, like a little soil or a small stream, it may merit inclusion. Respectfully submitted in reply.

Third Question
Meng Yan
Associate Examiner Du, Instructor, comments: 〔“The diagrams of the Changes and Ordering the World (Jingshi): what is the same is also different.”〕〔“What is different is fundamentally the same; distinguishing…”〕

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
其異而歸之同非用心于內者不能
考試官教諭林　批〔筆力雅健不獨達于理數爾已〕
考試官學正毛　批〔誦之心目豁然于其心伏犧之心〕
學康節之學者也
易畫成而天下之道盡其體經世成而天
下之道盡其用夫陰陽消息之變鬼神造
化之功天地萬物之理固有渺茫無象而
不可測度者非伏犧氏之仰觀俯察而筆
之於易畫卦立爻稽實待虛則天下之道
===
何以盡其體耶故奇偶剛柔生而天地之
撰神明之德自昭然于畫象之間矣天時
人事之始終古今世道之成敗萬事萬物
之消長固有盈縮相乘而不可臆料者非
康節邵氏之內聖外王而作皇極經世因
理推數因數達理則天下之道何以盡其
用耶故元會運世著而天地之心天下之
故自了然於推步之下矣是天地之秘非
犧氏無以明犧氏之精非康節無以闡先
punctuated:
其異而歸之同，非用心于內者不能。
考試官教諭林，批〔筆力雅健，不獨達于理數爾已。〕
考試官學正毛，批〔誦之，心目豁然，于其心伏犧之心〕學康節之學者也。
易畫成而天下之道盡其體，經世成而天下之道盡其用。夫陰陽消息之變，鬼神造化之功，天地萬物之理，固有渺茫無象而不可測度者。非伏犧氏之仰觀俯察，而筆之於易，畫卦立爻，稽實待虛，則天下之道何以盡其體耶？故奇偶剛柔生，而天地之撰、神明之德，自昭然于畫象之間矣。天時人事之始終，古今世道之成敗，萬事萬物之消長，固有盈縮相乘而不可臆料者。非康節邵氏之內聖外王，而作《皇極經世》，因理推數，因數達理，則天下之道何以盡其用耶？故元會運世著，而天地之心、天下之故，自了然於推步之下矣。是天地之秘，非犧氏無以明；犧氏之精，非康節無以闡。先
translation_en:
…their differences and bring them back to their underlying unity: only someone who applies his mind inwardly can accomplish this.
Examiner Lin, an Instructor, comments: “The writing is elegant and vigorous; it does more than merely show a grasp of principle and number.”
Examiner Mao, an Instructor, comments: “Reading this aloud opens the mind and eyes. In his heart he takes Fuxi’s heart as his own [?] and studies the learning of Kangjie.”
When the diagrams of the Changes were completed, the Way of all under Heaven was fully expressed in its substance; when Ordering the World was completed, the Way of all under Heaven was fully expressed in its operation. The changes wrought by the waxing and waning of yin and yang, the creative workings of spirits, and the principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things certainly contain aspects so obscure and formless that they cannot be fathomed. Had Fuxi not looked upward and examined downward, recording these things in the Changes, drawing the trigrams and establishing their lines, examining what was manifest and awaiting what was not yet manifest, how could the Way of all under Heaven have been fully expressed in its substance? Thus, once the odd and even, the firm and yielding, came into being, the workings of Heaven and Earth and the potency of spiritual intelligence became plainly evident in the diagrams and images.
The beginnings and endings of celestial seasons and human affairs, the successes and failures of the world’s course past and present, and the waxing and waning of all affairs and things certainly involve increases and decreases acting upon one another that cannot be guessed at. Had Shao Kangjie not embodied inward sageliness and outward kingliness and composed Supreme Principles for Ordering the World (Huangji jingshi), inferring numbers from principles and comprehending principles through numbers, how could the Way of all under Heaven have been fully expressed in its operation? Thus, once the chronological cycles of yuan, hui, yun, and shi were set forth, the heart of Heaven and Earth and the reasons underlying the world’s affairs became clear through calculation. Accordingly, without Fuxi there was no means of illuminating the mysteries of Heaven and Earth; without Kangjie there was no means of expounding the essence of Fuxi’s thought. The Prior-…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
天之學其數之體乎皇極之數其易之用
乎而又何同異之懸絕哉請因執事之問
而敷陳之以終其說天下之道方其始也
渾渾噩噩而不可爲方體浩浩蕩蕩而不
可爲限量天地之化莫究其端倪萬物之
變莫知其眹兆其尊卑之定位卑高之肆
陳動靜之常度象形之昭布人但見其運
行而已爾但見其森列而已爾但見其往
來屈伸而已爾而陰之所以爲陰陽之所
===
以爲陽則又孰得而知之天開人文伏犧
氏生焉于是乎仰觀于天文俯察于地理
畫一奇以象陽畫一偶以象陰剛柔相摩
八卦相盪引而伸之觸類而長之大抵一
分爲二一者太極二則兩儀矣二分爲四
四則四象所謂太陽太陰少陽少陰者是
也四分爲八八則八卦所謂乾兌離震巽
坎艮坤者是也八分爲十六十六分爲三
十二三十二分爲六十四而其變無窮天
punctuated: 天之學，其數之體乎？皇極之數，其易之用乎？而又何同異之懸絕哉？請因執事之問，而敷陳之，以終其說。天下之道，方其始也，渾渾噩噩而不可爲方體，浩浩蕩蕩而不可爲限量。天地之化，莫究其端倪；萬物之變，莫知其眹兆。其尊卑之定位，卑高之肆陳，動靜之常度，象形之昭布，人但見其運行而已爾，但見其森列而已爾，但見其往來屈伸而已爾。而陰之所以爲陰，陽之所以爲陽，則又孰得而知之？天開人文，伏犧氏生焉。于是乎仰觀于天文，俯察于地理，畫一奇以象陽，畫一偶以象陰。剛柔相摩，八卦相盪，引而伸之，觸類而長之。大抵一分爲二，一者太極，二則兩儀矣；二分爲四，四則四象，所謂太陽、太陰、少陽、少陰者是也；四分爲八，八則八卦，所謂乾、兌、離、震、巽、坎、艮、坤者是也；八分爲十六，十六分爲三十二，三十二分爲六十四，而其變無窮，天
translation_en: …the learning of Prior Heaven: is it not the substance of these numbers? Are the numbers of the Supreme Ultimate (Huangji) not the functioning of the Changes? How, then, could their similarities and differences place them so far apart? Allow me to elaborate in response to your question, honored examiner, and thus complete my account. At its inception, the Way of all under Heaven was undifferentiated and could not be given a definite shape or substance; it was vast and boundless and could not be circumscribed or measured. No one could fathom the beginnings of the transformations of Heaven and Earth; no one could discern the first signs of changes in the myriad things. As for the fixed positions of the exalted and the lowly, the array of things low and high, the constant measures of movement and stillness, and the manifest display of images and forms, people merely saw their motions, their ordered ranks, and their coming and going, contraction and expansion. But who could know what makes yin yin and yang yang? Heaven inaugurated human culture, and Fu Xi was born. He looked upward to observe the patterns of Heaven and downward to examine the configurations of Earth. He drew a single unbroken line to symbolize yang and a divided line to symbolize yin. The firm and yielding interacted, and the eight trigrams impelled one another. He extended them and developed them by following their affinities. Broadly speaking, one divides into two: the one is the Supreme Polarity, and the two are the Two Modes. Two divides into four: the four are the Four Images, namely greater yang, greater yin, lesser yang, and lesser yin. Four divides into eight: the eight are the Eight Trigrams, namely Qian, Dui, Li, Zhen, Xun, Kan, Gen, and Kun. Eight divides into sixteen, sixteen into thirty-two, and thirty-two into sixty-four, and their transformations are inexhaustible; Heaven…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
下之能事畢矣陰陽動靜之道于是乎形
焉天地萬物之理于是乎發焉至宋而有
康節邵氏者出反覆乎大易之旨默契乎
犧氏之心深得於易而數學爲精其於始
畫之八卦也則見其陰陽先後之數於八
卦之正位也則見其陰陽消息之數於八
卦之因重也則見其陰陽流行之數於六
十四卦之方圓也則見其陰陽對待之數
於陽九陰六之用也則見其萬物之數故
===
作經世以覺天下衍易一圖曰一動一靜
之間者卽易之所謂太極也天地四象圖
曰太陽太陰少陽少陰少剛少柔太剛太
柔者卽易之所謂四象也天地始終之數
圖曰元會運世歲月日辰水火土石者卽
易之六十四卦也六十四卦數圖曰一一
起于南八八脩於北者卽易之八卦之數
也至於一元消息之數圖四象體用之數
圖則又何莫而非易之萬物之數耶故總
punctuated: 下之能事畢矣。陰陽動靜之道於是乎形焉，天地萬物之理於是乎發焉。至宋而有康節邵氏者出，反覆乎大易之旨，默契乎犧氏之心，深得於易，而數學爲精。其於始畫之八卦也，則見其陰陽先後之數；於八卦之正位也，則見其陰陽消息之數；於八卦之因重也，則見其陰陽流行之數；於六十四卦之方圓也，則見其陰陽對待之數；於陽九陰六之用也，則見其萬物之數。故作《經世》以覺天下。《衍易一圖》曰：「一動一靜之間者」，卽易之所謂太極也。《天地四象圖》曰：「太陽、太陰、少陽、少陰、少剛、少柔、太剛、太柔者」，卽易之所謂四象也。《天地始終之數圖》曰：「元、會、運、世、歲、月、日、辰、水、火、土、石者」，卽易之六十四卦也。《六十四卦數圖》曰：「一一起于南，八八脩於北者」，卽易之八卦之數也。至於《一元消息之數圖》、《四象體用之數圖》，則又何莫而非易之萬物之數耶？故總
translation_en:
…all undertakings under Heaven are fully encompassed. Here the Way of yin and yang, movement and stillness, takes form; here the principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are revealed. In the Song there emerged Shao Kangjie, who pondered repeatedly the purport of the great Book of Changes and attained an unspoken accord with the mind of Fuxi. His understanding of the Changes was profound, and he was especially accomplished in the study of numbers. In the eight trigrams as first drawn, he discerned the numbers governing the sequence of yin and yang; in the proper positions of the eight trigrams, the numbers governing their waxing and waning; in the doubling of the eight trigrams, the numbers governing their circulation; in the square and circular arrangements of the sixty-four hexagrams, the numbers governing their complementary opposition; and in the operation of nine as yang and six as yin, the numbers of the myriad things.

He therefore composed Ordering the World (Jingshi) to enlighten all under Heaven. What Diagram One Expounding the Changes describes as “that which lies between a movement and a stillness” is precisely what the Changes calls the Supreme Ultimate. What the Diagram of the Four Images of Heaven and Earth names as “greater yang, greater yin, lesser yang, lesser yin, lesser firmness, lesser yielding, greater firmness, and greater yielding” are precisely what the Changes calls the Four Images. What the Diagram of the Numbers of the Beginning and End of Heaven and Earth names as “epochs, conjunctions, cycles, generations, years, months, days, double-hours, water, fire, earth, and stone” corresponds to the sixty-four hexagrams of the Changes. What the Diagram of the Numbers of the Sixty-four Hexagrams describes as “one-one beginning in the south and eight-eight extending [?] in the north” is precisely the numerical scheme of the eight trigrams of the Changes. As for the Diagram of the Numbers of Waxing and Waning within One Epoch and the Diagram of the Numbers of the Substance and Function of the Four Images, how could these, too, be anything other than the numbers of the myriad things in the Changes? Thus, taking together…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
其書而論之其道一本於犧畫但其用字
立意自爲一家引經引義別爲一說若其
宗要則明道所謂加一倍法也是故由用
而之體則自一而二自二而四自四而八
自八而十六自十六而三十二自三十二
而六十四卽體而之用則自六十四而三
十二自三十二而十六自十六而八自八
而四自四而二自二而一一者太極也所
謂一動一靜之間也天奇地偶之畫陽九
===
陰六之數四千九十有六之變萬有一千
五百二十之策何以加于此哉是其作用
雖不同而實則伏犧所畫之卦也夫道生
天地而太極者道之全體也太極生兩儀
兩儀生四象四象生而後天地之道備焉
陰陽變于上而日月星辰生剛柔化于下
而水火土石成象動于上而萬時之消長
盈虛以變而起體交于下而萬物之動植
飛走以類而應然時之與物又皆有數以
punctuated:
其書而論之，其道一本於犧畫，但其用字立意，自爲一家；引經引義，別爲一說。若其宗要，則明道所謂加一倍法也。是故由用而之體，則自一而二，自二而四，自四而八，自八而十六，自十六而三十二，自三十二而六十四；卽體而之用，則自六十四而三十二，自三十二而十六，自十六而八，自八而四，自四而二，自二而一。一者，太極也，所謂一動一靜之間也。天奇地偶之畫，陽九陰六之數，四千九十有六之變，萬有一千五百二十之策，何以加于此哉？是其作用雖不同，而實則伏犧所畫之卦也。
夫道生天地，而太極者，道之全體也。太極生兩儀，兩儀生四象，四象生而後天地之道備焉。陰陽變于上，而日月星辰生；剛柔化于下，而水火土石成。象動于上，而萬時之消長盈虛以變而起；體交于下，而萬物之動植飛走以類而應。然時之與物，又皆有數以
translation_en:
…considering his book as a whole, its Way is rooted entirely in Fuxi’s drawn trigrams. Yet his wording and conception constitute a school of their own; his citations of the classics and their meanings form a distinct interpretation. As for its essential principle, it is what Mingdao called the method of doubling. Thus, proceeding from function to substance, one goes from one to two, from two to four, from four to eight, from eight to sixteen, from sixteen to thirty-two, and from thirty-two to sixty-four. Proceeding from substance to function, one goes from sixty-four to thirty-two, from thirty-two to sixteen, from sixteen to eight, from eight to four, from four to two, and from two to one. This one is the Supreme Ultimate, what is called the interval between movement and stillness. How could the lines representing Heaven’s oddness and Earth’s evenness, the numbers nine for yang and six for yin, the 4,096 transformations, or the 11,520 divining stalks add anything to this? Thus, although its workings differ, in substance these are the hexagrams drawn by Fuxi.
Now the Way generates Heaven and Earth, and the Supreme Ultimate is the complete substance of the Way. The Supreme Ultimate generates the Two Modes; the Two Modes generate the Four Images; and once the Four Images arise, the Way of Heaven and Earth is complete. Yin and yang change above, giving rise to the sun, moon, stars, and celestial markers; the hard and soft transform below, forming water, fire, soil, and stone. Images move above, and the waning and waxing, fullness and emptiness of all periods of time arise through change. Substances interact below, and the myriad things—moving and rooted, flying and running—respond according to their kinds. Yet both times and things also possess numbers by which…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
存乎其間數者何也道之運也理之會也
陰陽之度也萬物之紀也定於幽而驗於
明藏於微而顯於著原於一而行之以爲
萬窮天下之數而復歸於一推之於天地
而後萬物之理昭焉於陰陽而後萬
物之數覩焉故其書以日月星辰水火土
石盡天地之體用以暑寒晝夜雨風露雷
盡天地之變化以性情形體走飛草木盡
萬物之感應以元會運世歲月日辰盡天
===
地之終始以皇帝王伯易書詩春秋盡聖
賢之事業而陰陽之消長古今之治亂較
然可見矣噫天下之道至大也非伏犧氏
之畫易則道之體無以見故卦成而斯道
之明方如日之中天有以啓萬古之蒙瞶
而體盡之矣天下之道至精也非邵氏之
經世則道之用無以達故數成而斯道之
行方如水之行地有以開萬古之否塞而
用盡之矣彼所謂易主卜筮經世主推步
punctuated:
存乎其間。數者何也？道之運也，理之會也，陰陽之度也，萬物之紀也。定於幽而驗於明，藏於微而顯於著，原於一而行之以爲萬，窮天下之數而復歸於一。推之於天地而後萬物之理昭焉，於陰陽而後萬物之數覩焉。故其書以日月星辰、水火土石盡天地之體用，以暑寒晝夜、雨風露雷盡天地之變化，以性情形體、走飛草木盡萬物之感應，以元會運世、歲月日辰盡天地之終始，以皇帝王伯、《易》《書》《詩》《春秋》盡聖賢之事業，而陰陽之消長、古今之治亂較然可見矣。

噫！天下之道至大也，非伏犧氏之畫《易》，則道之體無以見。故卦成而斯道之明，方如日之中天，有以啓萬古之蒙瞶，而體盡之矣。天下之道至精也，非邵氏之《經世》，則道之用無以達。故數成而斯道之行，方如水之行地，有以開萬古之否塞，而用盡之矣。彼所謂《易》主卜筮，《經世》主推步
translation_en:
…exist within them. What are numbers? They are the operation of the Way, the convergence of principles, the measures of yin and yang, and the ordering framework of the myriad things. They are determined in obscurity and verified in the light, concealed in the subtle and revealed in the manifest. They originate in the One and unfold into the myriad; exhaust all numbers under Heaven, and they return again to the One. Extend them to Heaven and Earth, and the principles of the myriad things become clear; extend them to yin and yang, and the numbers of the myriad things become visible. Thus his book uses the sun, moon, stars, and celestial stations, together with water, fire, earth, and stone, to encompass the substance and functioning of Heaven and Earth. It uses heat, cold, day, and night, together with rain, wind, dew, and thunder, to encompass their transformations. It uses nature, feelings, form, and body, together with running creatures, flying creatures, grasses, and trees, to encompass the mutual stimulation and response of the myriad things. It uses epochs, assemblies, cycles, and generations (yuan, hui, yun, shi), together with years, months, days, and double hours, to encompass the endings and beginnings of Heaven and Earth. It uses the August Ones, thearchs, kings, and hegemons, together with the Changes, Documents, Odes, and Spring and Autumn Annals, to encompass the undertakings of sages and worthies. Thus the waxing and waning of yin and yang, and order and disorder in antiquity and the present, can be clearly seen.

Ah! The Way of all under Heaven is supremely great. Without Fuxi’s drawing of the figures of the Changes, the substance of the Way could not have been revealed. Thus, once the hexagrams were completed, the illumination of this Way was like the sun at the zenith: it could dispel the ignorance and blindness of all ages, fully revealing its substance. The Way of all under Heaven is supremely subtle. Without Master Shao’s Ordering the World (Jingshi), the functioning of the Way could not have been fully expressed. Thus, once his numerical system was completed, the operation of this Way was like water flowing across the earth: it could clear the obstructions of all ages, fully expressing its functioning. As for the assertion that the Changes is chiefly concerned with divination and Ordering the World chiefly with calendrical and astronomical calculation…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
者則其形迹之似耳而非邵子用易之本
旨也若夫楊氏之太玄八十一首關氏之
洞極二十七象司馬氏之潜虛五十五行
皆不知而作者也而又何足以語易哉雖
然聖人以天地爲一體以萬物爲一身善
救而不棄曲成而不遺然後可以成能其
中故時不能以違天物不能以違時聖人
不能以違物時不違天故天運而必變物
不違時故時變而必化聖人不能違物故
===
物化而必順天之時由人之事乎人之事
由天之時乎興事而應時者其惟人乎故
聖人者雖因數以察時而亦必興事以合
天天苟不違而况於人乎况於鬼神乎是
易之數雖寓於事物而易之理則具之人
心故曰復其見天地之心乎又曰以此洗
心退藏于密善學易者能于吾心而求之
則天地之道萬物之理固自有機之不可
遏者矣觀康節之詩曰思慮未起鬼神莫
punctuated:
者，則其形迹之似耳，而非邵子用易之本旨也。若夫楊氏之太玄八十一首、關氏之洞極二十七象、司馬氏之潜虛五十五行，皆不知而作者也，而又何足以語易哉？

雖然，聖人以天地爲一體，以萬物爲一身，善救而不棄，曲成而不遺，然後可以成能其中。故時不能以違天，物不能以違時，聖人不能以違物。時不違天，故天運而必變；物不違時，故時變而必化；聖人不能違物，故物化而必順。天之時由人之事乎？人之事由天之時乎？興事而應時者，其惟人乎？故聖人者，雖因數以察時，而亦必興事以合天。天苟不違，而况於人乎？况於鬼神乎？是易之數雖寓於事物，而易之理則具之人心。故曰：「復，其見天地之心乎？」又曰：「以此洗心，退藏于密。」善學易者，能于吾心而求之，則天地之道、萬物之理，固自有機之不可遏者矣。觀康節之詩曰：「思慮未起，鬼神莫
translation_en:
…such claims concern only their apparent similarity in outward form; they do not express Master Shao’s fundamental purpose in using the Changes. As for the eighty-one heads of Master Yang’s Supreme Mystery (Taixuan), the twenty-seven images of Master Guan’s Penetrating the Ultimate (Dongji), and the fifty-five forms of Master Sima’s Fathoming the Void (Qianxu), these are all works composed without understanding. How, then, could they suffice for discussing the Changes?

Nevertheless, the sage regards Heaven and Earth as one body, and the myriad things as one person. He is skilled at saving and abandons nothing; he brings things to fulfillment in all their particular circumstances and overlooks nothing. Only then can he accomplish his work among them. Thus the seasons cannot depart from Heaven, things cannot depart from the seasons, and the sage cannot depart from things. Since the seasons do not depart from Heaven, they necessarily change as Heaven moves; since things do not depart from the seasons, they necessarily transform as the seasons change; since the sage cannot depart from things, he must follow their transformations. Do Heaven’s seasons depend upon human affairs? Or do human affairs depend upon Heaven’s seasons? Is it not human beings alone who undertake affairs in response to the times? Thus, although the sage examines the times through numbers, he must also undertake affairs in accord with Heaven. If even Heaven does not oppose him, how much less will human beings, or ghosts and spirits?

Thus, although the numbers of the Changes reside in affairs and things, its principles are fully present in the human heart. Hence it says: “Return: do we not see here the heart of Heaven and Earth?” It also says: “With this, they cleanse their hearts and withdraw into secrecy.” If those skilled in studying the Changes can seek it within their own hearts, then the Way of Heaven and Earth and the principles of the myriad things surely possess an incipient impulse that cannot be restrained. Consider the poem by Kangjie, which says: “Before thoughts arise, ghosts and spirits cannot …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
知不由乎我更由乎誰此非心學之要乎
又曰心無妄思足無妄走人無妄交物無
妄受此非無妄之道乎噫安得康節之學
而與之論易謹對

李滚寛

教也爲甚大由孔子興觀羣怨之旨則知
詩之切於日用也爲甚詳然有本焉不可
以襲取也然有辭焉不可以淫比也然有

李滚寛

…know. If it does not depend on me, on whom else does it depend?” Is this not the essential point of learning directed toward the mind? He also says: “Let the mind entertain no wayward thoughts; let the feet take no wayward steps; form no improper associations with others; accept no things improperly.” Is this not the Way of Freedom from Falsehood? Li Gunkuan 李滚寛
Associate Examiner Fan, Instructor, comments: 〔Judging from your discussion of the Odes, you must be someone who has studied the “Zhou Nan” and “Shao Nan,” using your own understanding to apprehend the poets’ intentions and gaining insight thereby.〕

Examiner Mao, School Instructor, comments: 〔To treat poetry as mere literary embellishment is an error of its latter-day decline [?]. If you can seek it in intention and inspiration, are you not skilled at returning to its source?〕

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
不可以弱滯也然有體焉不可以類拘也
然有意焉不可以實泥也詩之義大矣哉
是故仁義中正其本也溫厚和平其辭也
閎深雅淡其思也情會神應其興也宮商
相宜其聲也高朗暢達其調也感發懲創
其體也言近旨遠其意也詩亡久矣果能
此焉雖未敢自附於聖人刪述之後而於
春秋數子或可庶幾矣乎不然强排以為
工牽合以為奇本體不識意興俱亡而曰
===
我能賦我能賦謂之曰刪後無詩也不其
然乎道以器離音與心異其與陽刺而漢
無所聞顯頌而漫不知荅相去也何遠哉
執事下策承學而以詩為問且有取春秋
之人蓋亦憫大雅不作而叔季猶存而以
遺音絕倡復望於今日也誦毛萇之傳徒
得其言檢元凱之編未究其旨誠何足以
知之請以所聞為明問復可乎嘗讀三百
篇之序說而知詩之所由作矣書曰詩言
punctuated:
不可以弱滯也。然有體焉，不可以類拘也；然有意焉，不可以實泥也。詩之義大矣哉！是故仁義中正，其本也；溫厚和平，其辭也；閎深雅淡，其思也；情會神應，其興也；宮商相宜，其聲也；高朗暢達，其調也；感發懲創，其體也；言近旨遠，其意也。詩亡久矣！果能此焉，雖未敢自附於聖人刪述之後，而於春秋數子，或可庶幾矣乎！不然，强排以為工，牽合以為奇，本體不識，意興俱亡，而曰：「我能賦！我能賦！」謂之曰「刪後無詩」也，不其然乎？道以器離，音與心異，其與陽刺而漢無所聞，顯頌而漫不知荅，相去也何遠哉？
執事下策，承學而以詩為問，且有取春秋之人，蓋亦憫大雅不作而叔季猶存，而以遺音絕倡復望於今日也。誦毛萇之傳，徒得其言；檢元凱之編，未究其旨，誠何足以知之？請以所聞為明問復，可乎？嘗讀三百篇之序說，而知詩之所由作矣。《書》曰：「詩言
translation_en:
…it must not be feeble or stagnant. Poetry also has its forms, which must not be confined by categories; it has its meaning, which must not be bound to literal particulars. How great is the significance of poetry! Thus benevolence, righteousness, centrality, and correctness constitute its foundation; gentleness, generosity, peace, and harmony characterize its diction; breadth, depth, refinement, and simplicity characterize its thought. The meeting of feelings and the response of the spirit constitute its evocative impulse; the fitting coordination of gong and shang notes constitutes its sound; loftiness, clarity, fluency, and freedom characterize its cadence. Stirring the feelings and chastening faults constitute its essential character; accessible words with far-reaching implications constitute its meaning. Poetry has long been lost! If one could truly achieve these things, although one would not presume to place oneself in the succession following the Sage’s editing and transmission, one might perhaps approach the achievement of those few masters of the Spring and Autumn period. Otherwise, if one takes forced arrangement for craftsmanship and strained connections for originality, without recognizing poetry’s fundamental character, with meaning and evocative impulse alike lost, yet declares, “I can compose! I can compose!”—would it not indeed be fitting to say of this, “After the Sage’s editing, there is no poetry”? When the Way becomes divorced from its vehicle, and sound differs from what is in the heart, how far is this from openly voiced criticism that goes entirely unheard, or manifest praise to which one heedlessly knows no reply [?]?
You, sir, have issued a policy question to those pursuing learning, asking about poetry and drawing upon people of the Spring and Autumn period. Presumably you too lament that the great odes are no longer composed, while the habits of a declining age persist, and hope that today the surviving strains and interrupted song may be renewed. If, in reciting Mao Chang’s Commentary, one gains only its words, and, in examining Yuan Kai’s compilation, one has not fathomed its meaning, how could this truly suffice to understand poetry? May I offer what I have learned in response to your illuminating question? I have read the prefaces and explanations of the Three Hundred Poems and thereby learned how poetry came to be composed.
