title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
志歌永言聲依永律和聲論樂者祖焉而
詩則其章矣此詩之始也三代治化之隆
功德之盛有所製作頌以登于清廟雅以
奏于朝廷皆達關雎麟趾之意而音響節
奏出焉是以皆可被之管弦格之上下至
於列國之詩亦陳之巡狩之日以觀政化
而行夫黜陟之典以示勸懲此詩之敎也
夫何東遷以還天子之尊下同列國黍離
之什降爲國風而時事可知矣故曰詩亡
===
然後春秋作雖然非詩之亡也雅亡也至
於風也者下里曲巷婦人女子情感意會
短歌長謠往往達意興而中音節亦足以
感人而動物豈唯三代之時敎化素洽之
所易能情同心同直道而行雖至今猶有
存者知者于詩亡而求之野焉亦思過半
矣而風豈俱亡哉刪後無詩之言豈亦獨
見于雅歟若夫端本正辭蘊思達興審聲
諧調比體逆意以復古雅以備今樂遠以
punctuated: 志，歌永言，聲依永，律和聲。」論樂者祖焉，而詩則其章矣。此詩之始也。三代治化之隆，功德之盛，有所製作，頌以登于清廟，雅以奏于朝廷，皆達關雎、麟趾之意，而音響節奏出焉。是以皆可被之管弦，格之上下。至於列國之詩，亦陳之巡狩之日，以觀政化，而行夫黜陟之典，以示勸懲。此詩之敎也。夫何東遷以還，天子之尊，下同列國，《黍離》之什降爲國風，而時事可知矣。故曰：「詩亡，然後春秋作。」雖然，非詩之亡也，雅亡也。至於風也者，下里曲巷，婦人女子，情感意會，短歌長謠，往往達意興而中音節，亦足以感人而動物。豈唯三代之時敎化素洽之所易能？情同心同，直道而行，雖至今猶有存者。知者于詩亡而求之野焉，亦思過半矣，而風豈俱亡哉？刪後無詩之言，豈亦獨見于雅歟？若夫端本正辭，蘊思達興，審聲諧調，比體逆意，以復古雅，以備今樂，遠以
translation_en:
…the intent; song prolongs the words; musical sounds follow that prolongation; the pitch standards harmonize the sounds.” Those who discuss music take this as their foundation, while poetry constitutes its articulated text. This is the origin of poetry. At the height of good government and moral transformation under the Three Dynasties, when achievements and virtue flourished, compositions were made: the Eulogies were presented in the Pure Temple, and the Elegantiae performed at court. All conveyed the meaning of “The Ospreys Cry” (Guanju) and “The Qilin’s Feet” (Linzhi), from which their sounds and rhythms emerged. Thus all could be set to pipes and strings and reach those above and below. As for the poems of the various states, these too were presented during royal inspection tours, so that government and moral transformation could be observed and the prescribed demotions and promotions carried out, thereby giving encouragement and warning. This was the instructive function of poetry.

Yet how was it that, after the eastward migration, the exalted Son of Heaven sank to the same standing as the rulers of the various states, and the poems of the “Millet Droops” (Shuli) group were relegated to the Airs of the States? From this one can understand the circumstances of the age. Hence the saying: “Only after poetry had vanished were the Spring and Autumn Annals composed.” Nevertheless, it was not poetry that vanished; it was the Elegantiae. As for the Airs, in humble villages and winding lanes, women and girls, moved by feeling and stirred in thought, would sing short songs and long ballads. These often expressed their thoughts and inspirations while fitting musical rhythms, and were sufficient to move people and affect other beings. Was this something readily accomplished only in the Three Dynasties, when moral instruction had long permeated society? People share the same feelings and hearts, and proceed along the straightforward Way; even today, examples of this still survive. Those who understand, seeking poetry among the common people after its disappearance, have already grasped the greater part of the matter. How, then, could the Airs all have vanished? Might the assertion that there was no poetry after the editorial selection likewise refer solely to the Elegantiae?

As for setting the foundation aright and rectifying the diction, nurturing thought and expressing inspiration, examining sounds and harmonizing melodies, comparing forms and tracing the intended meaning, so as to restore the ancient Elegantiae and furnish the music of the present, reaching back into the distant past to…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
追二帝三王之隆近以宣
聖文神武之化政同敎同涵育有得于古也又
奚難焉使樂正雅頌各得其所亦存乎其
人已矣考之孔子所刪三百篇之詩乃商
周祭祀燕享及房中所歌者其篇章宛然
三代之舊也雖取之以寓勸懲其所逸亦
多矣豈皆于善惡無所感創哉要之音節
或于律呂弗協故刪而去之孔子大聖固
不煩師承音譜相傳不可謂初無有也大
===
戴禮云凡雅二十六篇其八篇可歌晉志
亦云漢末杜夔傳舊雅樂有鹿鳴騶虞伐
檀文王四曲皆古聲辭其後改作新聲舊
曲遂廢至唐開元鄉飲酒禮其所奏樂乃
有鹿鳴四牡皇華嘉魚南山魚麗關雎葛
覃卷耳鵲巢采蘩采蘋一十二篇而聲已
不可得聞宋趙彥肅傳此十二詩之譜叶
諸律呂爲開元遺聲朱子疑古樂滅亡已
久工師何所考知不謂其然蓋亦史闕文
punctuated: 追二帝三王之隆，近以宣聖文神武之化，政同敎同，涵育有得于古也，又奚難焉？使樂正，雅頌各得其所，亦存乎其人已矣。考之孔子所刪三百篇之詩，乃商周祭祀、燕享及房中所歌者，其篇章宛然三代之舊也。雖取之以寓勸懲，其所逸亦多矣，豈皆于善惡無所感創哉？要之，音節或于律呂弗協，故刪而去之。孔子大聖，固不煩師承，音譜相傳，不可謂初無有也。《大戴禮》云：「凡雅二十六篇，其八篇可歌。」《晉志》亦云：「漢末杜夔傳舊雅樂，有《鹿鳴》《騶虞》《伐檀》《文王》四曲，皆古聲辭。」其後改作新聲，舊曲遂廢。至唐開元鄉飲酒禮，其所奏樂乃有《鹿鳴》《四牡》《皇華》《嘉魚》《南山》《魚麗》《關雎》《葛覃》《卷耳》《鵲巢》《采蘩》《采蘋》一十二篇，而聲已不可得聞。宋趙彥肅傳此十二詩之譜，叶諸律呂，爲開元遺聲。朱子疑古樂滅亡已久，工師何所考知，不謂其然，蓋亦史闕文
translation_en:
…to emulate, in the distant past, the flourishing age of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, and, nearer at hand, to spread the transforming influence of our sage ruler’s civil virtue and divine martial prowess. With government and instruction alike matching those of antiquity, what difficulty would there be in nurturing the people with something of the success achieved in ancient times? To set music right and give the Court Hymns and Temple Hymns their proper places likewise depends only upon finding the right person.

Examining the three hundred poems as edited by Confucius, we find that they were songs used for sacrifices, banquets, and performances within the inner chambers under the Shang and Zhou. Their texts clearly preserve the old forms of the Three Dynasties. Although he selected poems to convey encouragement and admonition, many were omitted. Could all of these have lacked the power to move people toward goodness or warn them against evil? In essence, some of their musical rhythms may not have accorded with the pitch standards, and so he deleted them. Confucius, as a great sage, certainly had no need to trouble himself with instruction from a teacher; nevertheless, one cannot say that musical notation had never previously been transmitted.

The Elder Dai’s Record of Rites states: “There are twenty-six Court Hymns in all, eight of which can be sung.” The Treatise in the History of the Jin also states: “At the end of the Han, Du Kui transmitted the old ceremonial music. There were four pieces—‘The Deer Call,’ ‘The Zouyu,’ ‘Felling Sandalwood,’ and ‘King Wen’—all with ancient melodies and words.” Subsequently, new melodies were composed, and the old pieces fell out of use. By the Kaiyuan era of the Tang, the music performed at the district drinking ceremony included twelve poems: ‘The Deer Call’ (Luming), ‘Four Stallions’ (Si mu), ‘Splendid Flowers’ (Huang hua), ‘Fine Fish’ (Jia yu), ‘South Mountain’ (Nanshan), ‘Fish in the Wicker Trap’ (Yu li), ‘The Ospreys Cry’ (Guan ju), ‘Spreading Kudzu’ (Ge tan), ‘Cocklebur’ (Juan er), ‘The Magpie’s Nest’ (Que chao), ‘Gathering White Southernwood’ (Cai fan), and ‘Gathering Duckweed’ (Cai pin). Yet their melodies can no longer be heard.

Zhao Yansu of the Song transmitted musical notation for these twelve poems, harmonizing them with the pitch standards and presenting them as surviving melodies from the Kaiyuan era. Master Zhu doubted this: ancient music had long since disappeared, so on what evidence could the music masters have ascertained it? He did not accept the claim as true. This, too, presumably reflected the principle that a historian leaves gaps in the text…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
之遺意也程子謂詩如今之歌曲古詩音
調不可復見今之歌曲雖出時人之口而
亦有所沿襲如向所謂十二詩鹿鳴等六
篇詩云黃鍾清宮俗呼正宮關雎等六篇
詩云無射清商俗呼云越調雖名目不同
誠因今而求之古循俗而入于雅因聲以
考律正律以定器古樂或可復見矣亦可
謂達于樂之變者也則音譜之亡也雖非
一日要之後世失之是故時至春秋去古
===
未遠音譜似有可傳不然則列國君臣雖
交相雄長或講信脩睦于兩國之交或陳
師請盟于時見之會于是乎饗宴以成禮
肆樂以盡文陳詞以達意荅賦以敘情猶
知有取于章句而未肯視爲糟粕也不獨
魯衛晉鄭風流文雅萃于一時六月之雅
反出于西鄙之秦大明之詩載歌于南荆
之楚不可槩見乎以至齊之公族如慶封
弗虔于飲食之節而甘受相鼠之譏宋世
punctuated: 之遺意也。程子謂：「詩如今之歌曲，古詩音調不可復見。」今之歌曲雖出時人之口，而亦有所沿襲。如向所謂十二詩，鹿鳴等六篇，詩云黃鍾清宮，俗呼正宮；關雎等六篇，詩云無射清商，俗呼云越調。雖名目不同，誠因今而求之古，循俗而入于雅，因聲以考律，正律以定器，古樂或可復見矣。亦可謂達于樂之變者也。則音譜之亡也，雖非一日，要之後世失之。是故時至春秋，去古未遠，音譜似有可傳。不然，則列國君臣雖交相雄長，或講信脩睦于兩國之交，或陳師請盟于時見之會，于是乎饗宴以成禮，肆樂以盡文，陳詞以達意，荅賦以敘情，猶知有取于章句，而未肯視爲糟粕也。不獨魯衛晉鄭，風流文雅萃于一時，六月之雅反出于西鄙之秦，大明之詩載歌于南荆之楚，不可槩見乎？以至齊之公族如慶封，弗虔于飲食之節，而甘受相鼠之譏，宋世
translation_en:
…a surviving trace of that intention. Master Cheng said: “The Odes were like songs today; the melodies of the ancient Odes can no longer be recovered.” Although today’s songs come from the mouths of our contemporaries, they too inherit something from the past. Of the twelve odes mentioned above, the six beginning with “The Deer Call” are described as being in the clear gong mode of Huangzhong [?], commonly called zhenggong; the six beginning with “The Ospreys Cry” are described as being in the clear shang mode of Wuyi [?], commonly called yuediao. Although the names differ, if we truly seek the ancient through the present, proceed from popular music to refined music, examine the pitch standards through the sounds, and rectify those standards to tune the instruments, ancient music might yet be recovered. This too may be called understanding the transformations of music. Thus, although the loss of musical notation did not happen in a single day, it was, in the end, later generations that lost it.

By the Spring and Autumn period, antiquity was still not far distant, and musical notation seemingly remained available for transmission. Otherwise, although the rulers and ministers of the various states competed for supremacy, when they cultivated trust and friendly relations in dealings between two states, or arrayed their armies and sought covenants at meetings of rulers, how could they have held feasts to fulfill ritual, performed music to complete its ceremonial adornment, presented verses to convey their intentions, and recited answering odes to express their feelings? They still understood that the stanzas and lines had something to offer and were unwilling to regard them as mere dregs. Nor was it only in Lu, Wei, Jin, and Zheng that cultivated elegance flourished together in that age: the court hymn “The Sixth Month” was actually performed in Qin on the western frontier, and the ode “Great Brightness” was sung in Chu in the southern Jing region. Can we not discern the general picture from this? Even among the ruling lineage of Qi, someone such as Qing Feng, who failed to observe proper decorum at a feast, willingly exposed himself to the rebuke of “Look at the Rat”; and among the hereditary houses of Song…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
家如華定徙取遄亡之輕而弗知蓼蕭之
賦則又學與不學爾矣其曰它不暇論無
亦謂誠晉人也知晉之卿大夫已乎景仰
之餘亦嘗究心矣若子餘之於秦伯賦黍
苗釆菽之互荅也而使公子降拜受之晉
文之佐天子匡王國爲之兆矣不亦善乎
若叔向之於衛侯以齊侯鄭伯之求釋也
而告趙武請而許之盟主之宣明德正違
闕庶乎可矣抑豈私乎以至蘧罷楚之良
===
也如晉涖盟拜晉侯之享而賦旣醉皺以
事君必能養民叔向以是知蘧氏之得政
于楚也噫可以觀蘧罷矣非叔向其誰知
之亦可以觀叔向矣韓宣子晉之選也歷
聘侯國見易象春秋歎周禮盡在魯如齊
聘衛不辱君命君子以是知韓氏之有利
于晉也噫可以觀宣子矣而晉實有之亦
可以觀晉矣豈唯是也其它如趙武子觀
志于七子賦詩垂隴之地韓宣子獻馬丁
punctuated: 家如華定，徙取遄亡之輕，而弗知《蓼蕭》之賦，則又學與不學爾矣。其曰「它不暇論」，無亦謂誠晉人也，知晉之卿大夫已乎？景仰之餘，亦嘗究心矣。若子餘之於秦伯，賦《黍苗》《釆菽》之互荅也，而使公子降拜受之，晉文之佐天子、匡王國，爲之兆矣，不亦善乎？若叔向之於衛侯，以齊侯、鄭伯之求釋也，而告趙武，請而許之，盟主之宣明德、正違闕，庶乎可矣，抑豈私乎？以至蘧罷，楚之良也，如晉涖盟，拜晉侯之享，而賦《旣醉》，皺以事君，必能養民。叔向以是知蘧氏之得政于楚也。噫！可以觀蘧罷矣，非叔向，其誰知之？亦可以觀叔向矣。韓宣子，晉之選也，歷聘侯國，見《易象》《春秋》，歎周禮盡在魯。如齊，聘衛，不辱君命，君子以是知韓氏之有利于晉也。噫！可以觀宣子矣，而晉實有之，亦可以觀晉矣。豈唯是也？其它如趙武子觀志于七子賦詩，垂隴之地，韓宣子獻馬丁
translation_en:
…among the hereditary houses of Song, someone such as Hua Ding merely incurred the contempt expressed in the words “swiftly perish,” yet failed to understand the recitation of Luxuriant Southernwood (Liao xiao). Here again, the difference lay simply in having studied or not having studied. As for the statement, “There is no leisure to discuss the others,” might this mean that, being himself a man of Jin, he knew only Jin’s ministers and grandees? Beyond admiring them, I have also tried to examine the matter closely.

Consider Ziyu’s dealings with the Earl of Qin: when Millet Seedlings (Shu miao) and Gathering Beans (Cai shu) were recited in exchange, he had the ducal son descend the steps and bow to acknowledge the honor. This foreshadowed Duke Wen of Jin’s assistance to the Son of Heaven and his support of the royal realm. Was this not admirable? Consider also Shuxiang’s dealings concerning the Marquis of Wei: when the Marquis of Qi and the Earl of Zheng sought his release, Shuxiang informed Zhao Wu, who petitioned for it and obtained consent. This came close to what was required of the leader of the covenant: to manifest illustrious virtue and rectify transgressions and shortcomings. How could it have been merely a private favor?

Then there was Qu Ba [?], a worthy man of Chu. He went to Jin to attend a covenant ceremony and, in acknowledgment of the banquet given by the Marquis of Jin, recited Already Drunk (Ji zui). [The following character is doubtful.] In serving his ruler, he would surely be capable of nurturing the people. From this Shuxiang knew that the Qu lineage [?] would obtain governing authority in Chu. Ah! This allows us to assess Qu Ba; without Shuxiang, who would have recognized his worth? It also allows us to assess Shuxiang.

Han Xuanzi was an outstanding man of Jin. Traveling on diplomatic missions through the feudal states, he saw the Images of the Changes (Yi xiang) and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), and exclaimed that the rites of Zhou were all preserved in Lu. He went to Qi and undertook a mission to Wei, bringing no disgrace upon his ruler’s commission. From this, gentlemen knew that the Han lineage would benefit Jin. Ah! This allows us to assess Xuanzi; and since Jin actually possessed such a man, it also allows us to assess Jin.

Nor were these the only instances. There were others, such as Zhao Wuzi discerning the aspirations of seven gentlemen through their recitations of poems at Chuilong, and Han Xuanzi presenting horses [the final character is doubtful]…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
六卿載荅我將之詩又皆不能以悉舉者
也凡若此者雖皆假託一時一事之偶合
以濟其權變之私援引一字一句之強同
以售其敏捷之技固于雅言大旨槩乎未
聞先王言志觀風之義猶有不盡泯者殊
未可以大經大法責備于叔季之人才而
盡少之也何如慶華之多見于後世也哉
嗚呼先王之詩昔以導情也而今以寓言
昔以垂教也而今以取證昔以觀俗也而
===
今以禦辯要之音譜無正傳而葩藻有餘
思此春秋所以止於春秋而成周之盛無
復可想見也後之言詩者亦當知所考矣
朱子不云乎本之二南以求其端參之列
國以盡其變正之於雅以大其規和之於
頌以要其止且又不剖析於章句也而涵
濡其大綱不剽竊於近似也而融會其總
旨由是性情以之而正風俗以之而同脩
齊治平之道以之而次第可舉尚何遺音
punctuated:
六卿載荅《我將》之詩，又皆不能以悉舉者也。凡若此者，雖皆假託一時一事之偶合，以濟其權變之私；援引一字一句之強同，以售其敏捷之技，固于雅言大旨槩乎未聞，先王言志觀風之義猶有不盡泯者。殊未可以大經大法責備于叔季之人才，而盡少之也。何如慶華之多見于後世也哉！
嗚呼！先王之詩，昔以導情也，而今以寓言；昔以垂教也，而今以取證；昔以觀俗也，而今以禦辯。要之，音譜無正傳，而葩藻有餘思。此春秋所以止於春秋，而成周之盛無復可想見也。後之言詩者亦當知所考矣。朱子不云乎：「本之二南以求其端，參之列國以盡其變，正之於雅以大其規，和之於頌以要其止。」且又不剖析於章句也，而涵濡其大綱；不剽竊於近似也，而融會其總旨。由是性情以之而正，風俗以之而同，脩齊治平之道以之而次第可舉，尚何遺音
translation_en:
…the six ministers in turn replied with the ode “I Shall” (Wo jiang); these, too, are more examples than can be fully enumerated. In all such cases, they borrowed a chance correspondence with a particular occasion or event to serve their private purposes through expedient maneuvering, and cited forced similarities in a word or phrase to display their quick-witted skill. Granted, they had scarcely heard of the broad purport of these canonical utterances; nevertheless, the former kings’ purpose of expressing aspirations and observing local customs had not entirely vanished. We certainly cannot demand that the talented men of a declining age measure up in every respect to the great constant principles and rules, and disparage them all. How much better were they than the likes of Qing and Hua [?], so often seen in later ages!
Alas! The former kings’ Odes once guided the feelings, but now serve to convey indirect messages; once handed down instruction, but now furnish supporting evidence; once revealed customs, but now serve to parry arguments. In sum, their musical notation has no authentic transmission, while their splendid language offers lingering scope for reflection. This is why the Spring and Autumn age remained merely the Spring and Autumn age, and the flourishing of Chengzhou could no longer be envisioned. Those who discuss the Odes in later times should also know what to examine. Did Master Zhu not say: “Take the Two Southern Sections as the foundation to seek their beginnings; compare the Airs of the several states to comprehend their variations; set them right through the Elegantiae to broaden their scope; harmonize them through the Hymns to grasp their ultimate end”? Moreover, rather than merely dissecting chapters and phrases, one should steep oneself in their broad principles; rather than appropriating superficially similar expressions, one should comprehend their overall purport as a coherent whole. Through this, dispositions and feelings can be rectified, customs brought into accord, and the Way of cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world put into practice step by step. What then of the surviving strains…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
絕倡不見於今日之足患哉惟執事進而
教之
第五問
楊紹先
同考試官教授徐　批〔時務文字不在富麗秖是有益於時政便是𣪚陳家數此作得之〕
考試官教諭林　批〔今日兵食之弊正救之術條陳已悉矛其究心於時事者足驗有用之學〕
考試官學正毛　批〔議論切實有侃侃之風〕
===
安天下之勢者政也宜天下之時者通也
上下軍民之謂勢羸絀豐儉之謂時勢以
分安匪政曷以事以時宜匪通曷以是故
錢穀甲兵歸乎政也斟酌盈縮本乎通也
政行而分定則上食於下下食乎上民給
乎軍軍衛乎民錢穀甲兵通乎萬世然時
有盈虛財有豐約力有盛衰事或出於政
條畫一之外政或敝於臣工因循之久通
變以宜時所以濟乎其政也且㤗分之與
punctuated:
絕倡不見於今日之足患哉？惟執事進而教之。

第五問
楊紹先
同考試官教授徐　批〔時務文字不在富麗，秖是有益於時政，便是𣪚陳家數，此作得之。〕
考試官教諭林　批〔今日兵食之弊，正救之術，條陳已悉，矛其究心於時事者，足驗有用之學。〕
考試官學正毛　批〔議論切實，有侃侃之風。〕

安天下之勢者，政也；宜天下之時者，通也。上下軍民之謂勢，羸絀豐儉之謂時。勢以分安，匪政曷以？事以時宜，匪通曷以？是故錢穀甲兵歸乎政也，斟酌盈縮本乎通也。政行而分定，則上食於下，下食乎上，民給乎軍，軍衛乎民，錢穀甲兵通乎萬世。然時有盈虛，財有豐約，力有盛衰，事或出於政條畫一之外，政或敝於臣工因循之久。通變以宜時，所以濟乎其政也。且㤗分之與
translation_en:
…why, then, should it be cause for concern that the surviving strains and peerless songs are not heard today? I ask you, honored examiners, to offer further instruction.

Fifth Question
Yang Shaoxian
Associate Examiner Xu, Prefectural School Instructor, comments: 〔Writing on current affairs does not depend on richness and elegance. It need only benefit the government of the day: this is the manner of expository presentation [?], and this piece achieves it.〕
Examiner Lin, County School Instructor, comments: 〔The present abuses concerning military affairs and provisions, and the methods for correcting them, have all been set out fully. His close attention to current affairs [?] sufficiently demonstrates learning that can be put to use.〕
Examiner Mao, Departmental School Instructor, comments: 〔The arguments are pertinent and practical, with a forthright spirit.〕

What stabilizes the disposition of the realm is government; what accommodates the circumstances of the realm is adaptability. By “disposition” I mean superiors and inferiors, soldiers and civilians; by “circumstances” I mean weakness and shortage, abundance and scarcity. If the disposition of the realm is to be stabilized through proper distinctions of duty, how can this be done without government? If affairs are to be suited to their times, how can this be done without adaptability? Thus money, grain, arms, and troops fall within the province of government, while weighing surpluses against shortages rests upon adaptability. When government operates and duties are settled, those above are fed by those below, and those below are sustained by those above; civilians supply the soldiers, and soldiers protect the civilians. Money, grain, arms, and troops can thereby serve through all ages. Yet circumstances alternate between plenty and dearth, resources between abundance and scarcity, and strength between vigor and decline. Affairs may arise beyond the uniform provisions of governmental regulations, and government may deteriorate through officials’ prolonged adherence to routine. Adapting and changing to suit the times is therefore the means of sustaining government. Moreover, the great distinctions [?] and …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
政事非盡乎錢穀甲兵也而錢穀甲兵自
不能外也執事憂及二事策及山西承學
晉人也敢委之分外乎是故戎祀朝會百
官有司國資於錢穀舊矣自天官之法立
職貢賦式所以治小人養君子也西山之
民儉而能積絳翼之沃澤潞之饒西河之
殷盛天下稱其富也我
聖祖奄有海宇則壤成賦上給
宗藩次給軍伍百官之俸不及十一焉當時
===
官有餘財民有餘力真一方之財足供一
方之用也緊及今日百七十年矣地有定
畝賦有定數
宗枝日蕃祿加千倍宜病其不足矣獨怪夫
軍亡過半糧額猶前屯田之入冊籍徒存
天下根本非淺事也執事憂之無乃欲有
聞乎愚嘗熟察其故矣求用之裕究其耗
之端可也求財之充省其損之源可也傳
曰生之者衆食之者寡爲之者疾用之者
punctuated: 政事非盡乎錢穀甲兵也，而錢穀甲兵自不能外也。執事憂及二事，策及山西，承學晉人也，敢委之分外乎？是故戎祀朝會，百官有司，國資於錢穀舊矣。自天官之法立，職貢賦式，所以治小人、養君子也。西山之民儉而能積，絳翼之沃，澤潞之饒，西河之殷盛，天下稱其富也。我聖祖奄有海宇，則壤成賦，上給宗藩，次給軍伍，百官之俸不及十一焉。當時官有餘財，民有餘力，真一方之財足供一方之用也。緊及今日，百七十年矣。地有定畝，賦有定數，宗枝日蕃，祿加千倍，宜病其不足矣。獨怪夫軍亡過半，糧額猶前，屯田之入，冊籍徒存。天下根本，非淺事也。執事憂之，無乃欲有聞乎？愚嘗熟察其故矣。求用之裕，究其耗之端可也；求財之充，省其損之源可也。傳曰：「生之者衆，食之者寡，爲之者疾，用之者
translation_en: …government affairs do not consist entirely of money, grain, armor, and weapons; yet these certainly cannot be excluded. You, honored Examiner, express concern over these two matters, and your policy question addresses Shanxi. As a student and a native of Jin, dare I dismiss them as outside my responsibilities? Thus, for warfare, sacrifices, court audiences and assemblies, and the maintenance of officials and administrative offices, the state has long depended on money and grain. Since the establishment of the regulations of the Celestial Offices, the provisions for duties, tribute, taxation, and expenditure have served to govern the common people and support those who govern them. The people of Xishan are frugal and capable of accumulating reserves. The fertile lands of Jiang and Yi, the abundance of Ze and Lu, and the prosperity of Xihe are renowned throughout the realm for their wealth. When our sagely founding emperor took possession of all within the seas, he assessed the soil and established taxes, giving first priority to supporting the imperial princes and next to supporting the troops. The salaries of the civil officials accounted for less than one-tenth. At that time, the government had surplus resources and the people had strength to spare: truly, the wealth of a region sufficed to meet that region’s expenses. By the present day [?], one hundred and seventy years have passed. The acreage of the land is fixed, and the tax quotas are fixed, while the branches of the imperial clan multiply daily and their stipends have increased a thousandfold. It is understandable that insufficiency should now be a pressing problem. Yet it is puzzling that more than half the soldiers are missing while the grain quota remains unchanged, and that revenue from military agricultural colonies survives only as entries in the registers. These concern the foundations of the realm and are no trivial matters. In expressing concern over them, do you perhaps wish to hear an explanation? I have carefully examined their causes. To secure ample resources for expenditure, one should investigate how they are consumed; to ensure sufficient revenue, one should examine the sources of its depletion. The Commentary says: “Let those who produce it be many and those who consume it few; let those who make it be swift, and those who use it…”

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
舒方之今日豈一人之責乎蓋蠹財之端
在
宗室有四蝨財之本在軍民有三其在有司
軍衛有六焉何則蕃育滑於褻媵之雜進
應費糜於奢侈之敗度債負累於引誘之
徒過舉惑於投充之輩四者財之蠹也
宗室以之荒白幷没於豪隣侵欺僥倖於蠲
免逋欠抗違於强暴三者財之蝨也軍民
以之徵斂失於及時比併混於無等出納
===
苟於守藏踏荒白之不清覈蠲征之不切
追逋欠之無法屯租之弊循之民糧武官
不職甚於有司六者其官政之賸歟今日
之計不去四蠹財胡以節不治三蝨財胡
以充六賸不除如蠹蝨何哉是故媵妾之
數正則僞續清而不至冐其祿儉約之風
行則舉動中而不至濫其財法不廢於私
債祿可用於中槩例必行於撥置財可免
於滲卮如此可謂食之寡而用之舒矣多
punctuated:
舒。方之今日，豈一人之責乎？蓋蠹財之端，在宗室有四；蝨財之本，在軍民有三；其在有司軍衛，有六焉。何則？蕃育滑於褻媵之雜進，應費糜於奢侈之敗度，債負累於引誘之徒，過舉惑於投充之輩，四者財之蠹也，宗室以之。荒白幷没於豪隣，侵欺僥倖於蠲免，逋欠抗違於强暴，三者財之蝨也，軍民以之。徵斂失於及時，比併混於無等，出納苟於守藏，踏荒白之不清，覈蠲征之不切，追逋欠之無法，屯租之弊循之民糧，武官不職甚於有司，六者其官政之賸歟？
今日之計，不去四蠹，財胡以節？不治三蝨，財胡以充？六賸不除，如蠹蝨何哉？是故媵妾之數正，則僞續清而不至冐其祿；儉約之風行，則舉動中而不至濫其財；法不廢於私債，祿可用於中槩；例必行於撥置，財可免於滲卮。如此，可謂食之寡而用之舒矣。多
translation_en:
…slow in spending it. Compared with conditions today, can this be the responsibility of just one person? There are four sources of financial depletion among the imperial clan, three fundamental forms of financial parasitism among soldiers and civilians, and six abuses among the responsible civil authorities and military guards. Why is this? The multiplication of descendants becomes excessive through the indiscriminate admission of concubines; necessary expenditure is squandered through extravagance that breaches prescribed limits; debts accumulate through the activities of those who entice them into borrowing; and misconduct arises through the misleading influence of those who enter their service as dependents. These four things devour wealth, and the imperial clan is afflicted by them. Fallow and unregistered lands [?] are annexed and swallowed up by powerful neighbors; fraudulent appropriation exploits opportunities afforded by tax remissions; and arrears persist through the defiance of the strong and violent. These three things are parasites upon wealth, and soldiers and civilians are afflicted by them. Taxes are not collected at the proper time; comparative enforcement of payment [?] is confused by the absence of graded distinctions; receipts and disbursements are handled carelessly by treasury custodians; field inspections of fallow and unregistered lands [?] are inconclusive; scrutiny of remissions and assessments is inadequate; and recovery of arrears lacks proper methods. The abuses affecting military agricultural rents follow those affecting civilian grain taxes, while military officers neglect their duties even more than the civil authorities. Are these six things not excrescences upon official administration?
In planning for today, how can expenditure be restrained unless the four devourers are eliminated? How can revenues be made sufficient unless the three parasites are dealt with? If the six administrative excrescences remain, what can be done about the devourers and parasites? Thus, if the number of concubines is properly regulated, fraudulent claims to descent will be cleared away, preventing the illicit claiming of stipends. If habits of frugality prevail, conduct will observe due measure, preventing the reckless expenditure of wealth. If the law is not set aside on account of private debts, stipends can be used within proper limits [?]. If the regulations are invariably enforced against instigation and manipulation [?], wealth can be kept from draining away like liquid from a leaking vessel. Under such conditions, one could indeed say that those who consume are few and that spending is slow. More…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
訪知因以對老冊荒白之兼幷自明親給
糧由以嚴銷註蠲免之侵欺自著徵之及
時則民易完比併有等則人知勸出納清
弊則財不耗而荒白蠲征逋欠又特加之
意焉則生財節財我執其機如此可謂生
之衆而爲之疾矣夫區處之方曲盡無遺
然後覈逃亡之伍會出納之粟執其可質
較之將來果有羨餘裒多益寡或有未然
仍其舊貫則查解鹽之額扣其歲入之餘
===
復鹽法之初照行引開之地沮壞者有法
附餘者必盈雖不能盡足
宗室之祿雖不能通給歲歷之久較之往昔
其少舒乎此數者皆責之於下者也若夫
蠲免酌祿糧之應否災熟酌祿糧之損益
廟堂之議謂之如何或謂教之德藝應試入官
如唐宋之故事或謂給之公田制其穀祿
如功臣之田土或謂去冗員以移其祿或
謂遞減祿以寬其民或謂虛絕祀以存其
punctuated:
訪知因以對老冊，荒白之兼幷自明；親給糧由，以嚴銷註，蠲免之侵欺自著。徵之及時，則民易完；比併有等，則人知勸。出納清弊，則財不耗，而荒白、蠲征、逋欠，又特加之意焉，則生財節財，我執其機。如此，可謂生之衆而爲之疾矣。夫區處之方，曲盡無遺，然後覈逃亡之伍，會出納之粟，執其可質，較之將來。果有羨餘，裒多益寡；或有未然，仍其舊貫。則查解鹽之額，扣其歲入之餘，復鹽法之初，照行引開之地。沮壞者有法，附餘者必盈。雖不能盡足宗室之祿，雖不能通給歲歷之久，較之往昔，其少舒乎？
此數者，皆責之於下者也。若夫蠲免酌祿糧之應否，災熟酌祿糧之損益，廟堂之議謂之如何？或謂教之德藝，應試入官，如唐宋之故事；或謂給之公田，制其穀祿，如功臣之田土；或謂去冗員以移其祿；或謂遞減祿以寬其民；或謂虛絕祀以存其
translation_en:
…make inquiries into the circumstances and compare them with the old registers, and the engrossment of waste and unassessed land [?] will become clear of itself. Issue grain-tax notices personally and strictly control the cancellation of entries, and embezzlement and fraud involving tax remissions will reveal themselves. If collections are timely, the people can readily pay in full; if enforcement proceeds in graded steps [?], people will know to exert themselves. If abuses in receipts and disbursements are cleared away, resources will not be depleted. Give particular attention, moreover, to waste and unassessed land, tax remission and collection, and arrears: then the means of generating and conserving resources will be in our hands. This may be called having many who produce and working swiftly at production.
Once every detail of these arrangements has been fully addressed, investigate the household groups containing fugitives, audit grain receipts and disbursements, and retain verifiable figures for comparison in the future. If there truly is a surplus, take from abundance to supplement scarcity; if this has not been achieved, retain the established arrangements. Then examine the quota for salt from Jie, deduct the surplus from its annual receipts, restore the original salt regulations, and act according to the areas specified in the salt certificates [?]. Let there be legal sanctions for those who obstruct and undermine the system, and the supplementary surplus will surely be ample [?]. Although this may not fully meet the stipends of the imperial clan, and may not provide for all of them over many years, would it not afford some relief compared with the past?
These measures all place responsibility on those below. As for deciding whether stipend grain should be included in remissions, and adjusting its amount according to calamities or good harvests, what would the court’s deliberations propose? Some suggest teaching members of the imperial clan moral cultivation and practical accomplishments, allowing them to take examinations and enter office, following precedents of the Tang and Song. Others suggest granting them public fields and fixing their grain stipends, as with lands granted to meritorious officials. Some suggest eliminating superfluous officials and transferring their stipends; some suggest progressively reducing stipends to ease the burden on the people; some suggest leaving extinct sacrificial lines vacant in order to preserve their… [?]

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
祿均不得已之議也就中折之公田之給
不惟不能均其數抑且不能各如其便境
內冗官縣去一員歲俸不過數百僅一將
軍之祿耳況未可盡去耶世祿已定一旦
減祿非重祿同好之謂也何以服衆心乎
數者非宜時也執事爲萬世之慮志固遠
矣吾恐周官之財賦權不在玆乎爭始於
民之有欲兵興於訟之不終國資於甲兵
尚矣自司馬之法立六軍三軍二軍所以
警有衆待暴客也三晉之兵質而能勇晉
人用之以遏楚韓趙因之以抗秦李牧將
之以逐匈奴天下莫强焉我
聖祖俯察形勢建衛置兵外禦胡虜內備不虞
制於未亂保於未危也當時軍政嚴明將
士用命眞一方之兵足衛一方之民也太
平歷年百又七十矣前日之衛前日之兵
中土因循衰弱不振已可恥矣又重以邊
軍精鋭胡虜尚驕况兇狡不恭數年不靖
punctuated:
祿，均不得已之議也。就中折之，公田之給，不惟不能均其數，抑且不能各如其便。境內冗官，縣去一員，歲俸不過數百，僅一將軍之祿耳，況未可盡去耶？世祿已定，一旦減祿，非重祿同好之謂也，何以服衆心乎？數者非宜時也。執事爲萬世之慮，志固遠矣，吾恐周官之財賦權不在玆乎。
爭始於民之有欲，兵興於訟之不終，國資於甲兵尚矣。自司馬之法立，六軍、三軍、二軍，所以警有衆、待暴客也。三晉之兵質而能勇，晉人用之以遏楚，韓趙因之以抗秦，李牧將之以逐匈奴，天下莫强焉。我聖祖俯察形勢，建衛置兵，外禦胡虜，內備不虞，制於未亂，保於未危也。當時軍政嚴明，將士用命，眞一方之兵足衛一方之民也。太平歷年百又七十矣，前日之衛，前日之兵，中土因循，衰弱不振，已可恥矣。又重以邊軍精鋭，胡虜尚驕，况兇狡不恭，數年不靖。
translation_en:
…stipends: these are all proposals born of necessity. Weighing them, the provision of public fields would not only fail to equalize the amounts received but also fail to suit each recipient’s circumstances. As for superfluous officials within the territory, removing one official from a county would save no more than several hundred in annual salary—merely the stipend of a single General of the imperial clan. Moreover, could they all be removed? Hereditary stipends have already been fixed. Suddenly reducing them would hardly accord with the principle of granting generous stipends and sharing in others’ preferences; how could this win general acceptance? These measures are ill suited to the times. Your concern extends to ten thousand generations, and your purpose is indeed far-reaching. Yet I suspect that the fiscal discretion described in the Offices of Zhou does not lie in such measures.
Contention begins with the people’s desires; warfare arises when litigation finds no resolution. States have long relied upon arms. Since the establishment of the Methods of the Minister of War, the arrangements of six armies, three armies, and two armies have served to keep the populace vigilant and meet violent intruders. The soldiers of the Three Jin regions are plain and sturdy, yet courageous. The men of Jin employed them to check Chu; Han and Zhao relied on them to resist Qin; Li Mu led them to drive out the Xiongnu. None under Heaven were stronger. Our sagely founding ancestor surveyed the terrain and strategic circumstances, established guards, and stationed troops, outwardly resisting the northern foes and inwardly preparing against unforeseen trouble. He imposed order before disorder arose and secured the realm before danger appeared. At that time military administration was strict and clear, and officers and soldiers obeyed their commands: the troops of each region truly sufficed to protect its people. Peace has now endured for one hundred and seventy years. Those same guards and troops, through habitual neglect in the central regions, have grown weak and failed to recover their vigor—already a disgrace. Compounding this, although the frontier troops are elite, the northern foes remain arrogant; worse still, they are fierce, cunning, and defiant, and for several years there has been no peace…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
天下大勢非細故也執事憂之無乃欲有
聞乎愚嘗熟察其故矣夷之順逆視軍之
强弱耳軍之强弱視將之材否耳傳曰君
不擇將將不知兵卒不可用器械不利擬
之今日豈一人之責乎蓋爲軍之祟在將
領有六爲軍之賊在旗卒有三其雷同於
里胥者於有司亦有三焉何則行伍缺於
賣閑弓馬踈於安逸貧弱亡於剥削功罪
眩於名實升顯起於僥倖退縮長於驕奢
===
六者有一焉軍之祟也況兼於一軍乎長
團練而遺器械投私役而避差遣習頹惰
而長委靡三者有一焉軍之賊也況所於
一時乎清審蔽於冊籍發遣窩於押解回
銷埋捺於當房此雷同於吏胥而有司驕
於察之其害有三焉今日之計六祟不驅
軍胡以振三賊不殄軍胡以實三害不明
如軍伍之充何哉是故覈實支以查行伍
則賣閑者懼矣立賞罰以試藝略則安逸
punctuated:
天下大勢，非細故也。執事憂之，無乃欲有聞乎？愚嘗熟察其故矣。夷之順逆，視軍之强弱耳；軍之强弱，視將之材否耳。傳曰：「君不擇將，將不知兵，卒不可用，器械不利。」擬之今日，豈一人之責乎？蓋爲軍之祟，在將領有六；爲軍之賊，在旗卒有三；其雷同於里胥者，於有司亦有三焉。何則？行伍缺於賣閑，弓馬踈於安逸，貧弱亡於剥削，功罪眩於名實，升顯起於僥倖，退縮長於驕奢。六者有一焉，軍之祟也，況兼於一軍乎？長團練而遺器械，投私役而避差遣，習頹惰而長委靡。三者有一焉，軍之賊也，況所於一時乎？清審蔽於冊籍，發遣窩於押解，回銷埋捺於當房。此雷同於吏胥，而有司驕於察之，其害有三焉。
今日之計，六祟不驅，軍胡以振？三賊不殄，軍胡以實？三害不明，如軍伍之充何哉？是故覈實支以查行伍，則賣閑者懼矣；立賞罰以試藝略，則安逸
translation_en:
…The overall situation of the realm is no trifling matter. You, sir, are concerned about it; might you wish to hear something on the subject? I have carefully examined its causes. Whether the barbarians submit or rebel depends simply on the strength or weakness of our armies; the strength or weakness of our armies depends simply on whether their commanders are capable. A transmitted text says: “The ruler fails to select commanders; the commanders do not understand warfare; the soldiers cannot be employed; the weapons and equipment are ineffective.” Applied to the present day, can responsibility rest with a single person? Among commanders there are six evils that plague the army; among rank-and-file soldiers there are three practices that undermine it; and among the responsible officials there are also three abuses resembling those of village clerks. What are they? The ranks are depleted by selling exemptions from duty; archery and horsemanship deteriorate through ease and idleness; the poor and weak flee because of exploitation; merit and guilt are obscured by discrepancies between names and realities; advancement to prominence comes through undeserved good fortune; and timidity grows through arrogance and luxury. Any one of these six is a scourge upon the army. How much worse when they are combined in a single army! They devote themselves to militia drill while neglecting weapons and equipment [?]; they enter private service to evade official assignments; and they become accustomed to indolence, fostering listlessness. Any one of these three undermines the army. How much worse when they occur together [?]! Verification is obstructed by registers; dispatch is compromised by concealment during escorted conveyance [?]; and the return and clearance of records are suppressed in the office concerned. These practices resemble those of clerks, while the responsible officials are too arrogant to investigate them [?]. Here are three harmful abuses.
As for measures to take today: unless the six scourges are driven out, how can the army be reinvigorated? Unless the three destructive practices are eradicated, how can the army possess real strength? Unless the three abuses are brought to light, how can its ranks be filled? Thus, verify actual disbursements to inspect the muster rolls, and those who sell exemptions from duty will be afraid. Establish rewards and punishments to test military skills and strategic ability, and those who live in ease…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
者勤矣拊巡營部虛心引訪剥削者革矣
賞不遺賤罰不避貴功罪之狀斯明進以
勲給薦以廉能僥倖之門斯杜引之險阻
以習其勞試之艱辛以忍其性驕奢之氣
斯去矣又勉以大義進以詩禮鼓以廉恥
亦將可以責之知兵矣因閱武而展攻戰
之具則不利者有罰明事例以定跟伴之
名則私投者可革較材藝有勸懲之方則
委靡者可作其氣矣又結以恩信汰其老
===
弱戒其輕逞亦將可以責其用矣按絶户
而究其田産埋没者可以得其隙嚴廻銷
而併家屬窩觧者可以破其姦扣程限以
責批收埋㮣者可以攻其蔽則新充舊籍
營伍可充雷同於里胥當房者可以免其
盲矣夫經略大槩救敝補偏行之中土之
軍未免尺寸之益少復當時之盛轉其軍
政之機耳至於談及邊關之事責以安攘
之兵首重將帥之選並急芻糧之積馬檡
punctuated:
者勤矣。拊巡營部，虛心引訪，剥削者革矣。賞不遺賤，罰不避貴，功罪之狀斯明；進以勲給，薦以廉能，僥倖之門斯杜。引之險阻以習其勞，試之艱辛以忍其性，驕奢之氣斯去矣。又勉以大義，進以詩禮，鼓以廉恥，亦將可以責之知兵矣。因閱武而展攻戰之具，則不利者有罰；明事例以定跟伴之名，則私投者可革；較材藝有勸懲之方，則委靡者可作其氣矣。又結以恩信，汰其老弱，戒其輕逞，亦將可以責其用矣。按絶户而究其田産，埋没者可以得其隙；嚴廻銷而併家屬，窩觧者可以破其姦；扣程限以責批收，埋㮣者可以攻其蔽。則新充舊籍，營伍可充，雷同於里胥當房者可以免其盲矣。
夫經略大槩，救敝補偏，行之中土之軍，未免尺寸之益，少復當時之盛，轉其軍政之機耳。至於談及邊關之事，責以安攘之兵，首重將帥之選，並急芻糧之積，馬檡
translation_en:
…those who have been idle will become diligent. Visit the military camps and units, reassuring the troops and humbly inviting information, and those who exploit them will be removed. Let rewards overlook none of low standing and punishments spare none of high standing: the facts of merit and wrongdoing will then become clear. Advance men according to meritorious service [?], and recommend them for integrity and ability: the door to advancement by mere luck will then be closed. Lead them through difficult terrain to accustom them to toil, and test them with hardships to strengthen their endurance: their arrogance and extravagance will then disappear. Further encourage them through the great principles of duty, cultivate them through the Odes and rites, and inspire them with integrity and a sense of shame. They may then be expected to understand military affairs.
When reviewing the troops, have their implements of assault and battle displayed, and punish those whose equipment is unserviceable. Clarify the applicable regulations to establish who is properly designated an attendant, and those who privately enter such service can be removed. Assess their abilities and skills, with methods of encouragement and punishment, and the dispirited can have their resolve revived. Further bind them through kindness and trust, discharge the old and weak, and warn them against rash displays of prowess. They may then be expected to serve effectively.
Investigate extinct households and inquire into their landed property, and openings can be found through which to expose those who conceal it. Strictly enforce the return of documentation confirming completion of military transfers, and include family members in the inquiry [?], and the fraud of those who shelter men being escorted can be broken. Enforce journey deadlines and demand official receipts, and the concealment practiced by those who suppress documents [?] can be exposed. Thus new recruits can fill the old registers, and the ranks of the camps can be replenished; those who connive with village clerks and the clerks responsible for these matters can be freed from their blindness.
These are the broad outlines of military administration: remedying abuses and correcting imbalances. Applied to the forces of the interior, they cannot fail to yield some modest benefit, somewhat restoring their former strength and turning the workings of military administration around. As for affairs at the frontier passes, where troops are charged with securing peace within and repelling enemies without, the first priority is selecting generals and commanders, while accumulating fodder and grain is equally urgent. Horses should be selected [?]…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
健壯而調士擇能勇而藝堅甲利兵戒譏
嚴堡好諜而懼覲釁而動進不可測撼不
可搖蠢爾豺狼寧無畏乎若夫伸天威於
不毛之地著殊勳於不朽之年務勝窮遠
未可輕議或謂三關宜大連絡三邊互為
聲援如常山蛇勢可也或謂召募死士養
銳待時東寇則西軍深入以擣其虛西侵
則東軍北行以擬其後將必有得志者焉
或謂晝戰以馬彼之長技也不如夜戰以
===
步誘之於險乘其未騎長槍大劍必有成
其謀者焉或謂不與輕合止於把截量用
兵車塞其險隘以逸待勞戰守俱良是固
中國之長技也或謂戰勇氣也在倡之耳
不一大創不能遠懲決勝奮擊如澶淵故
事亦其明驗也均非治內之兵也就中取
之互為聲援列鎮同心縱無大勝亦無小
衄矣兵車塞險盡其險可也有遺險焉膠
柱鼓瑟矣乘夜步擊無月有險間諜可用
punctuated:
健壯而調，士擇能勇而藝，堅甲利兵，戒譏嚴堡，好諜而懼，覲釁而動，進不可測，撼不可搖。蠢爾豺狼，寧無畏乎？若夫伸天威於不毛之地，著殊勳於不朽之年，務勝窮遠，未可輕議。

或謂三關宜大連絡，三邊互為聲援，如常山蛇勢可也。或謂召募死士，養銳待時，東寇則西軍深入以擣其虛，西侵則東軍北行以擬其後，將必有得志者焉。或謂晝戰以馬，彼之長技也，不如夜戰以步，誘之於險，乘其未騎，長槍大劍，必有成其謀者焉。或謂不與輕合，止於把截，量用兵車，塞其險隘，以逸待勞，戰守俱良，是固中國之長技也。或謂戰，勇氣也，在倡之耳。不一大創，不能遠懲；決勝奮擊，如澶淵故事，亦其明驗也。

均非治內之兵也。就中取之，互為聲援，列鎮同心，縱無大勝，亦無小衄矣。兵車塞險，盡其險可也；有遺險焉，膠柱鼓瑟矣。乘夜步擊，無月有險，間諜可用，
translation_en:
…strong and sturdy, and train them; select soldiers who are capable and brave, and school them in martial skills. Make armor strong and weapons sharp, maintain vigilant patrols and inspections, and secure the forts. Make good use of spies while remaining wary, and watch for openings before acting [?]. Let advances be unfathomable and positions unshakable. Would those brutish jackals and wolves then have nothing to fear? As for extending Heaven’s might into barren lands and establishing extraordinary achievements that will endure forever, pursuing victory to the remotest reaches—such things must not be discussed lightly.

Some say that the Three Passes should be closely linked and the three frontier regions support one another, adopting the disposition of the snake of Changshan. Others say that we should recruit warriors willing to die, nurture their fighting strength, and await the right moment: when the enemy raids the east, the western army should penetrate deeply to strike where they are undefended; when they invade the west, the eastern army should march north to threaten their rear. Surely one of these forces would achieve its aim. Others say that daytime cavalry fighting is the enemy’s particular strength, and that it would be better to fight at night with infantry, lure them into difficult terrain, and take advantage of their not yet having mounted. With long spears and great swords, such a plan would surely succeed. Others say that we should avoid engaging them rashly and confine ourselves to interception, using war wagons as appropriate to block strategic defiles and awaiting the exhausted enemy with rested troops. This would serve both attack and defense well and is indeed China’s particular strength. Others say that battle depends on courage, which need only be stirred into action. Unless the enemy suffers one crushing defeat, they cannot be deterred for long. Fighting fiercely to secure victory, as in the historical precedent of Chanyuan, provides clear proof of this.

All these concern warfare distinct from maintaining order within the realm. To choose among them: if the garrisons support one another and act with one purpose, then even without a great victory, they will avoid even a minor defeat. Blocking strategic terrain with war wagons is feasible if every such point can be covered; if any are left uncovered, it is like gluing the tuning bridges in place and trying to play the zither. As for attacking at night with infantry, if there is no moon, the terrain is difficult, and spies can be employed…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
善矣否則虎穴取子矣臨期決機戒之愼
之可也不然數者非所以通乎時也執事
謂鞭撻四夷志固壯矣愚恐帝王之治夷
狄不如是乎抑愚於鹽法將領有餘慨焉
祖宗以鹽法助邊思極深長委利於商鼓其飛
輓貯積于彼戰守足備客兵有資召募有
恃雖有災傷價值騰踴無所憂之軍士有
仰堅其良心軍威自振非惟寬民力已耳
近日紛更舊法商人輸價轉運受餘銀之
===
賞邊境受空虛之敝及有水旱開市和糴
殊不知商販之粟昔日鹽價之粟也軍士
之價近日鹽課之銀也不樂其省顧喜其
煩何也況鹽價由運司解之京由該庫轉
之邊道途之艱防護之警出納之漁何惡
逸而好勞也或謂芻糧易見即有盜冒數
月之支居然難搶百兩入囊踪跡寥然矣
此爲身家則善矣如
國家大事何愚前謂急芻糧之積意以此也
punctuated:
善矣，否則虎穴取子矣。臨期決機，戒之愼之可也。不然，數者非所以通乎時也。執事謂鞭撻四夷，志固壯矣，愚恐帝王之治夷狄不如是乎！抑愚於鹽法、將領有餘慨焉。
祖宗以鹽法助邊，思極深長。委利於商，鼓其飛輓，貯積于彼，戰守足備，客兵有資，召募有恃；雖有災傷，價值騰踴，無所憂之。軍士有仰，堅其良心，軍威自振，非惟寬民力已耳。近日紛更舊法，商人輸價，轉運受餘銀之賞，邊境受空虛之敝。及有水旱，開市和糴。殊不知商販之粟，昔日鹽價之粟也；軍士之價，近日鹽課之銀也。不樂其省，顧喜其煩，何也？況鹽價由運司解之京，由該庫轉之邊，道途之艱，防護之警，出納之漁，何惡逸而好勞也？或謂芻糧易見，即有盜冒，數月之支，居然難搶；百兩入囊，踪跡寥然矣。此爲身家則善矣，如國家大事何？愚前謂急芻糧之積，意以此也。
translation_en:
…that would be good; otherwise, it would be like entering a tiger’s den to seize its cubs. When the moment comes to decide how to act, one must be wary and cautious. Otherwise, these various methods will not enable one to respond suitably to the circumstances. You speak of scourging the barbarians of the four quarters: your ambition is certainly bold, but I fear that this is not how true emperors and kings govern the barbarians! Moreover, I have further concerns about the salt regulations and military commanders.
Our imperial ancestors gave profound and far-reaching thought to supporting the frontiers through the salt regulations. By leaving profits to the merchants, they encouraged them to transport supplies swiftly and build up stocks there. There were ample provisions for both attack and defense, resources for troops deployed from elsewhere, and supplies on which recruitment could depend. Even when disasters damaged the crops and prices soared, there was no cause for anxiety. The soldiers had support they could rely upon, which strengthened their loyalty, and military prestige naturally rose. The benefits went beyond merely easing the burdens on the people.
Recently, the old regulations have been repeatedly altered. Merchants pay in money; the transport officials receive rewards from the surplus silver, while the frontier suffers from depleted stores. When floods or droughts occur, markets are opened for government grain purchases at agreed prices. Yet it is not understood that the grain now sold by merchants is the grain formerly delivered as payment for salt, and that the money paid by the soldiers is the silver now collected as salt revenue. Why take no pleasure in the simpler arrangement, but delight instead in complexity? Moreover, the salt payments are remitted to the capital by the Salt Distribution Commission and then forwarded to the frontier by the treasury concerned. There are the hardships of the journey, the alarms attending its protection, and the illicit gains extracted during disbursement and receipt. Why dislike ease and prefer toil?
Some say that fodder and grain are conspicuous: even if someone steals supplies or makes fraudulent claims, several months’ provisions are plainly difficult to snatch away, whereas a hundred taels slipped into a purse leave scarcely any trace. This may serve one’s private interests well, but what of the great affairs of the state? This is why I said earlier that building up stocks of fodder and grain was urgent.

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
近日武舉準文舉開科用之不爲無人然
不過險譎利害之徒未聞有忠心體
國仇敵忘家者也是果無其人哉作養之政
未及也愚以爲處會試中選之士亦倣文
舉量撥各部或專本部觀效辦事遇有邊
警或各處重大事情各部就事難問因觀
其才識亦廣其才識他日用廢人皆知之
信之下第之士責之該處兵備之官提調
課試充廣材略習演馳射進之文學開發
===
仁義涵養忠愛規其成效不患無其人矣
愚前謂重將帥之選意以此也不識司徒
司馬謂之如何其審處祿糧雖有舊典也
昔周公去文武之時未及百年施文武之
事已有不合者仰思繼日後能得之損益
其法多矣況今去
國初百七十年矣惟
聖天子軫念民艱議及元老多臣斟酌損益則
西山之民幸甚天下幸甚不然執事徒憂
punctuated:
近日武舉準文舉開科，用之不爲無人，然不過險譎利害之徒，未聞有忠心體國、仇敵忘家者也。是果無其人哉？作養之政未及也。愚以爲處會試中選之士，亦倣文舉，量撥各部，或專本部，觀效辦事。遇有邊警，或各處重大事情，各部就事難問，因觀其才識，亦廣其才識。他日用廢，人皆知之、信之。下第之士，責之該處兵備之官提調課試，充廣材略，習演馳射，進之文學，開發仁義，涵養忠愛，規其成效，不患無其人矣。愚前謂重將帥之選，意以此也。不識司徒、司馬謂之如何？
其審處祿糧，雖有舊典也，昔周公去文武之時未及百年，施文武之事已有不合者，仰思繼日，後能得之，損益其法多矣。況今去國初百七十年矣！惟聖天子軫念民艱，議及元老多臣，斟酌損益，則西山之民幸甚，天下幸甚！不然，執事徒憂……
translation_en:
Recently, military examinations have been instituted on the model of the civil examinations, so there is no lack of men to employ. Yet they are merely men of cunning and calculation over advantage and disadvantage; I have not heard of any who loyally care for the state and, in their hostility to its enemies, forget their own families. Is there truly no such man? Rather, measures for fostering and cultivating them have not reached far enough. In my humble opinion, successful candidates in the Metropolitan Examination should likewise be assigned, following the civil examination model, in appropriate numbers to the various ministries, or exclusively to their own ministry, so that their effectiveness in handling affairs may be observed. Whenever border alarms arise, or major incidents occur elsewhere, the ministries should question them on the difficulties presented by those affairs, thereby both assessing and broadening their abilities and understanding. When they are subsequently employed or set aside, everyone will understand and accept the decision. Candidates who fail should be placed under the supervision and examination of the military defense officials in their respective localities. Their abilities and strategic understanding should be enlarged; they should practice riding and archery, advance in literary learning, develop benevolence and righteousness, and cultivate loyalty and devotion. If concrete results are sought from this training, there will be no fear of lacking suitable men. This is what I meant earlier when I urged that greater weight be placed on selecting commanders. I wonder what the Ministers of Revenue and War would say to this.
As for carefully determining arrangements for salary grain, although established regulations exist, even the Duke of Zhou, living less than a hundred years after Kings Wen and Wu, found that some of their practices no longer suited the circumstances when put into effect. Only after pondering day after day [?] could he arrive at a solution, and he made many additions to and subtractions from their institutions. How much more is this so now, a hundred and seventy years after the founding of our dynasty! If only the sage Son of Heaven would take the people's hardships to heart, consult the senior statesmen and the assembled ministers, and weigh what should be removed or added, the people of Xishan would be most fortunate, and all under Heaven would be most fortunate! Otherwise, you, sir, will merely worry…

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text: 之已耳
punctuated: 之已耳。
translation_en: …about it, and that is all.

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
山西鄉試錄後序
歲丁酉秋八月山西鄉試事
竣錄亦遂成〔應禎〕作而歎曰
錄備四義可以
獻矣四者何也曰勞勞者序其秩
尚賢者表其氏崇雅者程其
辭守常者遵其
===
制遵
制則同程辭則式表氏則榮序秩
則勸錄備四義可以
獻矣自夫鄉舉里選之制廢也乃
糊名易書取人以言不亦難
乎自監臨以至百執事經畫
防範聿嚴以慎猶慮材遺弊
punctuated:
山西鄉試錄後序

歲丁酉秋八月，山西鄉試事竣，錄亦遂成。〔應禎〕作而歎曰：「錄備四義，可以獻矣。四者何也？曰：勞勞者，序其秩；尚賢者，表其氏；崇雅者，程其辭；守常者，遵其制。遵制則同，程辭則式，表氏則榮，序秩則勸。錄備四義，可以獻矣。自夫鄉舉里選之制廢也，乃糊名易書，取人以言，不亦難乎？自監臨以至百執事，經畫防範，聿嚴以慎，猶慮材遺弊
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shanxi Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the dingyou year [1537], the Shanxi Provincial Examination concluded, and its record was duly completed. Yingzhen rose and sighed, saying: “This record fulfills four purposes and may now be presented to the throne. What are these four? To reward those who have labored, it lists their official ranks; to esteem the worthy, it displays their names; to honor elegant writing, it presents their compositions as models; to uphold established practice, it follows the prescribed regulations. Following the regulations ensures uniformity; presenting compositions supplies models; displaying names confers honor; listing official ranks gives encouragement. This record fulfills four purposes and may now be presented to the throne.

“Ever since the system of recommending men from the districts and selecting them from the villages was abolished, candidates’ names have been concealed and their scripts recopied, and men have been selected on the basis of their written words. Is this not difficult? From the Supervising Official down to all those carrying out duties, arrangements and precautions have been strict and careful. Yet they still fear that talent may be overlooked and abuses …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
滋以貽訾議耳目心思精力
無遺至若聯次以昭有事而
崇卑殊焉其何以作于後也
故曰序秩則勸士之强學待
問孰不秉時思奮以致厥身
令也脩辭獲進則登明選公
固宜樹之風聲以示遠詔來
===
亦庶乎得名稱已故曰表氏
則榮聖人立法以式九圍繩
墨載陳規矩聿設方圓平直
者麗焉誰能違之高則厲下
則弱弗式弗登則錄可知矣
故曰程辭則式三晉之士自
古在昔豪傑挺生乃今涵育
punctuated:
滋，以貽訾議，耳目心思精力無遺。至若聯次以昭有事，而崇卑殊焉，其何以作于後也？故曰：「序秩則勸。」
士之强學待問，孰不秉時思奮，以致厥身令也？脩辭獲進，則登明選公，固宜樹之風聲，以示遠詔來，亦庶乎得名稱已。故曰：「表氏則榮。」
聖人立法以式九圍，繩墨載陳，規矩聿設，方圓平直者麗焉，誰能違之？高則厲，下則弱，弗式弗登，則錄可知矣。故曰：「程辭則式。」
三晉之士，自古在昔，豪傑挺生，乃今涵育
translation_en:
… proliferate and invite criticism; thus they devoted all their powers of observation, thought, and exertion, leaving nothing unattended. As for listing in sequence those who served in the examination, distinguishing their higher and lower ranks, how would this encourage those who come afterward? Hence the saying: “Setting out their ranks encourages them.”
Among scholars who study diligently and await questioning, who does not wish to seize the moment and exert himself, so that he may bring distinction to his person? When they gain advancement through polished writing, the elevation of the worthy is transparent and the selection impartial. It is certainly fitting to establish their reputation, making them known in distant places and to future generations; one may thereby also hope that their reputation accords with their own worth [?]. Hence the saying: “Displaying their names brings them honor.”
The sages established laws to serve as standards throughout the realm. The marking line was laid out, the compass and square put in place; the square and round, the level and straight all conformed to them. Who could depart from them? What is too high is excessive; what is too low is weak. What does not conform to the standard is not included: thus the principles governing inclusion in this record may be understood. Hence the saying: “Presenting model compositions provides a standard.”
Among the scholars of the Three Jin regions, outstanding men have arisen since ancient times. Now, nurtured …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
聖化業專藝精彙征並進視昔繁
盛顧人以額拘文以
制限其如遺于取錄何哉蓋上有
道揆而下有法守也故曰遵
制則同雖然遵
制尚矣豈唯山西然哉幅員萬里
經國分野不無東西南北之
===
異於是四義罔或異焉所謂
車同軌書同文行同倫也於
乎盛矣傳曰王天下有三重
焉其寡過矣乎洛爾多士幸
際
昌期爲下不倍亦宜無弗寡過
者也〔應〕〔禎〕從執事之後于玆
punctuated: 聖化，業專藝精，彙征並進，視昔繁盛。顧人以額拘，文以制限，其如遺于取錄何哉？蓋上有道揆，而下有法守也。故曰：「遵制則同。」雖然，遵制尚矣，豈唯山西然哉？幅員萬里，經國分野，不無東西南北之異，於是四義罔或異焉，所謂「車同軌，書同文，行同倫」也。於乎盛矣！傳曰：「王天下有三重焉，其寡過矣乎！」洛爾多士，幸際昌期，爲下不倍，亦宜無弗寡過者也。〔應〕〔禎〕從執事之後，于玆
translation_en:
…under the sage influence, they have become devoted to their studies and accomplished in their literary arts, advancing together in greater flourishing numbers than in the past. Yet candidates are constrained by quotas, and compositions by prescribed rules: what can be done about those omitted from selection? For those above have the Way as their measure, while those below have established laws to observe. Hence the saying: “Following the prescribed rules ensures uniformity.”

Nevertheless, honoring the prescribed rules is paramount; how could this apply only to Shanxi? Across a territory extending ten thousand li, the geographical divisions of the realm necessarily differ from east to west and north to south. Yet in these four principles there is no difference whatsoever. This is what is meant by “Carriages have the same wheel gauge, writing uses the same characters, and conduct follows the same ethical norms.” How magnificent!

The commentary says: “He who rules all under Heaven has three weighty responsibilities; surely he will make few errors!” O[?] you many scholars, fortunate to live in this flourishing age: if, as subjects, you do not act contrary to your superiors, you too should all make few errors. I, Yingzhen 〔應〕〔禎〕, following behind those charged with conducting the examination, here …

title: 嘉靖十六年山西鄉試錄
text:
末簡其何辭以綴歌鹿鳴而
賔興之行將有位矣敢賦假
樂之卒章以僭著相從之義
浙江杭州府新城縣儒學教
諭林應禎謹序
punctuated:
末簡，其何辭以綴？歌《鹿鳴》而賔興之，行將有位矣。敢賦《假樂》之卒章，以僭著相從之義。
浙江杭州府新城縣儒學教諭林應禎謹序。
translation_en:
…on this final leaf, what words may I append? We sing “The Deer Call” (Lu ming) and honor the candidates as guests in sending them forward; soon they will hold official positions. I venture to recite the final stanza of “Joy and Happiness” (Jia le), presuming thereby to express the meaning of our fellowship.
Preface respectfully composed by Lin Yingzhen, Instructor in the Confucian School of Xincheng County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang.
